name: Medical and Biological Chemistry
description: Complete study manual · 15 practical and laboratory class topics

topics.title: Introduction to medical chemistry. Chemistry and the environment. Chemistry of biogenic elements

goals.text: To teach the student the tasks of medical chemistry and the stages of studying it, the mathematical skills needed for chemical calculations, chemical pollution of the environment and its effect on health, the rules of work in a chemical laboratory, and the properties, biological significance and qualitative reactions of s-, p- and d-elements.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the subject and tasks of medical chemistry and its links with other medical sciences;
the concepts of the mole, molar mass, mass fraction and concentration;
the main chemical pollutants of the environment and their effects on the body;
the classification of biogenic elements (macro-, micro- and ultramicroelements);
the physical and chemical properties and biological significance of s-, p- and d-elements;
the qualitative reactions of important cations and anions.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: follow the safety rules of a chemical laboratory and give first aid;
do simple calculations with moles, mass and concentration;
identify ions of biogenic elements with qualitative reactions;
solve situational problems and explain the chemical basis of an element deficiency or excess.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: About 97 % of body mass is made up of the **organogenic** elements — C, H, O, N, P, S. Macroelements make up more than 10^−2^ % of the body, microelements 10^−3^–10^−5^ %, and ultramicroelements less than 10^−5^ %.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Flame colors: **“Sodium — a yellow sun, Potassium — a violet night, Calcium — a brick wall, Copper — a green leaf”**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: When diluting an acid, pour the **acid into the water**, never the reverse: if water is poured into concentrated H~2~SO~4~, the heat released boils the water instantly and the acid spatters.

sections.title: 1. The subject of medical chemistry and how to study it

blocks.text: **Medical chemistry** is the science that studies the laws of the chemical and physicochemical processes in a living organism, the properties of the substances that enter the body (food, drugs, poisons) and the methods used to analyze them. It brings together the parts of general, inorganic, physical and colloid, analytical and bioorganic chemistry that medicine needs, and it is the foundation for **biochemistry, normal physiology, pharmacology, hygiene and clinical laboratory diagnostics**.

For example, to understand the acid–base status of the blood (pH 7.35–7.45) one needs buffer systems; to understand water–electrolyte metabolism one needs solutions and osmosis; to understand how drugs act one needs the structure of organic compounds.
Stages of studying the subject

items: **Theory** — learn terms, definitions and laws by understanding their logic, not by rote.
**Formulas and equations** — write and balance reaction equations correctly.
**Calculation** — consolidate knowledge quantitatively by solving problems.
**Experiment** — check the theory with your own eyes in laboratory work.
**Medical interpretation** — link the result to the state of the body.

blocks.text: The calculations use **decimal logarithms** (pH, pK), **powers of ten** (10^−7^ mol/L), **proportions** and **unit conversions** (mL → L, mg → g, mmol → mol) most often. Checking the units at the end of every calculation prevents half of all mistakes.

parts.text: 1 mole of any substance contains 6.022·10^23^ particles. At standard conditions (0 °C, 101.3 kPa) 1 mole of a gas occupies 22.4 L.

blocks.text: The human body constantly exchanges matter with the environment: any chemical that enters with air, water or food eventually reaches the tissues. Substances released into the environment in amounts far above the natural cycle and harmful to living organisms are called **ecotoxicants**.

blocks.text: **Global problems:** the rise of CO~2~ and CH~4~ — the greenhouse effect; chlorofluorocarbons (freons) — destruction of the ozone layer and stronger ultraviolet radiation; the reaction of SO~2~ and NO~x~ with water — **acid rain** (pH < 5.6).

parts.text: The **Aral Sea disaster** is a vivid example of a regional ecological problem. Dust made of salt and pesticide residues blown from the dried seabed has increased respiratory diseases, anemia, and kidney and liver diseases in Karakalpakstan and Khorezm. The high mineral content of drinking water promotes kidney stone formation.

blocks.text: Chemical quality of drinking water

A person drinks 2–2.5 L of water a day, so the impurities in water act on the body constantly. Water **hardness** is determined by its Ca^2+^ and Mg^2+^ salts. **Temporary (carbonate) hardness** is caused by hydrogen carbonates and disappears on boiling: Ca(HCO~3~)~2~ → CaCO~3~↓ + CO~2~↑ + H~2~O (the scale in a kettle is the product of this reaction). **Permanent hardness** is caused by sulfates and chlorides; it does not disappear on boiling and is removed only by ion exchange or with soda.

parts.text: The composition of drinking water can cause **endemic diseases**: too little iodine in water — endemic goiter, too little fluorine — caries, too much — fluorosis, high mineralization — urolithiasis. Such diseases are distinguished by being linked to a geographical area.

sections.title: 3. Rules of work in a chemical laboratory

items: Work in the laboratory only in a lab coat; wear safety goggles and gloves when needed.
Eating, drinking and tasting reagents at the workplace are strictly forbidden.
Smell a substance without bending over the vessel: waft the air toward yourself with your hand.
When heating a test tube, never point its mouth at yourself or at a neighbor.
Work with volatile, toxic and odorous substances only in a **fume hood**.
When diluting concentrated acids, pour the **acid in a thin stream into the water**.
Draw a solution into a pipette with a **rubber bulb** (pipette filler), never by mouth.
Do not use flammable liquids (ether, alcohol, acetone) near an open flame.
After work, return the reagents to their places, clean the workplace and wash your hands.

parts.text: It is a mistake to “neutralize” acid on the skin immediately with an alkali: the heat of the neutralization reaction deepens the burn. First **plenty of water**, then a weak neutralizing solution.

blocks.text: Elements that are part of the body and perform a definite function in vital processes are called **biogenic elements**. V.I. Vernadsky showed that the elemental composition of the body reflects that of the Earth’s crust, yet living organisms accumulate some elements (C, N, P, I) thousands of times more than their surroundings.

blocks.text: Most of the body mass is made up of **oxygen (≈ 62 %)**, **carbon (≈ 21 %)**, **hydrogen (≈ 10 %)**, **nitrogen (≈ 3 %)**, **calcium (≈ 2 %)** and **phosphorus (≈ 1 %)**.

blocks.label: Figure 1.1
blocks.caption: Position of the biogenic elements in the periodic table: macroelements, microelements and organogenic elements are highlighted (drawn on the basis of D.I. Mendeleev’s periodic table).

blocks.text: The biological role of an element is linked to its **position in the periodic table**: s-elements act mainly as ions (Na^+^, K^+^, Ca^2+^, Mg^2+^) in electrolyte and structural roles; p-elements form the skeleton of biomolecules; d-elements, thanks to their variable valence and ability to form complexes, sit in the active center of **metalloenzymes**.

parts.text: One and the same element can be both essential and toxic: it all depends on the **dose**. For example, fluoride strengthens tooth enamel in small doses but causes **fluorosis** in excess; selenium deficiency causes cardiomyopathy, its excess causes selenosis.

sections.title: 5. Atomic structure and the periodic law — the key to understanding biogenic elements

blocks.text: The chemical and biological properties of an element are determined by its **electronic structure**. According to D.I. Mendeleev’s periodic law, the properties of elements depend periodically on the nuclear charge (atomic number). Depending on which orbital the outer electrons occupy, elements are divided into **s-, p-, d- and f-blocks**.

blocks.title: Table 1.6. Electron configuration of some biogenic elements and their form in the body
head: Element
Electron configuration
Block
Main form in the body

blocks.text: **Electronegativity** is the ability of an atom to attract the electrons of a bond. Because oxygen and nitrogen are highly electronegative, O–H and N–H bonds are polar and form **hydrogen bonds** — the properties of water, the secondary structure of proteins and the DNA double helix are based on them.

**Ionic radius** determines biological selectivity: Na^+^ (0.102 nm) and K^+^ (0.138 nm) differ in size, so ion channels in the membrane can tell them apart. Ions of similar size and charge can replace each other — this is called **isomorphous substitution** and underlies many poisonings.

parts.text: Interchangeable pairs: **Li ↔ Na, Tl ↔ K, Sr ↔ Ca, Cd ↔ Zn, Be ↔ Mg**. For example, radioactive ^90^Sr settles in bone in place of calcium and irradiates the bone marrow for a long time; thallium enters potassium channels and poisons the nervous system.

blocks.text: s-Elements are the elements in which the s-orbital of the outer electron shell is being filled: **group IA** (Li, Na, K) — the alkali metals, and **group IIA** (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba) — the alkaline earth metals. They are **soft, light, reactive metals**; they give up electrons easily and form stable ions with oxidation states +1 and +2.

**Chemical properties:** they react vigorously with water to form an alkali: 2Na + 2H~2~O → 2NaOH + H~2~↑. Metallic character and reactivity increase down a group (K is more reactive than Na). Their oxides and hydroxides are basic; Ca and Mg salts (carbonates, phosphates) are poorly soluble in water — this is the chemical basis of bone and stone formation.

parts.text: **Hyperkalemia** (K^+^ > 5.5 mmol/L) disturbs cardiac conduction and may lead to asystole; **hypokalemia** causes muscle weakness and arrhythmia. **Hypocalcemia** raises neuromuscular excitability and causes **tetany** (spasms). Lithium salts (Li~2~CO~3~) are used to treat bipolar disorder.

blocks.text: Regulation of calcium and phosphorus metabolism

About half of plasma calcium is in the **ionized** (active) form; the rest is bound to albumin and present as complex salts. The normal ionized Ca^2+^ level is 1.1–1.3 mmol/L. Three hormones keep it constant:

items: **Parathyroid hormone** (parathyroid glands) — releases Ca^2+^ from bone, increases Ca^2+^ reabsorption in the kidney and increases phosphate excretion: blood Ca^2+^ rises.
**Calcitriol** (the active form of vitamin D) — increases the absorption of Ca^2+^ and phosphate in the intestine.
**Calcitonin** (C cells of the thyroid gland) — stops the release of Ca^2+^ from bone and lowers its blood level.

parts.text: The laboratory usually measures **total** calcium. If blood albumin is low (liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), total calcium comes out low, while the active ionized calcium may be normal. In that case **corrected calcium** is calculated: Ca(corr.) = Ca(measured) + 0.02·(40 − albumin), where Ca is in mmol/L and albumin in g/L.

blocks.text: **Magnesium and calcium** are antagonists in many processes: Ca^2+^ triggers muscle contraction, while Mg^2+^ blocks calcium channels and lowers excitability. That is why magnesium sulfate is used for seizures in eclampsia and in some arrhythmias.

p-Elements are the elements of groups IIIA–VIIIA; p-orbitals are being filled in their outer shell. Non-metallic character increases from left to right across a period: B and Al are amphoteric, C, N, O, S and P are non-metals, and F, Cl, Br and I are the halogens (the most reactive non-metals). Most of them have variable oxidation states (nitrogen from −3 to +5) and form covalent bonds.

parts.text: Uzbekistan is an **iodine-deficiency endemic region**. Iodine deficiency enlarges the thyroid gland (endemic goiter), and deficiency during pregnancy causes cretinism in the child. This is why table salt is iodized (KIO~3~ is added).

blocks.text: **Dose-dependent effect of fluoride:** about 1 mg/L of fluoride in drinking water prevents caries, because F^−^ replaces OH^−^ in hydroxyapatite Ca~10~(PO~4~)~6~(OH)~2~ and forms acid-resistant **fluorapatite** Ca~10~(PO~4~)~6~F~2~. More than 1.5 mg/L causes spots on the enamel (fluorosis).

d-Elements (transition metals) are the elements in which the d-orbital of the next-to-outer shell is being filled (groups IB–VIIIB). Their common properties are **variable oxidation states** (Fe^2+^/Fe^3+^, Cu^+^/Cu^2+^), the **formation of complex compounds** and **colored** compounds. These very features make them an essential part of oxidation–reduction enzymes.

parts.text: In hemoglobin, iron binds O~2~ in the **Fe^2+^** state. Hemoglobin oxidized to Fe^3+^ — **methemoglobin** — cannot carry oxygen. Nitrites and some drugs (dapsone, local anesthetics) cause methemoglobinemia; it is treated with methylene blue.
To remember the metalloenzymes: **“Iron — respiration, Copper — oxidase, Zinc — carbonic anhydrase, Cobalt — B~12~, Molybdenum — xanthine”**.

blocks.text: Iron and copper metabolism

Only 1–2 mg of dietary iron is absorbed — roughly the amount lost daily with intestinal epithelium and skin. Iron is absorbed in the duodenum as **Fe^2+^** (ascorbic acid reduces Fe^3+^ to Fe^2+^ and improves absorption), is carried in the blood as **Fe^3+^** by the protein **transferrin**, and is stored in the liver and spleen as **ferritin** and hemosiderin. The body has no mechanism for actively excreting iron, so it accumulates after many blood transfusions.

parts.text: In **Wilson disease** copper is not excreted with bile and accumulates in the liver, the subcortical nuclei of the brain and the cornea. A greenish-brown **Kayser–Fleischer ring** appears at the edge of the cornea, and blood ceruloplasmin decreases. Treatment uses the copper-binding drug D-penicillamine.

blocks.text: Heavy metals (Hg^2+^, Pb^2+^, Cd^2+^, As^3+^) bind firmly to the **sulfhydryl (–SH) groups** of proteins and inactivate enzymes, which is why they are called **thiol poisons**. In addition, they displace essential metals: lead displaces zinc from δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase in heme synthesis and causes anemia.

The treatment of poisoning is based on **chelating antidotes**: the antidote forms a stable, water-soluble complex with the metal, which is excreted in the urine. The chemistry of complex formation is discussed in detail in topic 3.

parts.text: Signs of **chronic lead poisoning**: severe abdominal colic (lead colic), a gray line at the gum margin, basophilic stippling of red blood cells, anemia, weakness of the arms and legs. δ-Aminolevulinic acid increases in the urine.
Only the **calcium** salt CaNa~2~-EDTA is used to remove lead. Calcium-free Na~2~-EDTA also binds blood Ca^2+^ and can cause severe hypocalcemia and cardiac arrest.

blocks.text: A **qualitative reaction** is a reaction that allows an ion to be identified by a clear external sign (a precipitate, a color, a gas, a flame color). The reaction must be **sensitive** (detect even small amounts) and **selective** (specific).

parts.text: Calcium oxalate precipitates not only in the test tube but also in the body: when urine contains much Ca^2+^ and oxalate, **oxalate stones** form in the kidney — about 70–80 % of all kidney stones are of this type.

sections.title: 11. Methods for the quantitative determination of biogenic elements

blocks.text: A qualitative reaction shows that an ion is present, but in the clinic its **exact amount** must be known. Chemical and instrumental methods are used for this.

blocks.title: Table 1.13. Methods for the quantitative determination of elements
head: Method
Principle
What is determined in the clinic
rows: by the volume of reagent consumed
light absorption by a colored compound
intensity of emission of atoms excited in a flame
absorption of a characteristic wavelength by atomic vapor
Pb, Cd, Cu, Zn, Hg — trace amounts
dependence of the electrode potential on ion activity

blocks.text: Photometry is based on the **Beer–Lambert law**: the absorbance of a solution is directly proportional to the concentration of the colored substance and to the path length, A = ε·l·C. The concentration is found from a **calibration curve** built with standard solutions.

parts.text: In a modern clinical laboratory Na^+^, K^+^, Ca^2+^ and Cl^−^ are mostly measured with **ion-selective electrodes** within minutes, while trace amounts of heavy metals are determined by **atomic absorption**.

sections.title: 12. Nuclear chemistry and its significance in medicine (independent work)

blocks.text: **Radioactivity** is the spontaneous emission of radiation by unstable atomic nuclei, which turn into other nuclei. Atoms of the same element with different mass numbers are called **isotopes** (for example, ^12^C, ^13^C, ^14^C); radioactive isotopes are called **radionuclides**.

items: **α-decay** — a helium nucleus (^4^He) leaves the nucleus; the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number by 2; it travels only a few micrometers in tissue.
**β^−^-decay** — a neutron turns into a proton and an electron is emitted; the atomic number rises by 1.
**β^+^-decay** — a proton turns into a neutron and a positron is emitted; the positron annihilates with an electron, giving two γ-quanta (the basis of PET).
**γ-radiation** — a high-energy electromagnetic wave; it has the greatest penetrating power.

blocks.text: **Law of radioactive decay:** N = N~0~·e^−λt^, where λ = ln2 / T~½~. The **half-life** (T~½~) is the time in which half of the radionuclide atoms decay. The unit of activity is the **becquerel** (1 Bq = 1 decay/s); absorbed dose is measured in **grays** (Gy), equivalent dose in **sieverts** (Sv).

blocks.title: Table 1.14. Radionuclides used in medicine
head: Radionuclide
T~½~
Use
rows: treatment of thyroid cancer and thyrotoxicosis

parts.text: For diagnostics, **short-lived**, mainly **γ-emitting** radionuclides (^99m^Tc) are chosen, so the patient receives little radiation. For treatment, **β-emitters** that destroy tissue (^131^I) are used.

blocks.text: Biological effects of ionizing radiation

Radiation acts on tissue in two ways. In the **direct effect** a quantum or particle itself ionizes the DNA or protein molecule and breaks bonds. The **indirect effect** is the main one: since ≈ 70 % of tissue is water, radiation splits water (**radiolysis**): H~2~O → H· + ·OH. The free radicals formed, especially the hydroxyl radical ·OH, damage DNA, membrane lipids and enzymes.

blocks.title: Table 1.15. Single whole-body radiation dose and its consequences
head: Equivalent dose
Consequence
rows: no clinical signs, the long-term risk of tumors rises slightly
lymphocytes in the blood decrease, usually without symptoms
without treatment about half of those exposed die

blocks.text: The radiosensitivity of cells depends on how fast they divide (**law of Bergonié and Tribondeau**): bone marrow, intestinal epithelium, germ cells and lymphocytes are the most sensitive, while nerve and muscle cells are resistant. The three main ways of protection from radiation are **time** (spend little time near the source), **distance** (the dose falls with the square of the distance) and **shielding** (lead and concrete against γ-radiation).

parts.text: In an accident at a nuclear power plant radioactive ^131^I is released and accumulates in the thyroid gland. To prevent this, the population is given **potassium iodide** tablets (130 mg for adults): the gland becomes saturated with stable iodine and does not take up radioactive iodine.

skills.title: Skill: identifying cations and anions with qualitative reactions

items: Pour 1–2 mL of the test solution into a clean test tube.
Add the reagent dropwise (3–5 drops) and mix.
Record the observed sign (color of the precipitate, color change, gas).
Check the solubility of the precipitate (for example, add ammonia to AgCl or acetic acid to CaC~2~O~4~).
Write the reaction equation in molecular and ionic form.
Conclusion: state which ion is present in the solution.

skills.title: Skill: identifying a metal ion by its flame color

items: Dip a nichrome (or platinum) wire into concentrated HCl and heat it in the flame until it no longer colors the flame.
Dip the wire into the test salt solution.
Place the wire in the colorless part of the burner flame.
Observe the flame color; for potassium, look through blue cobalt glass (it blocks the yellow color of sodium).
Clean the wire again with HCl after each sample.

skills.title: Skill: calculating the activity and remaining amount of a radionuclide

items: Find the half-life (T~½~) of the radionuclide in a table.
Express the elapsed time in the same unit as T~½~ and find the number of half-lives: n = t / T~½~.
Calculate the remaining activity: A = A~0~ / 2^n^ (if n is not a whole number, A = A~0~·e^−λt^, λ = 0.693 / T~½~).
Write the result with its unit (MBq or kBq) and check that it makes sense: the activity can never exceed the initial value.
Draw a medical conclusion: estimate how long the patient remains a source for the people around them.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A patient is receiving a 0.9 % sodium chloride solution (normal saline). Take the density of the solution as 1 g/mL (M(NaCl) = 58.5 g/mol).
cases.ask: How many grams of NaCl are in 500 mL of the solution? What is its molar concentration?
cases.answer: The mass of 500 mL of solution is 500 g; m(NaCl) = 500 · 0.009 = 4.5 g. n(NaCl) = 4.5 / 58.5 = 0.077 mol; C = 0.077 / 0.5 = 0.154 mol/L (≈ 154 mmol/L). Each NaCl gives two ions, so the osmolarity is ≈ 308 mOsm/L — close to blood plasma (isotonic).

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: A one-year-old child was fed formula prepared with well water. The child’s lips and nails are blue, and the cyanosis does not decrease when oxygen is given. The blood is brownish.
cases.ask: What condition is suspected? What is its chemical basis, and how is it treated?
cases.answer: Nitrate (methemoglobin) poisoning. Nitrates in the well water are reduced to nitrite in the intestine; nitrite oxidizes the Fe^2+^ of hemoglobin to Fe^3+^ — methemoglobin cannot bind O~2~, so giving oxygen does not help. Treatment: methylene blue (it returns Fe^3+^ to Fe^2+^ via NADPH-methemoglobin reductase), ascorbic acid; change the water source.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient with thyroid cancer received ^131^I with an activity of 3700 MBq (T~½~ = 8 days).
cases.ask: What activity remains in the body after 24 days (ignore physiological excretion)? Why is ^131^I chosen?
cases.answer: 24 days = 3 half-lives: A = 3700 · (1/2)^3^ = 3700 / 8 = 462.5 MBq. Iodine is actively taken up only by thyroid cells; the β-particles of ^131^I travel a few millimeters in tissue and destroy precisely the gland (tumor) cells, while its γ-radiation allows the process to be followed by scintigraphy.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: A 45-year-old man working at a battery plant complains of severe abdominal colic and weakness. Examination shows a gray line at the gum margin; the blood test shows anemia and basophilic stippling of red blood cells.
cases.ask: Poisoning with which element is suspected? What is its mechanism of action? Which antidote is used and why exactly its calcium salt?
cases.answer: This is chronic **lead** poisoning (battery production is a main source). Pb^2+^ binds the –SH groups of enzymes and displaces zinc from δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase in heme synthesis — heme synthesis is disturbed, anemia develops and δ-ALA increases in the urine. The antidote is **CaNa~2~-EDTA** (calcium disodium edetate) or succimer: Pb^2+^ takes the place of Ca^2+^ in the complex, forming a water-soluble complex that is excreted in the urine. Calcium-free Na~2~-EDTA would bind blood Ca^2+^ and cause dangerous hypocalcemia.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: Water from a village well was analyzed: 1 L of water contains 120 mg of Ca^2+^ and 36 mg of Mg^2+^ (the equivalent mass of Ca is 20, of Mg 12 g/mol).
cases.ask: Calculate the total hardness of the water (mEq/L) and compare it with the drinking water standard. What could drinking such water for a long time lead to?
cases.answer: Ca^2+^: 120 / 20 = 6 mEq/L; Mg^2+^: 36 / 12 = 3 mEq/L. Total hardness = 6 + 3 = **9 mEq/L** — above the norm (≤ 7 mEq/L), the water is **hard**. Long-term consumption increases calcium salts in the urine and raises the risk of **urolithiasis**. Softening the water with an ion-exchange filter is recommended.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: A patient with liver cirrhosis has total calcium of 1.9 mmol/L (normal 2.2–2.6) and albumin of 25 g/L (normal 35–50). There are no signs of tetany.
cases.ask: Calculate the corrected calcium. Does the patient have true hypocalcemia?
cases.answer: Ca(corr.) = 1.9 + 0.02·(40 − 25) = 1.9 + 0.3 = **2.2 mmol/L** — at the lower limit of normal. The low total calcium is due to **decreased albumin**: bound calcium is reduced, while active ionized calcium is sufficient. That is why there is no tetany. To be sure, ionized calcium (normal 1.1–1.3 mmol/L) should be measured directly.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: For a bone scan a patient was injected at 8:00 with a ^99m^Tc preparation with an activity of 740 MBq (T~½~ = 6 hours).
cases.ask: What will the remaining activity in the patient’s body be at 20:00 and at 8:00 the next day (ignore excretion)?
cases.answer: 12 hours = 2 half-lives: A = 740 / 2^2^ = **185 MBq**. 24 hours = 4 half-lives: A = 740 / 2^4^ = 740 / 16 ≈ **46 MBq**. In one day the activity falls 16-fold — this is the advantage of short-lived ^99m^Tc in diagnosis. In addition, the preparation is partly excreted in the urine, so the patient is advised to drink plenty of fluids.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A 28-year-old woman complains of weakness, dizziness and hair loss; her periods are heavy and prolonged. Tests: hemoglobin 90 g/L, serum iron 6 µmol/L, ferritin 8 µg/L.
cases.ask: What is the condition? What does ferritin show? In what form and with what should an iron preparation be taken?
cases.answer: **Iron deficiency anemia**: hemoglobin, serum iron and ferritin are decreased. Ferritin is an indicator of iron **stores**; its sharp decrease means the stores are exhausted (the cause is chronic blood loss). Iron is well absorbed in the intestine in the **Fe^2+^** form, so ferrous salts (FeSO~4~) are recommended, and taking them with **ascorbic acid** increases absorption. They are not taken together with tea, milk or antacids, which bind iron into insoluble compounds.

topics.title: Solutions. Colligative properties of solutions. Fundamentals of titrimetric analysis

goals.text: To teach the student the laws of dissolution of substances and gases in water (Henry’s and Sechenov’s laws), the colligative properties of solutions (Raoult’s and van ’t Hoff’s laws), the ways of expressing concentration, the fundamentals of titrimetric analysis and the neutralization method, and the determination of gastric juice acidity.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: solubility and the factors affecting it, Henry’s and Sechenov’s laws;
Raoult’s law, freezing point depression and boiling point elevation;
the concepts of osmosis, osmotic pressure, van ’t Hoff’s law and the isotonic coefficient;
mass fraction, molar, normal (equivalent) and molal concentration, and titer;
titration, the working solution, the equivalence point, alkalimetry and acidimetry;
the transition ranges of acid–base indicators.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: convert one type of concentration into another;
calculate the osmotic pressure of solutions and distinguish iso-, hypo- and hypertonic solutions;
perform a titration with a burette correctly;
determine and interpret the free, bound and total acidity of gastric juice.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Colligative properties depend **not on the nature of the solute but on the number of particles**. That is why 1 mole of NaCl (2 ions) raises the osmotic pressure about twice as much as 1 mole of glucose.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Indicators: **“Methyl orange — red in acid, Phenolphthalein — pink in alkali”**. Phenolphthalein is colorless in acidic and neutral media.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The law of equivalents C~n1~·V~1~ = C~n2~·V~2~ is written with **normal** concentration. If molar concentration is used, the stoichiometry of the reaction (for example, H~2~SO~4~ + 2NaOH) must be taken into account separately.

blocks.text: A **solution** is a **homogeneous** system of variable composition made of two or more components. The component present in the larger amount is the **solvent**, and the one in the smaller amount is the **solute**. The main solvent of the body is **water**: it makes up ≈ 60 % of the adult body mass, and thanks to its polarity it dissolves ionic and polar substances well (“like dissolves like”).

**Solubility** is the maximum mass of a substance that can dissolve in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature. A solution in this state is called **saturated**. For most solids, solubility increases with temperature; for gases it is the opposite — it **decreases**.
Solubility of gases

**Henry’s law:** at constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid: C = k~H~·p. **Dalton’s law:** from a gas mixture, each gas dissolves according to its own partial pressure.

**Sechenov’s law:** gases are less soluble in electrolyte solutions than in pure water: lg(C~0~ / C) = k·C~salt~. That is why the physical solubility of oxygen in blood plasma is lower than in pure water — most of the oxygen is carried bound to hemoglobin.

parts.text: **Caisson (decompression) disease:** at depth, under high pressure, much nitrogen dissolves in the blood. If a diver surfaces quickly, the pressure falls sharply and nitrogen comes out as bubbles that block the vessels (gas embolism). Treatment is to raise the pressure again in a **hyperbaric chamber** and lower it slowly. **Hyperbaric oxygenation** works on the same law.

sections.title: 2. Water as a biological solvent. Composition of body fluids

blocks.text: The water molecule is bent (≈ 104.5°) and strongly **polar**; the molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other. As a result, water has a high heat capacity and heat of vaporization — it stabilizes body temperature and cools the body through sweating. Its high dielectric constant (ε ≈ 80) makes it easy for ionic compounds to dissociate in water.

Water in the adult body (≈ 60 % of body mass) is distributed between two main compartments: **intracellular fluid** — ≈ 40 % of body mass, and **extracellular fluid** — ≈ 20 % (interstitial fluid ≈ 15 % and blood plasma ≈ 5 %). The compartments differ sharply in ionic composition; this difference is maintained by Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase.

blocks.text: The daily **water balance** in an adult is about 2.5 L: water comes from drinking (≈ 1.5 L), water in food (≈ 0.7 L) and **metabolic water** formed by the oxidation of nutrients (≈ 0.3 L); it leaves with urine (≈ 1.5 L), evaporation through skin and breath (≈ 0.9 L) and feces (≈ 0.1 L).

parts.text: The type of **dehydration** is determined by plasma sodium: **isotonic** (vomiting, diarrhea — water and salt are lost equally), **hypertonic** (more water is lost — fever, not drinking; Na^+^ > 145 mmol/L, cells lose water) and **hypotonic** (more salt is lost; Na^+^ < 135 mmol/L, cells swell). Different solutions are infused for each type.

blocks.text: **Equivalence number (z)**: for an acid — the number of exchangeable H^+^ ions (z = 2 for H~2~SO~4~), for a base — the number of OH^−^ (z = 2 for Ca(OH)~2~), for a salt — the metal valence multiplied by the number of its atoms (z = 6 for Al~2~(SO~4~)~3~). The molar mass of the equivalent is M~eq~ = M / z.
**Conversion formulas:** C = ω·ρ·10 / M (ω in %, ρ in g/mL) and T = C~n~·M~eq~ / 1000. Example: for 36.5 % HCl (ρ = 1.18 g/mL), C = 36.5 · 1.18 · 10 / 36.5 = 11.8 mol/L.

parts.text: In the clinical laboratory, concentrations are given mainly in **mmol/L** (glucose 3.3–5.5 mmol/L), while drug solutions are labeled in **percent** and **mg/mL** (1 % = 10 mg/mL).

blocks.text: Diluting solutions and clinical solutions

When a solution is diluted, the amount of solute does not change, so the **dilution rule** applies: C~1~·V~1~ = C~2~·V~2~. For example, to prepare 200 mL of a 5 % solution from 40 % glucose, V~1~ = 5 · 200 / 40 = 25 mL of the concentrate is taken and water is added up to 200 mL.

parts.text: Concentrated **KCl solution** must never be injected intravenously directly (as a bolus) — it causes cardiac arrest. It is always diluted and given slowly, usually at a rate not exceeding 10–20 mmol of K^+^ per hour.

blocks.text: Properties of a solution that depend only on the number of particles are called **colligative properties**: lowering of the solvent vapor pressure, freezing point depression, boiling point elevation and osmotic pressure.
**Raoult’s 1st law:** the relative lowering of the solvent vapor pressure above a solution equals the mole fraction of the solute: (p~0~ − p) / p~0~ = χ(solute).

**Raoult’s 2nd law:** the freezing point depression and the boiling point elevation of a solution are proportional to its molal concentration: ΔT~f~ = K·C~m~ (cryometry), ΔT~b~ = E·C~m~ (ebulliometry). For water, the cryoscopic constant K = 1.86 K·kg/mol and the ebullioscopic constant E = 0.52 K·kg/mol.

For electrolytes the **isotonic coefficient** (van ’t Hoff factor) i is introduced into the formulas: i = 1 + α(ν − 1), where α is the degree of dissociation and ν is the number of ions formed from one molecule. For non-electrolytes i = 1.

parts.text: Blood plasma freezes at −0.56 °C. From this its **osmolality** is found: C = 0.56 / 1.86 ≈ 0.3 mol/kg (≈ 300 mOsm/kg). Cryometry (osmometry) is used in the clinic to measure plasma and urine osmolality.

sections.title: 5. Osmosis and osmotic pressure. Van ’t Hoff’s law

blocks.text: **Osmosis** is the one-way diffusion of solvent molecules through a semipermeable membrane from a less concentrated solution into a more concentrated one. The extra pressure that must be applied to the solution to stop osmosis is called the **osmotic pressure** (π).

**Van ’t Hoff’s law:** π = i·C·R·T, where C is the molar concentration (mol/L), R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and T is the absolute temperature. The osmotic pressure of blood plasma at 37 °C is **740–780 kPa** (7.3–7.7 atm). About 3.5–4 kPa of it is created by proteins — this is the **oncotic pressure**, which keeps water inside the vessels.

parts.text: Hypertonic solutions are used on purpose in practice: a dressing soaked in **10 % NaCl** draws fluid out of a purulent wound; **25 % MgSO~4~** holds water in the intestine and acts as a laxative; **mannitol** and **15–20 % glucose** draw water from tissue into the blood in cerebral edema. Large intravenous volumes of hypotonic fluid cause hemolysis.

blocks.text: Osmolarity, osmolality and tonicity

**Osmolarity** is the number of osmotically active particles in 1 L of solution (mosmol/L), **osmolality** — the number of particles per 1 kg of solvent (mosmol/kg). In dilute biological fluids they are almost equal. The normal plasma osmolality is **285–295 mosmol/kg**; it can be estimated as: Osm = 2·[Na^+^] + [glucose] + [urea] (all in mmol/L).

Substances that cross the membrane freely (urea, ethanol) quickly equalize inside and outside the cell and do not cause water movement. Therefore cell volume is determined only by the **effective osmolality — tonicity** created by particles that do not cross the membrane. For example, 5 % glucose is isotonic in a test tube, but in the body glucose enters cells and is used, so the solution effectively acts like free water.

Water exchange across the capillary wall is determined by **Starling forces**: at the arterial end the hydrostatic pressure exceeds the oncotic pressure and water leaves for the tissue; at the venous end the oncotic pressure prevails and water returns to the blood. When albumin falls (< 20–25 g/L) the oncotic pressure drops, water stays in the tissue and **edema** develops.

parts.text: In **hemodialysis** blood exchanges with dialysis fluid across a semipermeable membrane: urea, creatinine and excess K^+^ leave the blood down the concentration gradient, while proteins and blood cells remain. Excess water is removed by applying pressure to the membrane (ultrafiltration).

blocks.text: **Titrimetric (volumetric) analysis** is a quantitative method based on measuring the volume of a reagent solution of exactly known concentration that is used up in complete reaction with the analyte. A solution of exactly known concentration is called a **working (standard) solution**; adding it dropwise from a burette to the analyte solution is called **titration**.

The moment when the reagent has reacted with the analyte in an equivalent amount is called the **equivalence point**. It is detected by the color change of an indicator (or by an instrument — a pH meter); the moment actually observed is called the **end point of titration**. The calculation is based on the **law of equivalents**: C~n1~·V~1~ = C~n2~·V~2~.

blocks.label: Figure 2.1
blocks.caption: Titration setup: a burette clamped to a stand and the solution being titrated in a conical flask (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA).

items: **Primary standard** — a pure, stable substance whose composition matches its formula exactly; an accurately weighed portion of it is used to find the concentration of the working solution: **borax** Na~2~B~4~O~7~·10H~2~O for HCl, **oxalic acid** H~2~C~2~O~4~·2H~2~O for NaOH.
**Volumetric glassware:** burette (25 or 50 mL, read to 0.1 mL), Mohr pipette, volumetric flask.
The burette is read at the **bottom of the meniscus**, with the eye level with the meniscus.

sections.title: 7. The neutralization method. Alkalimetry and acidimetry

blocks.text: The neutralization method is based on the reaction between acids and bases. **Alkalimetry** is the determination of acids (and acid salts) with a working solution of an alkali (NaOH, KOH); **acidimetry** is the determination of bases (and salts that give an alkaline medium on hydrolysis) with a working solution of an acid (HCl).

The dependence of pH on the volume of titrant added during titration is called the **titration curve**. Near the equivalence point the pH changes sharply — this is the **titration jump**. When 0.1 M HCl is titrated with 0.1 M NaOH, the jump runs from pH 4.3 to 9.7, and pH = 7 at the equivalence point.

blocks.label: Figure 2.2
blocks.caption: Titration curve of a strong acid (0.1 M HCl) with a strong base (0.1 M NaOH) and the color change ranges of indicators (drawn from calculated data).

parts.text: The color change range of the indicator must lie **within the titration jump**. When a weak acid (CH~3~COOH) is titrated with a strong base, the equivalence point lies in the alkaline region (pH ≈ 8.7), so **phenolphthalein** is chosen; when a weak base (NH~3~) is titrated with a strong acid — **methyl orange**.

blocks.text: Depending on how it is carried out, titration is of three kinds:

items: **Direct titration** — the analyte is titrated directly with the standard solution (HCl with NaOH).

**Back (residual) titration** — a known excess of the standard solution is added to the analyte, and the unreacted residue is titrated with another solution. It is used when the reaction is slow or the substance is volatile (NH~3~, CaCO~3~).
**Replacement (substitution) titration** — the analyte is reacted with a reagent, and another substance formed in an equivalent amount is titrated (in iodometry the liberated I~2~ is titrated).

blocks.text: **Main calculation formulas.** From the law of equivalents: C~n~(X) = C~n~(titrant)·V(titrant) / V(X). Mass of the substance: m(X) = C~n~(titrant)·V(titrant)·M~eq~(X) / 1000 (V in mL). In back titration the number of equivalents that reacted equals the difference between the amount added and the residue.

**Standardization of the working solution.** Because NaOH absorbs CO~2~ from the air, its solution cannot be prepared from an exact weighed amount; its concentration is determined against an exact weighed amount of oxalic acid: H~2~C~2~O~4~ + 2NaOH → Na~2~C~2~O~4~ + 2H~2~O. The equivalent molar mass of oxalic acid dihydrate is 126 / 2 = 63 g/mol.

parts.text: The results of parallel titrations should not differ from each other by more than **0.1 mL**. If the difference is larger, the titration is repeated.

blocks.text: **Acid–base indicators** are weak organic acids or bases that change color depending on the pH of the medium. According to **Ostwald’s ionic theory**, the undissociated molecule of the indicator (HInd) and its anion (Ind^−^) have different colors: HInd ⇄ H^+^ + Ind^−^. The **chromophore theory** explains the color change by a rearrangement of the molecular structure (chromophore groups).
The color change is seen roughly in the range pH = pK~Ind~ ± 1. The pH value at which the color changes completely is called the **titration index** (pT).

sections.title: 10. Laboratory work: determination of gastric juice acidity

blocks.text: **Principle of the method:** the acids of gastric juice are titrated with a 0.1 M NaOH working solution in the presence of two indicators (Michaelis method). First the **free HCl** is titrated (dimethylaminoazobenzene, pH 2.9–4.0 — the red color turns orange), then, in the same sample, the **total acidity** (phenolphthalein — until a pink color appears). Total acidity includes free HCl, HCl bound to proteins, and acid phosphates and organic acids.
Equipment:
filtered gastric juice, 0.1 M NaOH, 0.5 % alcoholic dimethylaminoazobenzene and 1 % alcoholic phenolphthalein, a burette, a 5 mL pipette, conical flasks.

items: Measure 5 mL of filtered gastric juice into a flask with a pipette.
Add 1 drop of dimethylaminoazobenzene and 2 drops of phenolphthalein (the juice turns red).
Add 0.1 M NaOH dropwise from the burette until the red color turns **orange**; record the volume used (V~1~) — this is the **free HCl**.
Continue the titration: the color first becomes yellow, then a **pink** color appears; titrate until it persists for 30 seconds and record the total volume (V~2~) — this is the **total acidity**.
Calculate the bound acidity: total − free.

blocks.text: Calculation:

Acidity is expressed in **titration units** (t.u.) — the number of milliliters of 0.1 M NaOH needed to neutralize 100 mL of gastric juice. With a 5 mL sample: acidity = V(NaOH) · 20 t.u. Numerically this equals mmol/L.

parts.text: In modern gastroenterology, gastric acidity is measured mostly by **intragastric pH-metry** (fasting pH in the body of the stomach 1.5–2.0). Still, the titration method shows well the concept of acidity and the medical use of the neutralization method.

blocks.text: Formation of hydrochloric acid in the stomach

HCl is produced by the **parietal cells** of the fundic glands of the stomach. Inside the cell, with the help of **carbonic anhydrase**, the reaction CO~2~ + H~2~O → H~2~CO~3~ → H^+^ + HCO~3~^−^ takes place. H^+^ ions are pumped into the gastric lumen by **H^+^/K^+^-ATPase** (the proton pump), and Cl^−^ follows them through channels. HCO~3~^−^ goes into the blood — that is why blood and urine become slightly alkaline after a meal (the **“alkaline tide”**).

parts.text: **Proton pump inhibitors** (omeprazole and others) irreversibly block H^+^/K^+^-ATPase and sharply reduce HCl production — they are the main drugs for treating peptic ulcer and reflux esophagitis. **Antacids** (Al(OH)~3~, Mg(OH)~2~), in contrast, bind acid already formed by a neutralization reaction.

skills.title: Skill: titration with a burette

items: Rinse the burette with distilled water, then 2 times with the working solution.
Fill the burette with the working solution slightly above the zero mark, remove the air bubble from the tip and bring the level to zero.
Measure the analyte solution into a flask with a pipette and add the indicator.
Control the burette stopcock with the left hand and swirl the flask constantly with the right hand while adding the titrant dropwise.
Near the equivalence point add the titrant one drop at a time; stop when the color persists for 30 seconds.
Read the volume at the bottom of the meniscus to 0.05 mL.
Repeat the titration at least 3 times; if the results differ by no more than 0.1 mL, take the mean.

skills.title: Skill: calculating osmotic pressure and identifying the type of solution

items: Find the molar concentration of the substance (C = ω·ρ·10 / M).
Determine the isotonic coefficient (non-electrolyte — 1, NaCl — ≈ 2, CaCl~2~ — ≈ 3).
Convert the temperature to kelvin (37 °C = 310 K).
Calculate the pressure in kPa with the formula π = i·C·R·T.
Compare the result with the plasma pressure (740–780 kPa) and decide whether the solution is iso-, hypo- or hypertonic.

skills.title: Skill: preparing a solution of a given concentration

items: Write down the required volume and concentration of the solution (%, mol/L or mmol/L).
If it is prepared from a dry substance, calculate the mass: m = ω·m(solution) or m = C·V·M.
If it is prepared from a concentrate, find its volume from the dilution rule: V~1~ = C~2~·V~2~ / C~1~.
Weigh the substance or measure the concentrate with a pipette, transfer it to a volumetric flask, add distilled water to the mark and mix.
Label the vessel with the name of the solution, its concentration and the date of preparation.

Approximately how much metabolic water is formed daily by the oxidation of nutrients?

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A patient’s gastric juice was examined. When 5 mL of filtered juice was titrated, 0.4 mL of 0.1 M NaOH was used to the dimethylaminoazobenzene end point and a total of 1.2 mL to the phenolphthalein end point.
cases.ask: Calculate and interpret the free, bound and total acidity.
cases.answer: Free HCl = 0.4 · 20 = 8 t.u.; total acidity = 1.2 · 20 = 24 t.u.; bound = 24 − 8 = 16 t.u. Total acidity (normal 40–60) and free HCl (normal 20–40) are reduced — **hypoacidity**. This is typical of chronic atrophic gastritis; the patient should be referred for gastroscopy and biopsy.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: A hypertonic solution is needed to clean a purulent wound. The laboratory assistant prepared a 10 % NaCl solution (ρ = 1.07 g/mL, M(NaCl) = 58.5 g/mol, i = 1.9).
cases.ask: Calculate the osmotic pressure of the solution at 37 °C. Why does it act on the wound?
cases.answer: C = 10 · 1.07 · 10 / 58.5 = 1.83 mol/L. π = i·C·R·T = 1.9 · 1.83 · 8.314 · 310 ≈ 8960 kPa — about 12 times higher than the plasma pressure (740–780 kPa). By osmosis, water is drawn from the wound tissue and pus into the dressing, and the wound is cleaned.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: In an emergency, a patient was mistakenly given 1 liter of distilled water intravenously. Soon the urine turned reddish and pain appeared in the lower back.
cases.ask: What happened? Explain the physicochemical basis.
cases.answer: Distilled water is hypotonic to plasma. By osmosis, water enters the red blood cells, makes them swell and burst — **hemolysis**. Free hemoglobin passes into the urine (hemoglobinuria) and may block the renal tubules, causing acute kidney injury. Only isotonic solutions (0.9 % NaCl, 5 % glucose) or other solutions prescribed for a medical indication are given intravenously.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: An elderly patient with diabetes mellitus was brought in unconscious. Tests: Na^+^ 150 mmol/L, glucose 25 mmol/L, urea 10 mmol/L.
cases.ask: Calculate and assess the plasma osmolality. What happens in the cells?
cases.answer: Osm = 2·150 + 25 + 10 = **335 mosmol/kg** — well above normal (285–295), a **hyperosmolar state**. Because the extracellular fluid has become hypertonic, water leaves the cells, including brain cells — cellular dehydration causes the loss of consciousness. In treatment, fluids and insulin are given to lower the osmolality **gradually** (a rapid fall risks cerebral edema).

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: A pharmacy has to prepare 500 mL of 0.9 % NaCl solution (take the density of the solution as 1 g/mL, M(NaCl) = 58.5 g/mol).
cases.ask: How many grams of NaCl are needed? What are the molar concentration and osmolarity of the solution?
cases.answer: m(NaCl) = 0.009 · 500 = **4.5 g**. 1 L contains 9 g: C = 9 / 58.5 ≈ **0.154 mol/L** (154 mmol/L). NaCl dissociates into two ions (i ≈ 2): osmolarity ≈ 2 · 154 = **308 mosmol/L** — close to plasma, the solution is isotonic.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: A patient with hypokalemia (K^+^ 2.8 mmol/L) is to be given 40 mmol of K^+^. The ward has 7.5 % KCl solution (≈ 1 mmol of K^+^ per 1 mL).
cases.ask: How many mL of KCl are needed? How should it be given correctly? At least how long should the infusion last (the rate must not exceed 10 mmol per hour)?
cases.answer: 40 mmol / 1 mmol/mL = **40 mL** of 7.5 % KCl. It is not given as a bolus — it is **diluted** in 1 L of isotonic solution and given as a drip. At a rate of 10 mmol per hour the infusion lasts at least 40 / 10 = **4 hours**. ECG and blood K^+^ are monitored during treatment.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: To standardize an NaOH solution, 0.1260 g of oxalic acid dihydrate (H~2~C~2~O~4~·2H~2~O, M~eq~ = 63 g/mol) was dissolved and titrated with phenolphthalein. 20.0 mL of NaOH was used.
cases.ask: Calculate the normality of the NaOH solution.
cases.answer: Number of equivalents of oxalic acid: n = 0.1260 / 63 = 0.002 mol-eq. By the law of equivalents NaOH also reacted in an amount of 0.002 mol-eq: C~n~(NaOH) = 0.002 / 0.0200 = **0.1 mol-eq/L (0.1 N)**. Since a weak acid was titrated, phenolphthalein was the right choice.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A child with nephrotic syndrome has swelling of the face and legs and fluid in the abdomen. There is much protein in the urine; blood albumin is 15 g/L (normal 35–50).
cases.ask: Explain the physicochemical mechanism of the edema. Why does an albumin infusion help only temporarily?
cases.answer: Albumin is lost in the urine and has decreased in plasma — the **oncotic pressure** has fallen. The balance of Starling forces is disturbed: at the venous end of the capillary water does not return to the blood and remains in the tissues — **edema** and ascites develop. When albumin is infused intravenously, the oncotic pressure rises temporarily and water is drawn from the tissues into the blood (usually given together with a diuretic). But because albumin is again lost in the urine, the effect is short; the main treatment is treating the kidney disease itself.

topics.title: Complex compounds. Inner complex compounds (chelates)

goals.text: To teach the student Werner’s coordination theory, the structure, naming and stability in solution of complex compounds, the nature of their chemical bonds, inner complex compounds (chelates) and chelation therapy, the fundamentals of complexometry and the determination of calcium in blood serum; to explain the chemical basis of stone diseases.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concepts of complexing agent, ligand, coordination number, inner and outer sphere;
the classification and naming rules of complex compounds;
instability and stability constants;
the donor–acceptor bond and hybridization in complex compounds;
chelates, the chelate effect and biologically important complexes (heme, chlorophyll, B~12~);
chelation therapy drugs and the fundamentals of complexometry.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the charge of the central atom and the coordination number from the formula of a complex;
carry out reactions that form and destroy complex compounds;
determine the calcium content of blood serum with Trilon B and interpret the result;
justify which complexing agent is used in heavy-metal poisoning.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Trilon B (EDTA) reacts with metal ions in a **1 : 1** ratio whatever their charge. This makes the calculation in complexometry very simple: n(Me) = n(Trilon B).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Order for reading a complex formula: **“Ligand — number — center — charge”**: [Cu(NH~3~)~4~]^2+^ is the tetra**ammine**copper(II) ion.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In lead poisoning, **calcium disodium** edetate (CaNa~2~EDTA) is used. Calcium-free Na~2~EDTA also binds the Ca^2+^ of the blood and causes life-threatening hypocalcemia.

blocks.text: **Complex compounds** are compounds that contain molecules or ions (ligands) arranged in a definite order around a central atom (ion) and that exist as separate particles even in solution. Their structure was explained in 1893 by **A. Werner** (Nobel Prize in 1913).

items: **Complexing agent (central atom)** — usually an ion of a d-element: Fe^2+^, Fe^3+^, Cu^2+^, Co^3+^, Zn^2+^, Ag^+^, Pt^2+^.
**Ligands** — molecules or anions bound to the central atom: H~2~O, NH~3~, Cl^−^, CN^−^, OH^−^, amino acids.
**Coordination number** — the number of donor atoms bound directly to the central atom (most often 2, 4 or 6).
**Inner sphere** — the central atom and the ligands, written in square brackets; **outer sphere** — the ions outside the brackets, which separate easily in solution.

blocks.text: For example, in K~4~[Fe(CN)~6~]: the central ion is Fe^2+^, the ligand is CN^−^, the coordination number is 6, the inner sphere is [Fe(CN)~6~]^4−^ and the outer sphere is 4K^+^. The charge of the complex ion = charge of the central ion + charges of the ligands: (+2) + 6·(−1) = −4.

The number of bonds a ligand forms with the central atom is called its **denticity**: **monodentate** (NH~3~, H~2~O, Cl^−^, CN^−^), **bidentate** (ethylenediamine, oxalate, glycinate), **polydentate** (EDTA — 6-dentate, hexadentate).

parts.text: **Cisplatin** [Pt(NH~3~)~2~Cl~2~] is the best-known complex drug. In the cell its chloride ligands are replaced by water, and platinum binds to the nitrogen of guanine in DNA, “stitching” the strands together — division of the tumor cell stops. It is used in testicular, ovarian and lung cancer; its main adverse effect is nephrotoxicity.

blocks.text: Complexes with the same composition but differing in the structure of the inner sphere or in the spatial arrangement of the ligands are called **isomers**. Isomers can differ sharply in their properties, including biological activity.

blocks.title: Table 3.2. Types of isomerism of complex compounds
head: Type of isomerism
Essence
Example
rows: identical ligands are next to each other (cis) or opposite each other (trans)
the complex and its mirror image cannot be superimposed
an ion is exchanged between the inner and outer sphere
a water molecule is in the inner or outer sphere

parts.text: Only **cis**-[Pt(NH~3~)~2~Cl~2~] (cisplatin) is active against tumors: two neighboring guanines of DNA bind in place of the two adjacent chlorides and bend the strand. **Transplatin** cannot form such a bridge and is useless as a drug. Newer-generation platinum drugs are **carboplatin** (less nephrotoxic) and **oxaliplatin** (in colorectal cancer).

blocks.text: **Werner’s experiment** made it possible to distinguish the inner and outer spheres: when AgNO~3~ is added to a solution of CoCl~3~·5NH~3~, only two thirds of the chloride precipitates as AgCl. Therefore the third chloride is bound directly to cobalt and the formula is [Co(NH~3~)~5~Cl]Cl~2~.

sections.title: 3. Equilibrium and stability of complex compounds in solution

blocks.text: In solution a complex compound first dissociates completely along the outer sphere (like a strong electrolyte): [Ag(NH~3~)~2~]Cl → [Ag(NH~3~)~2~]^+^ + Cl^−^. The inner sphere breaks down only very slightly and stepwise: [Ag(NH~3~)~2~]^+^ ⇄ Ag^+^ + 2NH~3~.

This equilibrium is described by the **instability constant**: K~inst~ = [Ag^+^]·[NH~3~]^2^ / [[Ag(NH~3~)~2~]^+^]. Its reciprocal is the **stability constant**: β = 1 / K~inst~. The smaller K~inst~, the more stable the complex.

blocks.title: Table 3.3. Instability constants of some complexes (25 °C)
head: Complex ion
K~inst~

blocks.text: Formation of a stable complex can dissolve poorly soluble substances: AgCl dissolves in ammonia because the Ag^+^ ions are bound into [Ag(NH~3~)~2~]^+^, and [Ag^+^] in solution falls below the solubility product of AgCl. Conversely, a strong precipitating agent destroys a complex: when KI is added to [Ag(NH~3~)~2~]^+^, AgI precipitates.
Factors affecting the stability of complexes

items: **Charge and radius of the central ion:** a large charge and small radius attract the ligand more strongly (Fe^3+^ complexes are usually more stable than Fe^2+^ complexes).
**Series of divalent 3d metals (Irving–Williams series):** Mn^2+^ < Fe^2+^ < Co^2+^ < Ni^2+^ < Cu^2+^ > Zn^2+^ — copper complexes are the most stable.
**Nature of the ligand:** the basicity of the donor atom and polydenticity (the chelate effect) increase stability.

**pH of the medium:** in an acidic medium H^+^ ions compete with the metal for the donor atoms of the ligand and the complex breaks down; in an alkaline medium the metal may precipitate as a hydroxide.

blocks.text: **Worked example.** In a solution containing 0.1 M [Ag(NH~3~)~2~]^+^ and 1 M excess NH~3~, the concentration of free Ag^+^ is: [Ag^+^] = K~inst~·[complex] / [NH~3~]^2^ = 5.9·10^−8^ · 0.1 / 1 = 5.9·10^−9^ mol/L. Such a tiny amount of free metal ion explains the biological importance of complexes: there is almost no “free” Cu^2+^ or Fe^3+^ in the body — they are bound to proteins.

sections.title: 4. The nature of the chemical bond in complex compounds

blocks.text: The bond between the central atom and a ligand is a **donor–acceptor (coordinate)** bond: the ligand (donor) supplies a lone electron pair and the central atom (acceptor) takes it into its empty orbitals. According to valence bond theory, the orbitals of the central atom hybridize, and the geometry of the complex depends on the type of hybridization.

blocks.title: Table 3.4. Type of hybridization and shape of complexes
head: Coordination number
Hybridization
Shape
Example

blocks.text: **Crystal field theory** shows that the electric field of the ligands splits the d-orbitals of the central atom by energy. Visible light is absorbed when an electron moves from one d-level to another — that is why complexes of d-elements are **colored**: [Cu(H~2~O)~4~]^2+^ is light blue, [Cu(NH~3~)~4~]^2+^ deep blue, hemoglobin red.

Compounds in which a polydentate ligand forms several bonds with the central atom and so creates a **ring (cycle)** are called **inner complex compounds** or **chelates** (Greek *chele* — a crab’s claw). The most stable are chelates with **five- and six-membered** rings.

blocks.label: Figure 3.1
blocks.caption: An example of an inner complex compound — copper(II) glycinate [Cu(NH~2~CH~2~COO)~2~]: each glycinate ion forms a five-membered ring with copper through nitrogen and oxygen (structural formula drawn with RDKit).

blocks.text: **The chelate effect:** even with the same donor atoms, a chelate is much more stable than a complex with monodentate ligands. The reason is entropy: one polydentate ligand displaces several water molecules, and the number of particles in solution increases (ΔS > 0).

parts.text: **Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning** is also a matter of complex formation: CO binds to the Fe^2+^ of heme ≈ 200–250 times more strongly than O~2~, forming **carboxyhemoglobin**. Treatment with 100 % oxygen and hyperbaric oxygenation shifts the equilibrium toward O~2~.

blocks.text: Cyanide poisoning — a clinical example of complex formation

The cyanide ion CN^−^ is a very strong ligand. It forms a stable complex with the **Fe^3+^ ion of cytochrome oxidase** in the mitochondria and stops the respiratory chain: the tissues cannot use oxygen (histotoxic hypoxia), while the blood remains saturated with oxygen — even venous blood is bright red.

rows: methemoglobin pulls CN^−^ away from cytochrome oxidase, forming cyanmethemoglobin
the low-toxicity thiocyanate is excreted in the urine
cyanocobalamin (vitamin B~12~) is formed and excreted in the urine

parts.text: In **metalloenzymes** the metal is firmly bound to the protein, and the enzyme loses activity if it is removed (carbonic anhydrase — Zn, cytochrome oxidase — Fe and Cu). In **metal-activated enzymes** the metal is loosely bound and increases activity when added from solution (Mg^2+^ for kinases).

blocks.text: **Chelation therapy** is the removal of toxic metal ions from the body by binding them into stable, water-soluble chelates that are excreted by the kidneys. The drug (complexing agent) must form a **more stable** complex with the toxic metal than with the essential metals of the body (Ca, Zn).

parts.text: **Pearson’s HSAB principle** (“soft with soft, hard with hard”): soft metals (Hg^2+^, Pb^2+^, Cd^2+^, As^3+^) bind stably to **sulfur** ligands, hard ions (Ca^2+^, Mg^2+^, Fe^3+^) to **oxygen** ligands. That is why thiol antidotes are used against mercury and arsenic.

sections.title: 7. Complex compounds in drugs and diagnostics

blocks.text: Complex formation is used in medicine not only to remove toxic metals but also to deliver a metal to the right place, to make it harmless and to release it slowly.

blocks.title: Table 3.8. Complex compounds used in medicine

parts.text: **Free Gd^3+^** is very toxic: because its radius is close to that of Ca^2+^, it blocks calcium channels and enzymes. That is why it is given only as a very stable chelate. In severe renal failure the agent stays in the body for a long time, partly dissociates, and a risk of **nephrogenic systemic fibrosis** appears — such patients are given the most stable macrocyclic agents.

blocks.text: When **sodium nitroprusside** breaks down, 5 CN^−^ ions are released together with NO. With prolonged or high-dose infusion cyanide may accumulate, so it is used for a short time and, if necessary, together with sodium thiosulfate.

**Complexometry** is a method based on titrating metal ions with a complexone (most often **Trilon B**, the disodium salt of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, Na~2~H~2~Y·2H~2~O). Trilon B forms a stable chelate with metal ions in a 1 : 1 ratio whatever their charge: Me^2+^ + H~2~Y^2−^ → MeY^2−^ + 2H^+^.

items: Because H^+^ is released in the reaction, the titration is done in the presence of a **buffer**: an ammonia buffer (pH ≈ 10) for the sum of Ca^2+^ + Mg^2+^, and NaOH (pH 12–13, Mg(OH)~2~ precipitates) for Ca^2+^ alone.

**Metal indicators** form colored complexes with the metal that are less stable than those with Trilon B: **eriochrome black T** (pH 10: wine-red with the metal, blue when free), **murexide** (pH 12: pink with Ca, violet when free).
At the equivalence point Trilon B pulls the metal out of the indicator complex, and the color of the free indicator appears.

parts.text: Complexometry is used to determine water **hardness** (the sum of Ca^2+^ and Mg^2+^, meq/L). Hard water increases the tendency to form kidney stones and gallstones; in some regions of Uzbekistan (Khorezm, Karakalpakstan) the hardness of drinking water is above the standard (7 meq/L).

blocks.text: Determination of water hardness

5 mL of ammonia buffer (pH ≈ 10) and Eriochrome Black T are added to 100 mL of water — Ca^2+^ and Mg^2+^ give a **wine-red** color with the indicator. On titration with Trilon B the metals are released from the indicator and the color changes to **blue**. Hardness: H = C~n~(Trilon B)·V(Trilon B)·1000 / V(water), mmol-eq/L.

parts.text: Complex formation is also used in laboratory practice: **K~2~-EDTA** is added to tubes for the complete blood count, and **sodium citrate** to tubes for coagulation tests and for blood transfusion. Both bind Ca^2+^ and stop blood clotting (Ca^2+^ is clotting factor IV).

blocks.text: Formation and study of complex compounds

items: **Copper ammine complex:** add NH~3~·H~2~O dropwise to CuSO~4~ solution — first a light blue precipitate of Cu(OH)~2~ forms, then it dissolves in excess ammonia to give deep blue [Cu(NH~3~)~4~]^2+^.

**Silver ammine complex:** add NaCl to AgNO~3~ (white AgCl), then add ammonia — the precipitate dissolves; add KI to the resulting solution — a yellow precipitate of AgI forms (the complex is destroyed).
**Prussian blue:** add K~4~[Fe(CN)~6~] to FeCl~3~ — a deep blue precipitate.
**Detecting the central ion in a complex ion:** add NaOH to K~3~[Fe(CN)~6~] solution — no Fe(OH)~3~ precipitate forms, because Fe^3+^ is held inside a stable complex.
Write an equation for each experiment and explain the observation.

blocks.text: Complexometric determination of calcium in blood serum

**Principle of the method:** in an alkaline medium (pH 12–13) the Ca^2+^ of serum forms a pink complex with murexide; on titration with Trilon B the calcium passes into the more stable CaY^2−^, and the color turns **violet**.

items: Place 1 mL of blood serum and 1 mL of distilled water in a flask.
Add 0.2 mL of 1 M NaOH and a pinch of a dry murexide mixture (with NaCl, 1 : 100) — the solution turns pink.
Titrate from a microburette with 0.0025 M Trilon B solution until the color turns violet.
Titrate a blank (without serum) in the same way and subtract the volume used.
Calculate: C(Ca^2+^) = C(Trilon B) · V(Trilon B) / V(serum).

blocks.text: **Example:** 0.96 mL of Trilon B was used in the titration. C(Ca) = 0.0025 · 0.96 / 1 = 0.0024 mol/L = **2.4 mmol/L** — normal (total calcium 2.2–2.6 mmol/L).

parts.text: **Hypercalcemia** (> 2.6 mmol/L) occurs in hyperparathyroidism, tumor metastases and hypervitaminosis D; **hypocalcemia** (< 2.2 mmol/L) in hypoparathyroidism, rickets, renal failure and acute pancreatitis. About 40 % of total calcium is bound to albumin, so the result is corrected in hypoalbuminemia.

sections.title: 10. Chemical basis of stone diseases (independent work)

blocks.text: Stones (calculi) form in a biological fluid when the concentration of the ions of a poorly soluble salt exceeds its **solubility product** (K~sp~), that is, when the fluid is **supersaturated**: [Ca^2+^]·[C~2~O~4~^2−^] > K~sp~(CaC~2~O~4~) = 2.3·10^−9^. Once a crystal nucleus forms, new layers are deposited on it.

blocks.title: Table 3.10. Main types of urinary stones
head: Type of stone
Share
Conditions of formation
Prevention
rows: plenty of water, limit oxalate-rich food, citrate
infection with urease-producing bacteria, alkaline urine

blocks.label: Figure 3.3
blocks.caption: A kidney stone made of calcium oxalate: its sharp-edged crystals injure the mucosa and cause hematuria (Wikimedia Commons).

blocks.text: **Inhibitors** of stone formation are citrate (it forms a soluble complex with Ca^2+^), magnesium (it gives a soluble salt with oxalate), pyrophosphate and proteins. That is why hypocitraturia increases the risk of stones, and **potassium citrate** is used to treat them.

parts.text: The type of stone depends on urine **pH**: urate stones form in acidic urine, phosphate and struvite stones in alkaline urine. Most gallstones, on the other hand, are **cholesterol** stones — cholesterol precipitates when it exceeds bile acids and phospholipids in the bile.

Compare the result with the normal range and write a conclusion.

skills.title: Skill: complexometric determination of the total hardness of water

items: Measure 100 mL of the water to be tested into a conical flask with a measuring cylinder.
Add 5 mL of ammonia buffer (pH ≈ 10) and a pinch of Eriochrome Black T — the solution turns wine-red.

Repeat the titration twice and take the mean volume.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A battery factory worker complains of colicky abdominal pain, weakness and headache. There is a gray line on his gums; the blood shows hypochromic anemia and basophilic stippling of red cells.
cases.ask: What poisoning is suspected? Which complexing agent is used to treat it, and why is its calcium form chosen?
cases.answer: Chronic lead poisoning (saturnism). Pb^2+^ blocks the enzymes of heme synthesis (δ-ALA dehydratase, ferrochelatase) — anemia develops. Treatment: edetate calcium disodium (CaNa~2~EDTA) intravenously; Pb^2+^ forms a more stable complex with EDTA than Ca^2+^ does, displaces the calcium, and PbY^2−^ is excreted in the urine. Calcium-free Na~2~EDTA would bind the blood calcium and could cause hypocalcemia and cardiac arrest. In children, succimer (DMSA) is given by mouth.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: To determine a patient’s serum calcium, 1 mL of serum was titrated with 0.0025 M Trilon B. Three titrations used 0.70, 0.72 and 0.71 mL, and the blank used 0.01 mL.
cases.ask: Calculate and interpret the calcium concentration. In which diseases can such a result occur?
cases.answer: Mean volume = 0.71 mL; subtracting the blank gives 0.70 mL. C(Ca) = 0.0025 · 0.70 / 1 = 0.00175 mol/L = 1.75 mmol/L — **hypocalcemia** (normal 2.2–2.6). Causes: hypoparathyroidism (for example, after thyroid surgery), vitamin D deficiency, chronic renal failure, acute pancreatitis. The albumin level should also be checked.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A 45-year-old man has gout and renal colic. Urine pH is 5.0; no stones are seen on X-ray, but ultrasound shows a stone in the kidney.
cases.ask: What type of stone is it? What is the chemically based treatment?
cases.answer: A uric acid (urate) stone: in acidic urine (pH < 5.5) uric acid is poorly soluble and crystallizes; urate stones are not visible on X-ray. Treatment is to alkalinize the urine with **potassium citrate** to pH 6.5–7.0: uric acid passes into the soluble urate ion (anionic form) and the stone may dissolve; plenty of fluids, allopurinol (reduces uric acid formation), and limiting purine-rich food.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: A laboratory worker suddenly lost consciousness while working with cyanide salts. The skin is reddish, venous blood is bright red like arterial blood, and the breath smells of bitter almonds.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanism of poisoning from the point of view of complex compounds. Which antidotes are used and what is their chemical basis?
cases.answer: CN^−^ forms a stable complex with the **Fe^3+^** ion of cytochrome oxidase and stops the respiratory chain — the tissues cannot use O~2~, so venous blood stays oxygen-saturated and bright red. Antidotes: 1) **sodium nitrite** (or amyl nitrite) converts part of the hemoglobin into methemoglobin (Fe^3+^), which pulls CN^−^ away from the enzyme to form cyanmethemoglobin; 2) **sodium thiosulfate**, with the help of rhodanese, converts CN^−^ into low-toxicity SCN^−^; 3) **hydroxocobalamin** binds CN^−^ to form cyanocobalamin, which is excreted in the urine. In addition, 100 % oxygen is given.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: To determine water hardness, 100 mL of water was titrated with 0.05 N Trilon B in the presence of ammonia buffer and Eriochrome Black T; 12.0 mL was used.
cases.ask: Calculate and assess the total hardness of the water.
cases.answer: H = 0.05 · 12.0 · 1000 / 100 = **6 mmol-eq/L**. The drinking water standard is ≤ 7 mmol-eq/L — the water is **moderately hard** and fit for drinking. At the end of the titration the color changes from wine-red to blue because Trilon B pulls Ca^2+^ and Mg^2+^ out of the indicator complex.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: A solution contains 0.1 mol/L [Ag(NH~3~)~2~]^+^ and 1 mol/L excess NH~3~ (K~inst~ = 5.9·10^−8^). KI was added to it until [I^−^] = 0.01 mol/L (K~sp~(AgI) = 8.3·10^−17^).
cases.ask: Calculate the concentration of free Ag^+^. Will AgI precipitate?
cases.answer: [Ag^+^] = 5.9·10^−8^ · 0.1 / 1^2^ = **5.9·10^−9^ mol/L**. Ion product: [Ag^+^]·[I^−^] = 5.9·10^−9^ · 0.01 = 5.9·10^−11^ — much larger than K~sp~(AgI) = 8.3·10^−17^, so **AgI precipitates** and the complex breaks down. The ammonia complex dissolves AgCl, but it cannot “hold” the very poorly soluble AgI.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: A patient with severe chronic renal failure needs a contrast-enhanced MRI to detect a brain tumor.
cases.ask: What risk is associated with giving a gadolinium contrast agent? What is its chemical cause and how can the risk be reduced?
cases.answer: The Gd^3+^ agent is excreted by the kidneys; in renal failure it stays in the body for a long time, part of the chelate dissociates and **free Gd^3+^** is released. Because the radius of free Gd^3+^ is close to that of Ca^2+^, it disturbs calcium-dependent processes and, accumulating in tissues, can cause **nephrogenic systemic fibrosis**. Ways to reduce the risk: choose the most stable **macrocyclic** agent at the minimum dose, use a non-contrast method if possible, and in dialysis patients perform dialysis soon after the examination.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A student was given a violet compound with the composition CoCl~3~·5NH~3~. When excess AgNO~3~ was added to a solution of 0.01 mol of it, 0.02 mol of AgCl precipitated.
cases.ask: Write the coordination formula of the compound, determine the charge of the central ion and the coordination number, and name it.
cases.answer: Each mole of the compound gave 2 mol of AgCl — so there are **two** Cl^−^ ions in the outer sphere and the third is in the inner sphere. Formula: **[Co(NH~3~)~5~Cl]Cl~2~**. The central ion is **Co^3+^** (x + 0 − 1 = +2, x = +3), the coordination number is **6** (5 NH~3~ and 1 Cl^−^), the shape is octahedral. Name: chloropentaamminecobalt(III) chloride.

topics.title: Acid–base equilibrium. Buffer systems

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the ion product of water and pH, buffer systems, their classification and mechanism of action, buffer capacity, the formulas for calculating the pH of buffer solutions, the buffer systems of the body, the alkaline reserve of the blood, acidosis and alkalosis, and to teach how to prepare phosphate buffer solutions of different pH.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the ion product of water, the concepts of pH and pOH, and the pH values of biological fluids;
the definition, classification and mechanism of action of buffer systems;
the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation and buffer capacity;
the buffer systems of blood (bicarbonate, phosphate, hemoglobin, protein) and their shares;
the concept of the alkaline reserve;
the types and causes of acidosis and alkalosis.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: calculate the pH of solutions of strong and weak electrolytes;
calculate and prepare a buffer solution of the required pH;
assess buffer capacity experimentally;
interpret the acid–base parameters of blood.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Blood pH is **7.35–7.45**. In the bicarbonate buffer [HCO~3~^−^] : [H~2~CO~3~] = **20 : 1**, so pH = 6.1 + lg20 = 7.4. The limits compatible with life are roughly pH 6.8–7.8.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Lungs — CO~2~, kidneys — HCO~3~^−^”**: in respiratory disorders the primary change is in pCO~2~, in metabolic disorders in HCO~3~^−^. In metabolic disorders, pH and the primary parameter change in the same direction (both ↓ or both ↑).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: A buffer holds pH only **up to a certain limit**: its working range is about pK~a~ ± 1. When one buffer component is used up (for example, HCO~3~^−^ in ketoacidosis), the pH changes sharply.

sections.title: 1. The ion product of water and the hydrogen ion exponent

blocks.text: Water is a very weak electrolyte: H~2~O ⇄ H^+^ + OH^−^. At 25 °C the **ion product of water** K~w~ = [H^+^]·[OH^−^] = 10^−14^. In a neutral medium [H^+^] = [OH^−^] = 10^−7^ mol/L.
The **hydrogen ion exponent** pH = −lg[H^+^], the **hydroxide exponent** pOH = −lg[OH^−^], and pH + pOH = 14. pH < 7 is acidic, pH = 7 neutral and pH > 7 alkaline.

items: **Strong acid:** pH = −lg C (for 0.01 M HCl, pH = 2).
**Strong base:** pOH = −lg C, pH = 14 − pOH (for 0.01 M NaOH, pH = 12).
**Weak acid:** pH = ½(pK~a~ − lg C) (for 0.1 M CH~3~COOH, pK~a~ = 4.76, pH = 2.88).
