blocks.text: According to the interaction between the dispersed phase and the medium, **lyophilic** systems (the particle interacts strongly with the solvent, forms spontaneously and is stable: solutions of proteins and starch) and **lyophobic** systems (weak interaction, a stabilizer is needed: metal sols, AgI sol) are distinguished.

sections.title: 2. Preparation and purification of colloidal solutions

items: **Dispersion methods** — breaking up large particles: mechanical (colloid mill), ultrasound, electric arc (Bredig’s method — metal sols), **peptization** (converting a precipitate into the colloidal state with an electrolyte or a surfactant).

**Condensation methods** — joining molecules and ions into particles: physical (solvent replacement — pouring an alcoholic solution of sulfur into water) and chemical (reduction, hydrolysis, exchange reactions): FeCl~3~ + 3H~2~O → Fe(OH)~3~ + 3HCl (in boiling water).

blocks.text: Colloidal solutions are purified from low-molecular impurities as follows: **dialysis** — passing ions and small molecules through a semipermeable membrane into pure solvent; **electrodialysis** — dialysis speeded up by an electric field; **ultrafiltration** — filtration through a membrane under pressure.

parts.text: **Hemodialysis (the “artificial kidney”)** is based on the principle of dialysis: the patient’s blood flows on one side of a semipermeable membrane and the dialysis solution on the other. Small molecules such as urea, creatinine and K^+^ pass into the solution, while proteins and blood cells stay in the blood. Fluid is removed by ultrafiltration. The **renal glomeruli** are a natural ultrafilter as well.

sections.title: 3. Structure of the colloidal particle (micelle). The electrokinetic potential

blocks.text: A particle of a lyophobic sol is a **micelle**. For example, when **excess KI** is added to AgNO~3~: AgNO~3~ + KI → AgI↓ + KNO~3~. According to the Paneth–Fajans rule, the AgI crystals (the core) adsorb the excess I^−^ ions from the solution.

Micelle formula: {[mAgI]·nI^−^·(n − x)K^+^}^x−^·xK^+^. Here [mAgI] is the **aggregate (core)**; nI^−^ are the **potential-determining ions**; (n − x)K^+^ are the counterions of the **adsorption layer**; {…}^x−^ is the **granule** (negatively charged); xK^+^ are the counterions of the **diffuse layer**.

blocks.label: Figure 8.1
blocks.caption: Structure of a micelle of the AgI sol formed with excess KI: the core, the potential-determining I^−^ ions and the K^+^ counterions of the adsorption and diffuse layers (diagram).

blocks.text: The potential between the core surface and the solution is the **thermodynamic (φ) potential**; the potential at the slipping boundary between the granule and the diffuse layer is the **electrokinetic (ζ, zeta) potential**. The greater the ζ-potential, the more strongly the particles repel each other and the more stable the sol.

parts.text: If AgNO~3~ is in excess, the potential-determining ions are Ag^+^ and the granule is **positively** charged: {[mAgI]·nAg^+^·(n − x)NO~3~^−^}^x+^·xNO~3~^−^. That is, the sign of the charge depends on which reagent is in excess.

items: **Electrophoresis** — movement of particles of the dispersed phase in an external electric field toward the oppositely charged electrode.
**Electroosmosis** — movement of the dispersion medium (the liquid) through a porous barrier or capillary in an electric field.
**Streaming potential** — a potential difference that arises when a liquid is forced through a porous barrier under pressure (the reverse of electroosmosis).
**Sedimentation potential** (Dorn effect) — the potential arising while particles settle (the reverse of electrophoresis).

blocks.text: The rate of electrophoresis is proportional to the ζ-potential (the Helmholtz–Smoluchowski equation). The charge of proteins depends on pH: above the isoelectric point (pI) they are negatively charged, below it positively.

blocks.title: Table 8.3. Electrophoretic fractions of serum proteins (normal)
head: Fraction
Share, %
Main proteins

parts.text: Serum protein electrophoresis is widely used in diagnosis: in **multiple myeloma** a narrow “M-spike” appears in the γ region, in **nephrotic syndrome** albumin falls and α~2~ rises, in **liver cirrhosis** albumin falls and the γ-globulins rise broadly, and in **acute inflammation** α~1~ and α~2~ rise. In treatment, **electrophoresis** (delivery of drug ions through the skin) is used as a physiotherapy method.

items: **Brownian motion** — the random movement of colloidal particles under the impacts of the molecules of the medium; it keeps colloids from settling (kinetic stability).
**Diffusion** — the spontaneous spreading of particles from higher to lower concentration; in colloids it is much slower than in true solutions.
**Osmotic pressure** — very small in colloidal solutions because the number of particles is small (the oncotic pressure of plasma is ≈ 3.5–4 kPa).
**Sedimentation** — the settling of particles under gravity; it is accelerated in an ultracentrifuge and makes it possible to determine the molecular mass of proteins.

blocks.text: **Optical properties:** colloidal particles scatter light. When a beam of light is passed through a colloidal solution from the side, a bright cone is seen — the **Tyndall effect** (not seen in a true solution). By **Rayleigh’s law** scattering is inversely proportional to the 4th power of the wavelength — so short-wavelength blue light is scattered more strongly (why the sky looks blue). Colloidal particles are visible in the **ultramicroscope** and the electron microscope.

parts.text: The **erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)** is based on the sedimentation property of blood as a disperse system: in inflammation fibrinogen and globulins increase, red cells stick together in “rouleaux” and settle faster. Normal values: men 2–10 mm/h, women 2–15 mm/h.

blocks.text: Nanoparticles in medicine

Particles 1–100 nm in size fall into the colloidal range; their deliberate design and use is called **nanomedicine**. Because of their size, nanoparticles can enter tissues and cells, drugs or antibodies can be attached to their surface, and they accumulate more in tumors because tumor vessels are leaky.

blocks.title: Table 8.4. Nanoparticles used in medicine
head: Nanoparticle
Structure
Use
rows: liposomal doxorubicin, amphotericin B — drugs with reduced toxicity
delivery of mRNA vaccines into cells
MRI contrast, treatment of iron deficiency

blocks.text: **Kinetic (sedimentation) stability** is the resistance of particles to settling (thanks to Brownian motion); **aggregative stability** is the resistance of particles to sticking together and growing. The factors of aggregative stability are the like charge of the particles (ζ-potential), the **solvate (hydrate) shell** and **protective colloids**.

**Coagulation** is the sticking together, growth and settling of colloidal particles. It is caused by temperature, stirring, adding an oppositely charged sol and, most often, **electrolytes**. The lowest concentration of an electrolyte needed to start coagulation is called the **coagulation threshold** (C~k~, mmol/L).

**The Schulze–Hardy rule:** coagulation is caused by the ion whose charge is opposite to that of the granule (the coagulating ion); its coagulating power is proportional to roughly the **6th power** of the charge. For singly, doubly and triply charged ions the thresholds are in the ratio 1 : (1/2)^6^ : (1/3)^6^ ≈ 730 : 11 : 1.

parts.text: **Protective colloids** (proteins, gelatin) coat the particles of a lyophobic sol and protect them from coagulation. In the blood, proteins keep particles of poorly soluble salts (calcium phosphate, cholesterol) in colloidal form; when this protective property weakens, **stone** formation becomes easier. Protargol and collargol are silver sols protected by protein.

sections.title: 7. Blood as a disperse system. Hemolysis and agglutination

blocks.text: Blood is a complex disperse system: the dispersion medium is **plasma** (a colloidal solution of proteins and a true solution of salts), the dispersed phase is the **formed elements** (blood cells, mainly red cells). The red cell surface is **negatively charged** by sialic acids (ζ ≈ −15 mV); the like charges repel the cells from each other and keep the suspension stable.

blocks.title: Table 8.5. Types of hemolysis
head: Type of hemolysis
Cause
Example

distilled water, infusion of a hypotonic solution

freezing and thawing, vigorous shaking, an artificial valve
improper storage and transport of blood

blocks.text: The **osmotic fragility (resistance) of red cells** is their tolerance to hypotonic NaCl solutions. Normally hemolysis begins in 0.46–0.48 % NaCl and is complete in 0.32–0.34 % solution. Decreased resistance (hemolysis beginning at a higher concentration) is typical of **hereditary spherocytosis**: spherical red cells take up little water before they burst.

**Agglutination** is the clumping of particles (red cells, bacteria) by antibodies; it is a special kind of coagulation. Blood grouping is based on the agglutination of red cell antigens by standard sera (anti-A, anti-B, anti-D).

parts.text: **Blood clotting** is the conversion of plasma from a sol into a **gel**: soluble fibrinogen is converted by thrombin into fibrin, which forms a three-dimensional network that traps blood cells and fluid. Later the clot contracts and serum is squeezed out (**retraction**) — this is the **syneresis** characteristic of gels.

sections.title: 8. Coarse disperse systems and colloidal surfactants

items: **Suspensions** — solid particles (> 100 nm) in a liquid: the BaSO~4~ contrast agent and many pediatric dosage forms; they are shaken before use.
**Emulsions** — one liquid as droplets in another: **direct** (oil in water, like milk) and **inverse** (water in oil, like butter). They are stabilized by **emulsifiers** (surfactants).
**Foams** and **aerosols** — disperse systems with gas; inhaled drugs are given as aerosols.

blocks.text: **Colloidal surfactants** (soaps, bile salts, phospholipids) above a certain concentration — the **critical micelle concentration** (CMC) — join into micelles: hydrophobic tails inside, hydrophilic heads outside. Water-insoluble substances (fats, cholesterol) “dissolve” inside the micelle — **solubilization**.

parts.text: In the intestine, **bile salts** emulsify fats into small droplets (increasing the surface on which lipase acts) and carry the products of fat digestion to the site of absorption as mixed micelles. When bile is lacking (obstructive jaundice), fats and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are not absorbed — **steatorrhea** develops. In parenteral nutrition, **lipid emulsions** stabilized with egg phospholipids are given intravenously.

blocks.text: Dosage forms as disperse systems

**Suspensions and emulsions** are thermodynamically unstable: over time the particles settle, emulsion droplets float to the top (creaming) and merge (**coalescence**) — the emulsion separates into layers. That is why emulsifiers and thickeners are added to them, and they are shaken before use.

parts.text: Much of the aerosol from a metered-dose inhaler deposits in the mouth. A **spacer** (holding chamber) retains large particles and slows the aerosol — the fraction of drug reaching the bronchi increases and side effects such as oral candidiasis decrease. It is especially recommended for children and the elderly.

sections.title: 9. Solutions of macromolecular compounds and gels

blocks.text: Proteins, polysaccharides and nucleic acids are **macromolecular compounds** (biopolymers). Although their solutions are true (molecular) solutions, the molecules are close in size to colloidal particles, so they have colloid-like properties: slow diffusion, inability to cross membranes, the Tyndall effect. They form spontaneously and are thermodynamically stable.

blocks.title: Table 8.7. Comparison of lyophobic sols and solutions of macromolecular compounds
head: Feature
Lyophobic sol
Macromolecular solution
rows: precipitates only with much salt (salting out)
precipitation is reversible — dissolves again in water

items: **Swelling** is the increase in volume of a macromolecular substance as it takes up solvent: **unlimited** (gelatin dissolves completely in hot water) and **limited** (gelatin only swells in cold water). Swelling depends on pH and is minimal at the isoelectric point.

**Salting out** — a large amount of a neutral salt (NH~4~)~2~SO~4~ strips the hydration shell from protein molecules and precipitates them; protein activity is preserved — used to separate proteins into fractions.

A **gel** is a three-dimensional network of macromolecules or colloidal particles that holds solvent: gelatin, agar, a blood clot, the vitreous body of the eye. Over time gels contract and expel liquid — **syneresis**; some gels liquefy when shaken and set again on standing — **thixotropy**.

**Donnan equilibrium** — in a system containing protein ions that cannot cross a membrane, small ions are distributed unequally on the two sides of the membrane; this contributes to the difference in ionic composition between cells and plasma.

blocks.text: **Viscosity.** The flow of a liquid through a tube is described by **Poiseuille’s law**: Q = π·r^4^·ΔP / (8·η·l). Volume flow is proportional to the 4th power of the vessel radius and inversely proportional to viscosity (η). The viscosity of blood is 4–5 times that of water and depends mainly on the **hematocrit** and the fibrinogen content.

parts.text: In **polycythemia** the hematocrit rises to 60–65 % and blood viscosity increases sharply: blood flow slows and the risk of thrombosis, stroke and myocardial infarction rises. Treatment lowers the hematocrit by bloodletting (phlebotomy). Conversely, in severe anemia viscosity falls, the heart works “against little resistance” and murmurs appear.

skills.title: Skill: writing the formula of a micelle

items: Write the reaction equation and identify the poorly soluble substance (the core).
Find which reagent is in excess: its ion that is part of the core becomes the potential-determining ion (Paneth–Fajans rule).
The other ion of the excess reagent is the counterion; part of it is in the adsorption layer, the rest in the diffuse layer.
Write the formula: {[m(core)]·n(potential-determining ion)·(n − x)(counterion)}^charge^·x(counterion).
Show the sign of the granule charge and the electrode toward which it moves in electrophoresis.

skills.title: Skill: identifying the coagulating ion

items: Determine the sign of the granule charge.
From the added electrolyte, choose the ion with a charge opposite to the granule — this is the coagulating ion.
Compare the ions by charge: the greater the charge, the lower the threshold.
Use the Schulze–Hardy ratio (≈ 730 : 11 : 1) to estimate the required concentration.
Conclusion: state which electrolyte is the strongest coagulant.

skills.title: Skill: determining the osmotic fragility of red cells

items: Prepare a series of NaCl solutions from 0.70 % to 0.30 % (every 0.02 %), 1 mL each, in test tubes.
Add one drop of heparinized blood to each tube, mix gently and leave for 1 hour (or centrifuge).
Record the highest concentration at which the upper part of the solution has turned pale pink — this is the **minimal resistance** (onset of hemolysis).
Find the tube in which the sediment has disappeared completely and the solution is clear red — this is the **maximal resistance** (complete hemolysis).
Compare the result with the norm (onset 0.46–0.48 %, complete 0.32–0.34 %).

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: In the laboratory an iron(III) hydroxide sol was prepared by adding FeCl~3~ solution dropwise to boiling water. FeO^+^ ions are adsorbed on the particle surface, and the counterion is Cl^−^.
cases.ask: Write the formula of the micelle. Which of NaCl, Na~2~SO~4~ and Na~3~PO~4~ is needed in the smallest amount to coagulate the sol?
cases.answer: {[mFe(OH)~3~]·nFeO^+^·(n − x)Cl^−^}^x+^·xCl^−^ — the granule is positively charged. Coagulation is caused by anions; by the Schulze–Hardy rule the triply charged PO~4~^3−^ is the strongest, then SO~4~^2−^, and Cl^−^ the weakest. So **Na~3~PO~4~** is needed in the smallest amount (the thresholds are in roughly the reverse order of 1 : 11 : 730).

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: Serum protein electrophoresis of a patient: albumin 38 %, α~1~ 4 %, α~2~ 8 %, β 10 %, and a narrow tall peak in the γ region (40 %). The patient complains of bone pain; ESR is 75 mm/h.
cases.ask: Interpret the electrophoretogram. Why is the ESR sharply increased?
cases.answer: The narrow tall peak in the γ region is a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-spike), typical of **multiple myeloma**; albumin is relatively reduced. The increase of large, positively charged proteins (paraprotein) in the plasma neutralizes the negative charge (ζ-potential) of the red cells; they stick together in “rouleaux” and settle quickly — the ESR rises sharply. The diagnosis is confirmed by immunofixation, Bence Jones protein in the urine and bone marrow examination.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient with obstructive jaundice has pale, fatty, shiny stools, and the prothrombin time is prolonged.
cases.ask: Explain these signs using the properties of disperse systems and colloidal surfactants.
cases.answer: Because the bile duct is blocked, bile salts do not reach the intestine. As colloidal surfactants they emulsify fats and, by forming mixed micelles, solubilize fats and fat-soluble vitamins. Without bile, fat stays as large droplets and lipase acts poorly — **steatorrhea**; vitamin K is not absorbed and the liver synthesizes little prothrombin — blood clotting slows. Treatment: restore bile flow and give vitamin K parenterally.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: For a positively charged iron(III) hydroxide sol the coagulation threshold of NaCl is 9.25 mmol/L.
cases.ask: Using the Schulze–Hardy rule, estimate the threshold for Na~2~SO~4~ and Na~3~PO~4~. Which ion is the coagulating ion?
cases.answer: The granule is positive, so the coagulating ions are the **anions**: Cl^−^, SO~4~^2−^, PO~4~^3−^. The thresholds are inversely proportional to the 6th power of the charge: for SO~4~^2−^ 9.25 / 2^6^ = 9.25 / 64 ≈ **0.14 mmol/L**, for PO~4~^3−^ 9.25 / 3^6^ = 9.25 / 729 ≈ **0.013 mmol/L**. That is, phosphate coagulates about 700 times more strongly than chloride.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: A child presenting with jaundice and an enlarged spleen had the osmotic fragility of red cells tested: hemolysis began in 0.60 % NaCl and was complete in 0.40 % solution. The blood smear shows many small, spherical red cells.
cases.ask: Assess the result and explain the mechanism.
cases.answer: Hemolysis began at a much higher concentration than normal (0.46–0.48 %) — osmotic resistance is **decreased** (fragility increased). This is typical of **hereditary spherocytosis**: because of a defect in membrane proteins (spectrin, ankyrin) the red cell is a sphere rather than a disc. A sphere has the smallest surface for its volume, so the membrane stretches and bursts after only a little water enters. Such red cells are also destroyed quickly in the spleen — hence the anemia, jaundice and enlarged spleen.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: The isoelectric point of albumin is pI = 4.9. Serum protein electrophoresis is carried out in veronal buffer at pH 8.6.
cases.ask: How is albumin charged under these conditions and toward which electrode does it move? What is observed in a pH 4.0 buffer?
cases.answer: pH 8.6 > pI — albumin loses protons, becomes **negatively** charged and moves toward the **anode** (+); being the smallest and most negatively charged of the serum proteins, it moves fastest and farthest. If pH 4.0 < pI, albumin takes up protons, becomes **positively** charged and moves toward the **cathode** (−). At pH = pI it does not move.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: A 6-year-old child with bronchial asthma was prescribed a metered-dose inhaler, but the attacks did not decrease; oral candidiasis appeared.
cases.ask: Explain the cause from the point of view of disperse systems. What solution would you suggest?
cases.answer: The aerosol leaves the inhaler at high speed; the child cannot coordinate pressing with inhaling, and **large particles** deposit in the mouth and pharynx by inertia. The fraction of 1–5 µm particles that reach the bronchi is small — the effect is poor; the glucocorticoid left in the mouth causes candidiasis. Solution: a **spacer** with a mask or mouthpiece — it retains large particles and slows the aerosol; rinsing the mouth after inhalation.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A patient with polycythemia has a hematocrit of 65 % (normal 40–48 %), headaches and facial redness. There is a history of a transient ischemic attack.
cases.ask: Explain the disturbance of blood flow from a physicochemical point of view. If, because of atherosclerosis, the vessel radius has also narrowed 2 times, how many times does the blood flow decrease?
cases.answer: When the hematocrit rises, blood **viscosity** increases sharply. According to Poiseuille’s law, flow is inversely proportional to viscosity — blood flows slowly, microcirculation is impaired and the risk of thrombus formation rises. Flow is proportional to the 4th power of the radius: if the radius decreases 2 times, flow decreases 2^4^ = **16 times** (the increased viscosity makes this even worse). Treatment: phlebotomy to bring the hematocrit below 45 %, antiplatelet agents.

topics.title: Fundamentals of organic chemistry. Main classes of organic compounds

goals.text: To teach the student the theory of the structure of organic compounds, isomerism and stereoisomerism, the electronic effects (inductive and mesomeric) that determine reactivity, the acidity and basicity of organic compounds, oxidation–reduction reactions, the classes of hydrocarbons and of compounds containing heteroatoms, and their medical significance.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: A.M. Butlerov’s theory of chemical structure;
structural and spatial isomerism, chirality, enantiomers, and D/L and R/S nomenclature;
inductive and mesomeric effects, conjugation and aromaticity;
the acidity and basicity of organic compounds according to Brønsted and Lewis;
the oxidation and reduction of alcohols, aldehydes and other compounds;
the classes of hydrocarbons and of compounds with the main functional groups.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify the functional groups and the class of a compound;
find a chiral carbon atom and draw the enantiomers;
explain the effect of substituents on acidity and basicity by electronic effects;
link the oxidation of organic substances in the body (ethanol, methanol) with medical conditions.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Natural **amino acids belong to the L series**, natural **monosaccharides to the D series**. Enantiomers have the same physical properties, but their biological effects can be completely different (the thalidomide tragedy).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The oxidation ladder: **alcohol → aldehyde → acid → CO~2~** (primary alcohol); secondary alcohol → **ketone**. In the body: ethanol → acetaldehyde → acetic acid (acetyl-CoA).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Methanol itself is not very toxic, but in the body it is oxidized to **formaldehyde** and **formic acid**: the optic nerve is damaged (blindness) and severe metabolic acidosis develops. The antidote is fomepizole or ethanol (they compete for alcohol dehydrogenase).

sections.title: 1. The theory of the structure of organic compounds

blocks.text: **Organic chemistry** is the chemistry of carbon compounds and their derivatives. More than 90 % of known substances are organic compounds; all biomolecules and most drugs belong to them.

items: The atoms in a molecule are joined in a definite **order** according to their valence; this order is called the **chemical structure** (A.M. Butlerov, 1861).
The properties of a substance depend not only on its composition but also on its **structure** — this is why **isomers** exist.
The atoms and groups of atoms in a molecule **influence each other**.
The structure can be deduced from the properties of a substance, and the properties from the structure.

blocks.text: In organic compounds the carbon atom is always **tetravalent**; it can be **sp^3^** (tetrahedral, 109.5°, alkanes), **sp^2^** (planar, 120°, alkenes, benzene, the carbonyl group) or **sp** (linear, 180°, alkynes) hybridized. Carbon atoms can form long chains and rings with each other — hence the endless variety of organic compounds.

sections.title: 2. Classification and nomenclature of organic compounds

blocks.text: According to the **carbon skeleton**, organic compounds are divided into acyclic (open-chain), carbocyclic (the ring consists only of carbon atoms) and heterocyclic (the ring contains N, O or S atoms) compounds; according to the **functional group**, into classes (alcohols, aldehydes, acids, amines and others). Compounds with several identical functional groups are called **polyfunctional**, and those with different groups **heterofunctional** (topic 10).

Naming by **IUPAC substitutive nomenclature**: 1) the **principal functional group** is identified — it enters the name as a suffix; 2) the longest **parent chain** containing this group is chosen; 3) the chain is numbered so that the principal group gets the lowest number; 4) the remaining groups are written as prefixes in alphabetical order with their position numbers.

Group

blocks.text: **Examples:** CH~3~−CH(OH)−COOH — 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid); HOOC−CH~2~−C(OH)(COOH)−CH~2~−COOH — 2-hydroxypropane-1,2,3-tricarboxylic acid (citric acid); CH~3~−CO−CH~2~−COOH — 3-oxobutanoic acid (acetoacetic acid); HO−CH~2~−CH~2~−NH~2~ — 2-aminoethanol (ethanolamine).

parts.text: **Trivial** (historical) names are often used in medicine: lactic, citric and acetic acid, glycerol, urea. Knowing them together with the IUPAC names makes it easier to understand the structure of drugs and metabolites.

Essence
Example

arrangement of substituents relative to a double bond or ring
because of a chiral center the molecule cannot be superimposed on its mirror image
L- and D-alanine, L- and D-glyceraldehyde

blocks.text: **Chirality** is the property of a molecule of not being superimposable on its mirror image (like the right and left hands). Most often it is caused by an **asymmetric (chiral) carbon atom** with four different substituents. Stereoisomers that are mirror images of each other are called **enantiomers**: they rotate the plane of polarized light by the same angle but in opposite directions; an equal mixture of them (a **racemate**) is optically inactive.

blocks.label: Figure 9.1
blocks.caption: The enantiomers of alanine: L-alanine (S) and D-alanine (R) — mirror images of each other; the chiral center is the α-carbon atom (structural formulas drawn with RDKit).

blocks.text: **Nomenclature:** **D/L** — relative to glyceraldehyde (in the Fischer projection, OH or NH~2~ at the chiral center on the right — D, on the left — L); **R/S** — by the priority of the substituents (the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules). Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not enantiomers (for example, glucose and galactose).

parts.text: **The thalidomide tragedy** (1957–1961): the drug given to pregnant women as a sedative was a racemate; one enantiomer was sedative and the other **teratogenic**, and ≈ 10 000 children were born with limb defects (the enantiomers interconvert in the body). Today many drugs are produced as the active enantiomer: **levodopa** (L-DOPA), **levothyroxine**, **esomeprazole**, **levocetirizine**.

blocks.text: Conformations

The different spatial shapes a molecule takes as a result of rotation about a single σ-bond are called **conformations**; they are not isomers and interconvert rapidly. In ethane, **staggered** (atoms far apart, low energy) and **eclipsed** (atoms aligned, high energy) conformations are distinguished; they are drawn as Newman projections.

The cyclohexane ring is not flat: its most stable shape is the **“chair”**, in which the angles are close to 109.5° and there is no strain; a less stable shape is the **“boat”**. In the chair conformation substituents are **equatorial** (in the plane of the ring, favorable) or **axial** (perpendicular to the plane). In β-D-glucopyranose all the large groups are equatorial — that is why glucose is the most abundant monosaccharide in nature.
The distribution of electron density in a molecule determines its reactivity. The shift of electron density is described by two kinds of electronic effects.

items: **Inductive effect (I)** — a shift of electron density along a chain of σ-bonds; it fades quickly with distance. **−I**: electronegative atoms and groups withdraw electrons (F, Cl, OH, NH~2~, NO~2~, COOH). **+I**: alkyl groups donate electrons (CH~3~, C~2~H~5~).

**Mesomeric effect (M)** — a shift of electron density along a conjugated π-system; it is transmitted along the chain without fading. **+M**: groups with a lone pair donate electrons to the π-system (−OH, −NH~2~, −OR, halogens). **−M**: groups withdraw electrons from the π-system (C=O, COOH, NO~2~, C≡N).

blocks.text: **Conjugation** is the formation of one delocalized electron cloud by π-bonds, or by a π-bond and a lone pair; it lowers the energy of the molecule and increases its stability. **Aromaticity** (Hückel’s rule): a planar cyclic conjugated system with (4n + 2) π-electrons is especially stable — benzene (6 π-electrons), pyridine, pyrrole, the purine bases.

A covalent bond can break in two ways. In **homolytic cleavage** each atom keeps one electron and **free radicals** are formed (under high temperature, radiation or peroxides). In **heterolytic cleavage** the electron pair stays with one atom and ions are formed: an **electrophile** lacking an electron pair (E^+^ — H^+^, NO~2~^+^, a carbocation) and a **nucleophile** with a lone pair (Nu^−^ — OH^−^, Cl^−^, NH~3~, H~2~O).

blocks.text: The **S~N~2 mechanism** is one-step: the nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group and the configuration is inverted. The **S~N~1 mechanism** is two-step: first the leaving group departs to form a carbocation, then the nucleophile adds; racemization is observed at a chiral center.

parts.text: **Alkylating anticancer drugs** (cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, busulfan) are strong electrophiles: they attach to the N7 atom of guanine in DNA by nucleophilic substitution and “cross-link” the strands. Rapidly dividing cells — tumor, bone marrow, hair follicles — are damaged most; hence their side effects are anemia, infections and hair loss.

sections.title: 6. Acidity and basicity of organic compounds

blocks.text: **Brønsted theory:** an acid is a proton donor, a base is a proton acceptor. **Lewis theory:** an acid is an electron-pair acceptor, a base an electron-pair donor. By the type of acidic center, OH-, SH-, NH- and CH-acids are distinguished; the strength of an acid is determined by the stability of its conjugate base (anion).

blocks.title: Table 9.4. Acidity of some organic compounds

blocks.text: **Basicity** is typical mainly of nitrogen compounds (the lone electron pair). Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia (+I effect): pK~a~ ≈ 10.6 for CH~3~NH~3~^+^ and 9.25 for NH~4~^+^. Aniline, however, is a very weak base (pK~a~ ≈ 4.6 for C~6~H~5~NH~3~^+^) because the nitrogen lone pair is conjugated with the benzene ring (+M).

parts.text: The degree of ionization of drugs determines their absorption: mainly the **un-ionized** form crosses membranes. Weak acids (aspirin, pK~a~ ≈ 3.5) are largely un-ionized in the acidic stomach and are partly absorbed there; weak bases (many alkaloids) are absorbed well in the more alkaline intestine. In poisoning, alkalinizing the urine speeds up the excretion of weak acids (salicylates, phenobarbital).

sections.title: 7. Oxidation and reduction of organic compounds

blocks.text: In organic chemistry **oxidation** is the addition of oxygen to a molecule or the removal of hydrogen, and **reduction** is the reverse. In the body these reactions are catalyzed by **dehydrogenases**; the hydrogen carriers are NAD^+^, NADP^+^ and FAD.

items: Primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid: CH~3~CH~2~OH → CH~3~CHO → CH~3~COOH.
Secondary alcohol → ketone: CH~3~CH(OH)CH~3~ → CH~3~COCH~3~ (acetone).
Lactate ⇄ pyruvate (lactate dehydrogenase, NAD^+^/NADH).
Thiols are oxidized to disulfides: 2R−SH → R−S−S−R (cysteine → cystine, disulfide bridges in proteins).

parts.text: In the liver, ethanol is oxidized by **alcohol dehydrogenase** to acetaldehyde and then by **aldehyde dehydrogenase** to acetic acid. Accumulation of acetaldehyde causes facial flushing, nausea and palpitations — **disulfiram** blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, produces exactly this state, and is used to treat alcoholism.

blocks.text: **Biotransformation of drugs and foreign substances.** In the liver **cytochrome P450** enzymes oxidize fat-soluble substances (hydroxylation, dealkylation) and introduce a polar group (phase I). Then glucuronic acid, sulfate or glutathione is attached to this group (phase II — conjugation), and the substance becomes water-soluble and is excreted in urine or bile. In some cases the oxidation product is more toxic than the parent compound.

blocks.text: **Crown ethers** are cyclic polyethers containing repeating −CH~2~−CH~2~−O− units. They were synthesized in 1967 by C. Pedersen (Nobel Prize in 1987 together with D. Cram and J.-M. Lehn). The oxygen atoms inside the ring surround a metal cation like a “crown” and form a strong complex.

blocks.label: Figure 9.2
blocks.caption: The complex of 18-crown-6 with the K^+^ ion: six oxygen atoms hold the cation in the ring cavity (skeletal formula, diagram).

items: **Selective binding:** the ring cavity must match the size of the cation: 12-crown-4 — Li^+^, 15-crown-5 — Na^+^, 18-crown-6 — K^+^.

**Ionophore action:** because the complex is hydrophobic on the outside, it carries the cation across a lipid membrane. Natural ionophores — the antibiotics **valinomycin** (K^+^) and **monensin** (Na^+^) — work on this principle and disturb the ion balance of the bacterial membrane.

**Prospects in medicine:** antimicrobial and antitumor effects are being studied; they are used in drug delivery, binding heavy metals and radionuclides, and making ion-selective electrodes (for measuring blood K^+^). Because crown ethers themselves are toxic, they are not yet widely used as clinical drugs.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A patient drank illegally sold “alcohol”. After 18 hours his vision became blurred and he had abdominal pain; blood pH 7.10, HCO~3~^−^ = 9 mmol/L.
cases.ask: What poisoning is suspected? Explain the chemical mechanism and the principle of treatment.
cases.answer: Methanol poisoning. Methanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase to **formaldehyde** and then by aldehyde dehydrogenase to **formic acid**. Formic acid causes severe metabolic acidosis and damages the mitochondria of the optic nerve (blindness). The delayed onset of symptoms is due to the time needed to form the metabolites. Treatment: **fomepizole** or ethanol (they occupy alcohol dehydrogenase competitively and stop methanol oxidation), sodium bicarbonate, hemodialysis, folate.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: Levodopa (L-DOPA) is used to treat Parkinson’s disease; its D-enantiomer is ineffective.
cases.ask: Why do the enantiomers of one substance act differently in the body?
cases.answer: Enzymes, receptors and transport proteins are **chiral** structures built from L-amino acids; they bind the substrate at three points and, like a “hand in a glove”, recognize only one enantiomer. L-DOPA crosses the blood–brain barrier via the amino acid transporter and is converted to dopamine by L-aromatic amino acid decarboxylase; the D-form is not a substrate of this enzyme. That is why the drug is produced as the active enantiomer.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: In severe salicylate (pK~a~ ≈ 3) poisoning, the patient was given sodium bicarbonate and the urine pH was raised to 7.5–8.0.
cases.ask: Why does this measure speed up the excretion of salicylates?
cases.answer: Mainly the **un-ionized** molecule is reabsorbed across the membrane of the renal tubules. In alkaline urine the weak acid passes almost completely into the anion (the salicylate ion); the anion cannot cross the membrane and is “trapped” in the urine (ion trapping). As a result reabsorption decreases and excretion increases several-fold. This shows the medical significance of acidity.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: After physical exercise a substance with the structure CH~3~−CH(OH)−COOH accumulates in muscle.
cases.ask: Give the trivial and IUPAC names of the substance. How many stereoisomers can it exist as, and which one is formed in the body?
cases.answer: This is **lactic acid**, IUPAC name **2-hydroxypropanoic acid**. The C-2 atom has four different substituents (H, OH, CH~3~, COOH) — it is a **chiral center**, so there are two enantiomers: L- and D-lactic acid (2^1^ = 2). In human muscle lactate dehydrogenase forms only **L-lactate**; D-lactate is formed by some intestinal bacteria and can cause D-lactic acidosis in intestinal diseases.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: A patient with lymphoma is being treated with cyclophosphamide. Two weeks later the white blood cell count fell sharply and the patient’s hair began to fall out.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanism of action of the drug from the point of view of the type of organic reaction. Why do the side effects occur in these particular tissues?
cases.answer: Cyclophosphamide is activated in the liver to form a strong **electrophile** — an alkylating metabolite. It attaches to the nucleophilic **N7** atom of guanine in DNA by **nucleophilic substitution (S~N~)**; its two functional groups “cross-link” the two strands and replication stops. The drug acts most strongly on **rapidly dividing** cells whose DNA is replicated often: tumor, bone marrow (leukopenia), hair follicles (alopecia), intestinal epithelium.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: A 55-year-old man who smokes 2 packs of cigarettes a day has been diagnosed with lung cancer. Tobacco smoke contains benzo[a]pyrene — a fused aromatic hydrocarbon that is itself relatively chemically inert.
cases.ask: How does an inert hydrocarbon become a carcinogen? What type of reaction leads to DNA damage?
cases.answer: Benzo[a]pyrene is oxidized in the liver and lungs by **cytochrome P450** enzymes into a **diol epoxide** (metabolic activation). The strained epoxide ring is a strong **electrophile**: it reacts with the nucleophilic amino group of guanine in DNA by **nucleophilic substitution**, forming a covalent adduct. During replication a wrong nucleotide is inserted at this site — a mutation (often in the p53 gene) and a tumor develops. In addition, tobacco smoke induces P450, so some drugs are broken down faster in smokers.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: The task was to write all the structural isomers corresponding to the molecular formula C~4~H~10~O.
cases.ask: How many isomers are there? Classify and name them. Which one is chiral?
cases.answer: There are **7** in total. **Alcohols (4):** butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol. **Ethers (3):** diethyl ether, methyl propyl ether, methyl isopropyl ether. Chain, position and functional-group isomerism occur here. The C-2 atom of **butan-2-ol** has four different substituents (H, OH, CH~3~, C~2~H~5~) — it is chiral and exists as two enantiomers.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: The porphyrin ring of heme has 18 conjugated π-electrons, while cyclooctatetraene has 8 π-electrons.
cases.ask: According to Hückel’s rule, which system is aromatic? How does the aromaticity of porphyrin show itself in its properties?
cases.answer: Hückel’s rule: an aromatic system has **4n + 2** π-electrons. 18 = 4 · 4 + 2 (n = 4) — porphyrin is **aromatic**; 8 = 4n (n = 2) — cyclooctatetraene is not aromatic (it is not even flat). The large conjugated aromatic system of porphyrin makes it stable and causes strong absorption of visible light — that is why heme and blood are **red**, and chlorophyll is green.

topics.title: Poly- and heterofunctional compounds as metabolites and drugs

goals.text: To teach the student the structure, properties and significance as metabolites and drugs of compounds that contain identical (polyfunctional) or different (heterofunctional) functional groups — polyhydric alcohols and phenols, polyamines, dicarboxylic acids, amino alcohols and catecholamines, hydroxy-, amino- and keto acids, and heterofunctional derivatives of benzene.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concept of poly- and heterofunctional compounds;
the properties and medical significance of glycerol, ethylene glycol, xylitol, sorbitol and mannitol;
polyhydric phenols and the quinone–hydroquinone redox system;
the significance of polyamines and dicarboxylic acids (oxalate, malonate, succinate, fumarate);
amino alcohols (ethanolamine, choline, acetylcholine) and catecholamines;
hydroxy and keto acids, and derivatives of salicylic and p-aminobenzoic acid.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify the functional groups of a compound and classify it;
explain the detection of polyhydric alcohols by the qualitative reaction with Cu(OH)~2~;
write interconversions of metabolites (lactate ⇄ pyruvate, succinate → fumarate);
link the chemical structure of drugs (aspirin, paracetamol, sulfonamides) with their mechanism of action.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: A **polyfunctional** compound has identical functional groups (glycerol — 3 OH), a **heterofunctional** compound has different groups (lactic acid — OH and COOH; amino acids — NH~2~ and COOH). Most metabolites are heterofunctional.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The series of dicarboxylic acids (C~2~–C~5~): **“Oh My, Such Good”** — oxalic, malonic, succinic, glutaric.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Ethylene glycol** (antifreeze) tastes sweet but is highly toxic: in the body it is oxidized to glycolaldehyde, glyoxylic and **oxalic** acid — severe acidosis and kidney damage by calcium oxalate crystals result. The antidote is fomepizole or ethanol.

blocks.text: Alcohols are mono-, di- or polyhydric by the number of hydroxyl groups, and primary, secondary or tertiary by the carbon that bears the OH. In **aromatic alcohols** the OH is attached not to the benzene ring but to a side chain (benzyl alcohol C~6~H~5~CH~2~OH); compounds with OH attached directly to the ring are called **phenols**.

items: **Ethanol** — its 70 % solution denatures proteins and has the strongest antiseptic action (96 % alcohol coagulates protein on the surface of microbes so quickly that it does not penetrate inside).
**Benzyl alcohol** — a preservative in injection solutions; toxic in newborns (“gasping syndrome”).
**Menthol** (a cyclic alcohol) — a cooling and distracting effect (validol, ointments).

blocks.title: Table 10.1. Polyhydric alcohols
head: Substance
Formula
Significance
rows: part of lipids (triglycerides, phospholipids); base for ointments and suppositories, laxative
sugar substitute; accumulates in the lens and nerves and contributes to diabetic complications

blocks.text: **Qualitative reaction:** in an alkaline medium polyhydric alcohols dissolve the Cu(OH)~2~ precipitate and form a **deep blue** complex (copper glycerate) — monohydric alcohols do not give this reaction. This is due to the increased acidity of neighboring OH groups and the formation of a chelate.

**Polyhydric phenols:** pyrocatechol (1,2-dihydroxybenzene), resorcinol (1,3-), hydroquinone (1,4-). The pyrocatechol residue is part of the **catecholamines**. Hydroquinone is easily oxidized to **quinone** and reduced back again: this reversible system is the basis of the work of **ubiquinone (coenzyme Q)** in the respiratory chain.

parts.text: In diabetes mellitus, during hyperglycemia glucose is reduced to sorbitol by **aldose reductase**. Sorbitol crosses membranes poorly and accumulates in the cells of the lens, nerves and kidneys, causing osmotic swelling — one mechanism of the development of **cataract, neuropathy and nephropathy**.

blocks.text: **Polyamines** are compounds with two or more amino groups. They are formed by decarboxylation of amino acids: **putrescine** H~2~N(CH~2~)~4~NH~2~ from ornithine and **cadaverine** H~2~N(CH~2~)~5~NH~2~ from lysine; **spermidine** and **spermine** are synthesized from putrescine.

items: At physiological pH polyamines carry several positive charges and bind to negatively charged **DNA and RNA**, stabilizing their structure; they are needed for cell division and growth.
Polyamines increase in rapidly dividing tissues and in **tumors**; inhibitors of the enzyme of their synthesis (ornithine decarboxylase), such as eflornithine, are used in treatment.
Putrescine and cadaverine are foul-smelling “cadaveric poisons” (ptomaines) formed when proteins putrefy.

blocks.title: Table 10.2. Dicarboxylic acids and their significance
head: Acid
Formula

rows: calcium oxalate stones; a product of ethylene glycol poisoning
a **competitive inhibitor** of succinate dehydrogenase; malonyl-CoA — in fatty acid synthesis
a Krebs cycle metabolite; FAD-dependent dehydrogenation turns it into fumarate
a metabolite of the Krebs and urea cycles
lysine and tryptophan metabolism; glutaric aciduria

blocks.text: **The succinate dehydrogenase reaction:** HOOC−CH~2~−CH~2~−COOH + FAD → HOOC−CH=CH−COOH + FADH~2~. Because malonate resembles succinate in structure, it binds to the active site of the enzyme but is not dehydrogenated — the classic example of **competitive inhibition**.

**The behavior of dicarboxylic acids on heating** depends on their structure: oxalic and malonic acids **decarboxylate** on heating (HOOC−CH~2~−COOH → CH~3~COOH + CO~2~), while succinic and glutaric acids lose water to form five- and six-membered **cyclic anhydrides**. Biological decarboxylation (of pyruvate, α-ketoglutarate) is also made easier by a carbonyl or carboxyl group next to the carboxyl group.

parts.text: Foods rich in **oxalate** are sorrel, spinach, rhubarb, cocoa and tea. Normally calcium binds oxalate in the intestinal lumen; when fats are poorly absorbed (intestinal diseases), calcium binds to fatty acids instead, much free oxalate is absorbed, and **enteric hyperoxaluria** and kidney stones develop.

items: **Ethanolamine (colamine)** HO−CH~2~−CH~2~−NH~2~ — part of the phospholipid phosphatidylethanolamine (cephalin); formed by decarboxylation of serine.
**Choline** HO−CH~2~−CH~2~−N^+^(CH~3~)~3~ — part of phosphatidylcholine (lecithin); protects the liver from fatty degeneration (a lipotropic factor).
**Acetylcholine** CH~3~CO−O−CH~2~CH~2~−N^+^(CH~3~)~3~ — the ester of choline, the mediator of parasympathetic and neuromuscular synapses; it is rapidly broken down by acetylcholinesterase.

blocks.text: **Catecholamines** are biogenic amines containing a pyrocatechol ring and an aminoethyl chain: **dopamine**, **norepinephrine** (noradrenaline) and **epinephrine** (adrenaline). They are synthesized from tyrosine: tyrosine → DOPA → dopamine → norepinephrine → epinephrine.

blocks.label: Figure 10.1
blocks.caption: Catecholamines: dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine — amino alcohols containing a pyrocatechol ring, a β-hydroxyl and an amino group (structural formulas drawn with RDKit).

parts.text: Organophosphate insecticides (chlorophos, malathion) and nerve agents irreversibly phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates: miosis, salivation, bronchospasm, convulsions. Treatment is **atropine** (an M-cholinergic blocker) and **oximes** that reactivate the enzyme. **Epinephrine** is the drug of first choice in anaphylactic shock.

blocks.text: **Biogenic amines** are formed by the **decarboxylation** of amino acids: R−CH(NH~2~)−COOH → R−CH~2~−NH~2~ + CO~2~. The reaction is catalyzed by decarboxylases that depend on pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B~6~). Biogenic amines have strong physiological effects at low concentrations — they are neurotransmitters, hormones and local regulators.

rows: allergic and inflammatory reactions, gastric juice secretion
mood, sleep, gut motility, vascular tone
the main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the CNS

blocks.text: The action of biogenic amines must be stopped quickly. They are oxidatively deaminated by **monoamine oxidase** (MAO) (R−CH~2~−NH~2~ → R−CHO + NH~3~), and catecholamines are in addition methylated by **catechol-O-methyltransferase** (COMT). The aldehydes formed are oxidized to acids and excreted in the urine (vanillylmandelic acid is the main catecholamine metabolite).

parts.text: **The “cheese reaction”:** if a patient taking MAO inhibitors (some antidepressants) eats tyramine-rich food (aged cheese, smoked meat, wine, soy sauce), tyramine is not broken down in the intestine and liver. It displaces noradrenaline from nerve endings — a **hypertensive crisis** develops. That is why such patients are advised to follow a special diet.

head: Group

Significance

product of anaerobic glycolysis (lactate); Krebs cycle; a ketone body; citrate — an anticoagulant (blood preservation)

blocks.text: Important reactions of heterofunctional acids: **lactate ⇄ pyruvate** (lactate dehydrogenase, NAD^+^/NADH); **pyruvate → acetyl-CoA + CO~2~** (oxidative decarboxylation); **decarboxylation of β-keto acids**: acetoacetate → acetone + CO~2~ (the smell of acetone on the breath in diabetes); **transamination**: amino acid + keto acid ⇄ new keto acid + new amino acid.

parts.text: Citrate binds Ca^2+^ ions (a chelate) and stops blood clotting — **sodium citrate** is used as an anticoagulant in stored blood and laboratory tubes. When blood with much citrate is transfused rapidly, hypocalcemia may develop — calcium preparations are given.

blocks.text: **Ketone bodies** are three substances formed in the liver from acetyl-CoA: **acetoacetate** (a β-keto acid), **β-hydroxybutyrate** (a β-hydroxy acid) and **acetone** (a product of the spontaneous decarboxylation of acetoacetate). In starvation, a carbohydrate-free diet and insulin deficiency, fatty acids are oxidized intensively, acetyl-CoA is not fully used in the Krebs cycle and is converted into ketone bodies.

items: The liver **does not use** ketone bodies (it lacks the enzyme that activates them) — it releases them into the blood.
The heart and skeletal muscles, the renal cortex and, in prolonged starvation, the **brain** use ketone bodies as an energy source.
Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are strong acids (pK~a~ 3.6 and 4.7): when produced in large amounts they consume the bicarbonate buffer and cause **ketoacidosis**.
Acetone is volatile and hardly metabolized — it is exhaled through the lungs, and the breath smells of **“rotten apples”**.

parts.text: **Paracetamol poisoning:** in a large dose part of the drug is converted in the liver into the toxic metabolite **NAPQI**; once glutathione (a thiol) is used up, NAPQI damages the proteins of hepatocytes. The antidote is **N-acetylcysteine**, which restores the glutathione supply. This clearly shows the protective role of the thiol group.

blocks.text: Structure and action: salicylates and sulfonamides

**Aspirin** transfers an acetyl group to the serine hydroxyl in the active site of cyclooxygenase (COX) — the enzyme is **irreversibly** inactivated. Platelets have no nucleus and cannot synthesize new enzyme, so a single small dose (75–100 mg) stops **thromboxane** synthesis for the whole life of the platelet (≈ 7–10 days) — the prevention of cardiovascular disease is based on this.

**Sulfonamides and trimethoprim** block two successive steps of folate synthesis: a sulfonamide, as a competitor of PABA, blocks dihydropteroate synthase, and trimethoprim blocks dihydrofolate reductase. Together (co-trimoxazole) they act **synergistically**. Humans obtain folate from food and do not have this enzyme — this is the basis of the drugs’ selective action.

parts.text: **Aspirin is not given** to children under 16 during a viral infection (influenza, chickenpox) — it can cause **Reye syndrome** (acute liver failure and cerebral edema). In children, paracetamol or ibuprofen is used to lower fever.

skills.title: Skill: detecting polyhydric alcohols (the Cu(OH)~2~ reaction)

items: Put 2 drops of CuSO~4~ and 1 mL of 10 % NaOH into a test tube — a light blue precipitate of Cu(OH)~2~ forms.
Prepare two tubes: add glycerol to one and ethanol to the other.
Shake and observe: in the tube with glycerol the precipitate dissolves and a deep blue solution forms.
In the tube with ethanol there is no change (a monohydric alcohol).
Conclusion: neighboring OH groups form a chelate complex of copper.

Determine the relative position of the groups (α, β, γ or ortho, meta, para).

Link the significance of the substance as a metabolite or drug with this structure.

skills.title: Skill: detecting ketone bodies in urine (Legal’s test)

items: Pour 1–2 mL of urine into a test tube.
Add 2–3 drops of freshly prepared 5 % sodium nitroprusside solution and 0.5 mL of 10 % NaOH — a red color appears.
Add a few drops of glacial acetic acid: the red color due to creatinine disappears, while if ketone bodies are present a **red-violet** color persists and intensifies.
Grade the result with “+” signs or compare the test-strip color with the scale.
Interpret a positive result together with the patient’s glucose level and clinical condition.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A car-repair shop worker drank antifreeze by mistake. A few hours later he appeared drunk, and then metabolic acidosis (pH 7.15) developed; many crystals were found in the urine, and urine output decreased.
cases.ask: Explain the chemical basis of the poisoning. What crystals were found in the urine, and what is the treatment?
cases.answer: The **ethylene glycol** in antifreeze is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase to glycolaldehyde → glycolic acid → glyoxylic acid → **oxalic acid**. The acids cause acidosis; oxalate forms poorly soluble **calcium oxalate** crystals with Ca^2+^ and damages the renal tubules (acute kidney injury). Treatment: **fomepizole** or ethanol (they occupy alcohol dehydrogenase competitively), sodium bicarbonate, hemodialysis.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: After working with an organophosphate insecticide, a gardener was brought in with constricted pupils, heavy salivation and sweating, shortness of breath and muscle twitching.
cases.ask: What is the biochemical cause of the symptoms? Which drugs are given?
cases.answer: The organophosphate irreversibly phosphorylates the serine in the active site of **acetylcholinesterase**. Acetylcholine is not broken down and accumulates in the synapses, constantly stimulating muscarinic (miosis, salivation, bronchospasm) and nicotinic (muscle twitching, then paralysis) receptors. Treatment: **atropine** (blocks M-cholinergic receptors) in large doses, **oximes** that reactivate the enzyme (pralidoxime), respiratory support.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient took 15 g of paracetamol within 1 day for a headache. At first there are no symptoms except nausea.
cases.ask: What is the danger? Explain the chemical mechanism and the action of the antidote.
cases.answer: The danger is severe liver damage (fulminant hepatitis). At normal doses paracetamol is conjugated with glucuronic and sulfuric acids and excreted; at large doses these pathways become saturated and much toxic **NAPQI** is formed via cytochrome P450. NAPQI is normally neutralized by the SH group of **glutathione**; once glutathione is used up, it binds to hepatocyte proteins and causes necrosis (symptoms appear after 1–3 days). **N-acetylcysteine**, as a source of cysteine, restores glutathione synthesis; the earlier it is given, the more effective it is.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: A teenager with type 1 diabetes mellitus missed his insulin injections. He has nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and deep, noisy breathing; his breath smells fruity. Glucose 24 mmol/L, blood β-hydroxybutyrate 5.2 mmol/L.
cases.ask: Why have the ketone bodies increased? How do they cause acidosis? What is the smell of the breath due to?
cases.answer: Without insulin, cells cannot use glucose and lipolysis increases in adipose tissue; β-oxidation of fatty acids in the liver produces much **acetyl-CoA**, which is converted into ketone bodies. β-Hydroxybutyrate 5.2 mmol/L (> 3) — **diabetic ketoacidosis**. Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are strong organic acids; they release H^+^, consume the bicarbonate buffer and cause metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap. The deep Kussmaul breathing is respiratory compensation. **Acetone**, formed by the decarboxylation of acetoacetate, is volatile and is exhaled.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: A woman taking an MAO inhibitor for depression ate aged cheese and drank red wine at a party. An hour later she had a severe headache and palpitations, and her blood pressure was 220/120 mm Hg.
cases.ask: Explain the biochemical mechanism of the hypertensive crisis.
cases.answer: Cheese and wine contain much **tyramine** — the decarboxylation product of tyrosine. Normally tyramine is broken down by **MAO** in the intestinal wall and liver. When MAO is blocked, tyramine enters the blood and displaces **noradrenaline** from sympathetic nerve endings; since noradrenaline is also not broken down by MAO, its effect is enhanced — vessels constrict and blood pressure rises sharply. This is called the “cheese reaction”; the patient should have been warned in advance to avoid tyramine-containing foods.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: Several customers who ate canned tuna at a restaurant developed flushing of the face and neck, headache, a burning sensation in the mouth and itching 20–30 minutes later. None of them had a history of allergy.
cases.ask: What is the chemical cause of the condition? How is it treated?
cases.answer: This is **scombroid poisoning**: in improperly stored fish, **histidine** is converted into **histamine** by bacterial decarboxylase. Histamine is not destroyed by cooking; eaten in large amounts it causes an allergy-like reaction (vasodilation, flushing, itching), but without an immune mechanism. Treatment is with **antihistamines** (H~1~ blockers, and H~2~ blockers if needed); severe cases are treated like an allergic reaction.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: A patient with a urinary tract infection was prescribed co-trimoxazole (sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim).
cases.ask: What is the biochemical basis for giving the two drugs together? Why do they hardly affect human cells?
cases.answer: Bacteria synthesize folic acid themselves. **Sulfamethoxazole** is a structural analog of PABA: it competitively takes the place of PABA at dihydropteroate synthase. **Trimethoprim** blocks the bacterial dihydrofolate reductase at the next step. Because two successive steps of one pathway are blocked, the effect is **synergistic** and bactericidal, and resistance develops slowly. Humans take folate ready-made from food (they have no dihydropteroate synthase), and trimethoprim acts on human reductase 50 000 times more weakly — this is the basis of the selective action.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A patient with Parkinson disease has been found to lack dopamine, but for treatment levodopa together with carbidopa was prescribed instead of dopamine itself.
cases.ask: Why is dopamine itself not given? What role does carbidopa play?
cases.answer: Dopamine is a polar amine that is positively charged at physiological pH; it **does not cross the blood–brain barrier**. Levodopa (L-DOPA) is an amino acid that enters the brain via the neutral amino acid transporter and is converted there into **dopamine** by DOPA decarboxylase. However, much of the levodopa is decarboxylated in the periphery before it reaches the brain, causing nausea and arrhythmias. **Carbidopa** blocks peripheral decarboxylase but does not itself enter the brain — the fraction of levodopa reaching the brain increases, and the dose can be reduced.

topics.title: Heterocyclic compounds as metabolites and drugs

goals.text: To give the student knowledge of the structure, aromaticity and acid–base properties of five- and six-membered heterocycles with one or more heteroatoms and of bicyclic (fused) heterocycles, and of the important metabolites, vitamins, neurotransmitters and drugs derived from them.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the classification and naming of heterocycles;
the pyrrole, furan, thiophene, imidazole, pyrazole and thiazole rings and their derivatives;
the pyridine, pyrimidine and piperidine rings and their derivatives;
bicyclic systems such as indole, purine, quinoline and pteridine;
the difference between pyrrole and pyridine nitrogen, and lactim–lactam tautomerism;
heterocyclic neurotransmitters (serotonin, histamine, melatonin) and important drugs.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify and name the heterocycle in the formula of a drug or metabolite;
assess the acid–base properties of a heterocycle from the type of nitrogen;
explain the clinical significance of purine metabolism and uric acid formation;
justify the action of antimetabolite drugs (5-fluorouracil, methotrexate, allopurinol) by their similarity to natural metabolites.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Pyrrole nitrogen** gives its lone pair to the aromatic sextet — it has almost no basic properties, and N−H is a weak acid. **Pyridine nitrogen** keeps its pair — a weak base (pK~a~ ≈ 5.2). **Imidazole** has both types of nitrogen — amphoteric, pK~a~ ≈ 7 (hence the buffer property of histidine).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“CUT the PY”**: Cytosine, Uracil, Thymine are PYrimidines; **“PURe As Gold”**: PURines are Adenine and Guanine. The reverse rule: the word **pyrimidine** is long but the ring is single; **purine** is short but has two rings.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Many powerful drugs are **antimetabolites** designed to resemble natural heterocyclic metabolites: 5-fluorouracil (uracil), 6-mercaptopurine (hypoxanthine), methotrexate (folate), allopurinol (hypoxanthine). They also act on rapidly dividing healthy cells — blood counts and mucous membranes must be monitored.

sections.title: 1. Classification of heterocyclic compounds. Five-membered rings with one heteroatom

blocks.text: **Heterocyclic compounds** are cyclic compounds whose ring contains, besides carbon, atoms of other elements (**heteroatoms**: N, O, S). They are classified by ring size (five-, six-membered), by the number and type of heteroatoms, and by the number of rings (monocyclic, fused). More than half of all drugs are heterocyclic compounds.

blocks.title: Table 11.1. Five-membered heterocycles with one heteroatom
head: Ring
Heteroatom
Important derivatives
rows: porphyrins (heme, chlorophyll), corrin (vitamin B~12~), bile pigments (bilirubin)
nitrofural, furazolidone (antimicrobial drugs); ribose and deoxyribose in the furanose form

blocks.text: Pyrrole is aromatic: the π-electrons of the four carbons and the lone pair of nitrogen together form a sextet of 6 π-electrons. That is why the nitrogen pair of pyrrole gives no basic properties, while N−H is a weak acid (pK~a~ ≈ 17). Four pyrrole rings joined by methine bridges form the **porphine** ring.

parts.text: When heme is broken down, the pyrrole ring system opens and a linear tetrapyrrole — **bilirubin** — is formed. Its accumulation in the blood causes **jaundice**. **Phototherapy**, used to treat neonatal jaundice, converts bilirubin under blue light into water-soluble isomers and speeds up its excretion.

blocks.text: **Porphyrin synthesis** starts from glycine and succinyl-CoA: first **δ-aminolevulinic acid** (δ-ALA) is formed, then two molecules of δ-ALA give **porphobilinogen**, which has a pyrrole ring; four porphobilinogen molecules combine to give the porphyrin ring, and finally Fe^2+^ is inserted into it to form heme.

parts.text: **Porphyrias** are inherited deficiencies of the enzymes of heme synthesis. Intermediate products accumulate: in acute porphyria δ-ALA and porphobilinogen increase in the urine, causing severe abdominal pain and neurological disturbances (the urine darkens in light); in cutaneous porphyrias porphyrins accumulate in the skin and cause blisters on exposure to sunlight.

blocks.title: Table 11.2. Azoles and their derivatives

Heteroatoms

rows: thiamine (vitamin B~1~); the thiazolidine ring — in penicillins

blocks.text: **Imidazole** has both types of nitrogen: one of the pyrrole type (N−H) and one of the pyridine type (basic). The pK~a~ of the imidazolium ion is ≈ 7.0 — very close to physiological pH. That is why histidine residues serve as **buffer** groups of proteins and as **proton carriers** in the active site of many enzymes (for example, serine proteases).

blocks.text: The nitrogen of **pyridine** does not give its lone pair to the aromatic system — it is a weak base (pK~a~ of the pyridinium ion ≈ 5.2). The pyridine ring is π-electron deficient: electrophilic substitution is difficult and nucleophilic attack is easy. **The active part of NAD^+^** is the pyridine ring of nicotinamide: it accepts a hydride ion (H^−^) and is reduced to NADH.

**Barbiturates** are derivatives of barbituric acid (pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione); they have hypnotic and anticonvulsant effects (phenobarbital). Barbituric acid itself is not pharmacologically active — two substituents at position 5 make it lipophilic and active.

sections.title: 4. Six-membered heterocycles containing oxygen and sulfur

blocks.text: **Pyran** is a six-membered ring with one oxygen atom. Its saturated form occurs in the **pyranose** form of monosaccharides (glucopyranose). **Benzopyran** (chromene) and **chromane**, fused with a benzene ring, form the basis of many plant substances and drugs.

parts.text: **Warfarin** is structurally similar to vitamin K; it blocks the enzyme that regenerates the active form of vitamin K (vitamin K epoxide reductase). As a result, less of the active forms of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X is formed in the liver. Treatment is monitored by the **INR**; if an overdose causes bleeding, **vitamin K** is given as the antidote.

blocks.text: **Lactim–lactam tautomerism:** in purines and pyrimidines with hydroxy groups (uracil, thymine, guanine, uric acid) a proton moves between oxygen and nitrogen: −N=C(OH)− ⇄ −NH−C(=O)−. Under physiological conditions the **lactam** (oxo) form predominates; it is this form that ensures correct hydrogen bonding between the bases in DNA. The rare lactim form can cause pairing errors — **point mutations**.

parts.text: **Uric acid** is the end product of purine metabolism in humans (xanthine oxidase: hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid). Its solubility is low (pK~a~ ≈ 5.4); when it rises in the blood, sodium urate crystals deposit in the joints — **gout**. **Allopurinol** (an isomer of hypoxanthine) blocks xanthine oxidase and reduces uric acid formation.

blocks.text: **Alkaloids** are natural compounds, found mainly in plants, that contain a nitrogen heterocycle, have basic properties and exert strong physiological effects. In the plant they occur as salts with acids; in medicine their water-soluble salts are mostly used (atropine sulfate, morphine hydrochloride). Alkaloids are classified by the type of heterocycle.

blocks.text: **General precipitating reagents for alkaloids:** Dragendorff’s reagent (potassium bismuth iodide — orange precipitate), Mayer’s reagent (potassium mercuric iodide — white precipitate), tannin and picric acid. They form poorly soluble salts and complexes with the nitrogen atom of alkaloids — used to detect alkaloids in forensic toxicology.

parts.text: Many alkaloids have a narrow margin between therapeutic and toxic doses. **Tannin** (strongly brewed tea) forms insoluble compounds with them — that is why tannin solution was formerly used for gastric lavage in oral alkaloid poisoning.

items: **Serotonin** (5-hydroxytryptamine) — from tryptophan by hydroxylation and decarboxylation; mood, sleep, appetite, gut motility, platelet aggregation. Drugs that block its reuptake (fluoxetine, sertraline) are used to treat depression.
**Melatonin** — formed from serotonin in the pineal gland (at night); it regulates the circadian rhythm.

**Histamine** — from the decarboxylation of histidine; allergic reactions (H~1~), HCl secretion in the stomach (H~2~), a mediator. H~1~ blockers (loratadine) and H~2~ blockers (famotidine) are widely used.
**Caffeine** and **theophylline** (methylxanthines) — block adenosine receptors and inhibit phosphodiesterase: they stimulate the CNS and dilate the bronchi.

blocks.text: Chemistry of heterocyclic antibiotics

The four-membered **β-lactam ring** of β-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) is highly strained and reactive. It acylates the serine hydroxyl of the bacterial transpeptidase (penicillin-binding protein) and inactivates it irreversibly — cell wall synthesis stops. Many bacteria hydrolyze this ring with the enzyme **β-lactamase** and become resistant; **clavulanic acid** and **tazobactam** bind β-lactamase and protect the antibiotic.

parts.text: **Fluoroquinolones** (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) and **tetracyclines** form insoluble chelates with Ca^2+^, Mg^2+^, Al^3+^ and Fe^2+^. If they are taken with milk, yogurt, antacids, iron or calcium preparations, their absorption falls several-fold. That is why these drugs are taken at least 2 hours apart from them.

skills.title: Skill: identifying the heterocycle from a formula

items: Pick out all rings in the formula and count the atoms in each.

If it is fused, say which rings it consists of (for example, benzene + pyrrole = indole).

skills.title: Skill: assessing the basicity of a nitrogen atom

items: Determine whether the lone pair of the nitrogen is part of the aromatic sextet.
If it is (pyrrole type), the basicity is very low.
If it is not (pyridine type), it is a weak base (pK~a~ ≈ 5).
A nitrogen in a saturated ring (piperidine, pyrrolidine) is a strong base like an aliphatic amine (pK~a~ ≈ 11).
If both types of nitrogen are present (imidazole), it is amphoteric, pK~a~ ≈ 7.

skills.title: Skill: detecting alkaloids with general precipitating reagents

items: Pour 1 mL of the test solution (for example, a solution of an alkaloid salt) into each of 2–3 test tubes and acidify with 1–2 drops of dilute HCl.
Add 2 drops of Dragendorff’s reagent to the first tube — an orange or reddish precipitate indicates an alkaloid.
Add Mayer’s reagent to the second tube — a white or yellowish precipitate is observed.
Add tannin solution to the third tube — a whitish-yellow precipitate forms.
As a control, perform the same reactions with distilled water and compare the results; confirm a positive result with specific reactions to identify the particular alkaloid.

cases.text: A 52-year-old man woke up at night after an evening of meat dishes and beer with sudden pain, redness and swelling of the big toe joint. Blood uric acid is 560 μmol/L (normal in men 200–420).
cases.ask: What is the diagnosis? Explain it in terms of the chemical structure of uric acid and state the principle of long-term treatment.
cases.answer: **An attack of gout.** Uric acid is a purine derivative (2,6,8-trioxopurine), the end product of purine metabolism; the purines in meat and beer increase its formation, and alcohol reduces its renal excretion. Uric acid is poorly soluble; when its blood level exceeds the saturation limit, sodium urate crystals deposit in a joint (especially the cooler peripheral joints) and cause inflammation. Long-term treatment: **allopurinol** or febuxostat (block xanthine oxidase), limiting purine-rich food and alcohol, plenty of fluids.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: A patient with colon cancer was prescribed a course of 5-fluorouracil. During treatment mouth ulcers (stomatitis), diarrhea and a fall in white blood cells were observed.
cases.ask: How does the drug work, and why do these adverse effects occur?
cases.answer: 5-Fluorouracil is an antimetabolite of uracil (F instead of H at position 5). In the body it is converted to fluorodeoxyuridylate, which irreversibly blocks **thymidylate synthase**: thymidine nucleotides are not formed, DNA synthesis stops and rapidly dividing tumor cells die. However, rapidly dividing healthy cells — the mucosa of the mouth and intestine and the bone marrow — are also damaged: stomatitis, diarrhea and leukopenia are due to this. Blood counts are monitored during treatment.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A student with allergic rhinitis complains in spring of a blocked nose, sneezing and watery eyes. Loratadine was recommended.
cases.ask: What is the chemical mediator of the symptoms, how is it formed, and how does the drug act?
cases.answer: The mediator is **histamine**: it is formed in mast cells by decarboxylation of histidine (histidine decarboxylase) and released on contact with the allergen. It is a biogenic amine with an imidazole ring that stimulates **H~1~ receptors**, increasing vascular permeability (swelling, nasal congestion) and irritating sensory nerves (itching, sneezing). Loratadine is an H~1~ receptor blocker; it prevents histamine from binding to the receptor.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: Two children ate jimsonweed seeds in a field. Their skin is red and dry, the pupils are dilated and do not react to light, there is tachycardia, the temperature is raised, and the children are agitated and delirious.
cases.ask: Poisoning with which substances? To which group of alkaloids do they belong and how do they act?
cases.answer: Jimsonweed contains **tropane alkaloids** — **atropine** and scopolamine. They are competitive antagonists of acetylcholine at M-cholinergic receptors: secretion of the salivary and sweat glands stops (dry skin, hyperthermia), the pupils dilate, the heart rate increases, and there is CNS excitation and delirium. Help: gastric lavage, activated charcoal (binds alkaloids well), cooling; in severe cases the cholinesterase inhibitor **physostigmine** increases acetylcholine and overcomes the blockade.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: A patient with a prosthetic heart valve takes warfarin (the INR should be 2.5–3.5). After he began to eat large amounts of spinach and cabbage, the INR fell to 1.6.
cases.ask: Why did the INR fall? Explain the relationship between warfarin and vitamin K.
cases.answer: Warfarin is a coumarin derivative; it blocks **vitamin K epoxide reductase**, which reactivates vitamin K, and reduces the formation of active clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). Spinach and cabbage contain a lot of **vitamin K**: the increased dietary vitamin K partly overcomes the effect of warfarin, more clotting factors are formed and the INR falls — the risk of thrombosis increases. The patient is advised to eat vitamin K-rich foods in a steady amount without sharp changes.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: A patient with a urinary tract infection took ciprofloxacin tablets every day with a glass of milk and, for heartburn, together with an antacid. After three days the fever and symptoms persist.
cases.ask: Explain the chemical reason for the failure of treatment. What would you advise?
cases.answer: The **keto and carboxyl groups** in the fluoroquinolone molecule form a stable, insoluble **chelate** with Ca^2+^ (milk), Mg^2+^ and Al^3+^ (antacid) ions. The chelate is not absorbed in the intestine — the antibiotic concentration in blood and urine does not reach an effective level. Advice: take ciprofloxacin with water, and take dairy products, antacids, iron and calcium preparations at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after the drug.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: A child’s otitis was treated with amoxicillin without effect. Culture showed a β-lactamase-producing Haemophilus. The doctor switched to amoxicillin + clavulanic acid.
cases.ask: Why did amoxicillin not work? How does clavulanic acid help?
cases.answer: The active part of amoxicillin is the strained **β-lactam ring**: it acylates transpeptidase and stops cell wall synthesis. The bacterial enzyme **β-lactamase** hydrolyzes and opens this ring — the antibiotic becomes inactive. **Clavulanic acid** also has a β-lactam structure: it binds β-lactamase irreversibly and inactivates it (a “suicide” inhibitor), so amoxicillin is preserved and acts.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A young man found unconscious has slow, shallow breathing (6 breaths per minute), pinpoint pupils and injection marks on his arm.
cases.ask: Poisoning with substances of which alkaloid group is suspected? How does the antidote act?
cases.answer: The clinical triad — coma, respiratory depression, **miosis** — is typical of poisoning with **opioids** (morphine, heroin — morphinan derivatives with an isoquinoline skeleton). They stimulate μ-opioid receptors in the brain and depress the respiratory center. The antidote is **naloxone**: its structure is close to that of morphine, but it does not activate the receptor; as a **competitive antagonist** it displaces the opioid from the receptor, and breathing recovers within minutes. Naloxone acts briefly, so the patient is kept under observation and the dose is repeated if necessary.
