topics.title: Carbohydrates. Structure and properties of monosaccharides. Di-, homo- and heteropolysaccharides

goals.text: To teach the student the main carbohydrates of food, the classification, stereoisomerism and cyclic forms of monosaccharides, their chemical properties (oxidation and reduction), their derivatives used in medicine, reducing and non-reducing disaccharides, and the structure and significance of homopolysaccharides and the heteropolysaccharides of connective tissue.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the classification of monosaccharides as aldoses/ketoses and by the number of carbons, the D/L series and epimers;
the pyranose and furanose forms, α- and β-anomers, and mutarotation;
the oxidation (aldonic and glucuronic acids) and reduction (sorbitol) of monosaccharides;
reducing (maltose, lactose, cellobiose) and non-reducing (sucrose, trehalose) disaccharides;
the structure of starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin and pectin;
the significance of hyaluronic acid, chondroitin sulfates and heparin.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write the Fischer and Haworth formulas of glucose;
explain the detection of reducing carbohydrates by the Trommer and Fehling reactions;
determine the composition of a disaccharide and the type of glycosidic bond;
explain the chemical basis of disorders of carbohydrate metabolism (lactase deficiency, diabetes mellitus).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: A disaccharide is **reducing** if one of its monosaccharides still has a **free hemiacetal (glycosidic) hydroxyl** (maltose, lactose). In sucrose both anomeric hydroxyls are used up in the bond — it is **non-reducing**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Disaccharides: **“Mal-Glu-Glu, Lac-Gal-Glu, Suc-Glu-Fru”** — maltose = glucose + glucose, lactose = galactose + glucose, sucrose = glucose + fructose.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Humans have no enzyme that breaks down **cellulose** (β-1,4-glycosidase): it is not digested, but as **dietary fiber** it stimulates gut motility and binds cholesterol and bile acids. Starch, on the other hand, has α-1,4 bonds and is easily broken down by amylase.

blocks.text: **Carbohydrates** are polyhydroxycarbonyl compounds and their derivatives; most have the general formula C~n~(H~2~O)~m~. They provide ≈ 50–60 % of dietary energy and are the main energy source; the brain and red blood cells use almost only glucose.

blocks.title: Table 12.1. The main carbohydrates of food
head: Carbohydrate
Type
Source

items: **By the carbonyl group:** aldoses (aldehyde group — glucose, galactose, ribose) and ketoses (keto group — fructose, ribulose).
**By the number of carbons:** trioses (glyceraldehyde, dihydroxyacetone), tetroses, pentoses (ribose, deoxyribose, xylose), hexoses (glucose, galactose, mannose, fructose).
**The D and L series** are defined by the configuration of the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group (C-5 in hexoses); natural monosaccharides belong mainly to the **D series**.

blocks.text: An aldohexose has 4 chiral carbons, so 2^4^ = 16 stereoisomers (8 pairs of enantiomers) exist. Diastereomers that differ at only one chiral center are called **epimers**: D-glucose and D-galactose are **C-4** epimers, D-glucose and D-mannose are **C-2** epimers.

In solution monosaccharides exist mainly in **cyclic** form: the carbonyl group forms an intramolecular hemiacetal with a hydroxyl of the same molecule. A six-membered ring is a **pyranose**, a five-membered one a **furanose**. The new chiral center that appears when the ring closes (C-1) is the **anomeric** center: OH below the plane of the ring (in the Haworth formula) — the **α**-anomer, above — the **β**-anomer.

blocks.label: Figure 12.1
blocks.caption: The α- and β-pyranose forms of D-glucose (Haworth projection): they differ only in the position of the hydroxyl at C-1 and interconvert in solution through the open form (diagram).

blocks.text: **Mutarotation** is the change of the specific rotation of a freshly prepared solution with time until it reaches an equilibrium value: α-D-glucose (+112°) and β-D-glucose (+18.7°) interconvert in solution through the open form; at equilibrium ≈ 36 % α and 64 % β (+52.5°).

rows: forms conjugates with bilirubin, drugs and toxins in the liver (detoxification)

blocks.text: **Reducing property:** aldoses (and ketoses in an alkaline medium) reduce alkaline Cu^2+^ solution: in the **Trommer** and **Fehling** reactions light blue Cu(OH)~2~ turns on heating into a brick-red precipitate of Cu~2~O; with **Tollens’** reagent a “silver mirror” forms.

items: **Amino sugars:** glucosamine, galactosamine (their N-acetyl derivatives are part of heteropolysaccharides); glucosamine is used as a chondroprotector in joint diseases.
**Deoxy sugars:** 2-deoxyribose — part of DNA.
**Ascorbic acid** (vitamin C) — a lactone derivative of glucose, a strong reducing agent; needed for collagen synthesis and iron absorption.
**Lactulose** (galactose + fructose) — a synthetic disaccharide not absorbed in the intestine: a laxative that reduces ammonia absorption in hepatic encephalopathy.

parts.text: In diabetes mellitus blood glucose combines non-enzymatically with the amino groups of proteins (**glycation**): glycated hemoglobin **HbA~1c~** reflects the mean glycemia over the last 2–3 months (normal < 5.7 %, in diabetes ≥ 6.5 %). Blood glucose is now measured by the glucose oxidase method; the Trommer and Fehling reactions are historical methods.

sections.title: 4. Qualitative reactions of carbohydrates and non-enzymatic glycation

blocks.text: Under the action of strong acids monosaccharides lose water to form **furfural** (from pentoses) or **hydroxymethylfurfural** (from hexoses); these give colored compounds with phenols. Many qualitative reactions are based on this.

blocks.title: Table 12.3. Qualitative reactions of carbohydrates
head: Reaction
Reagent
Result
What it detects

blocks.text: **Enolization in alkaline medium:** glucose, mannose and fructose can interconvert through a common **enediol** intermediate (the Lobry de Bruyn–van Ekenstein rearrangement). That is why fructose also shows reducing properties in an alkaline medium. In the body the isomerization of glucose 6-phosphate to fructose 6-phosphate (phosphoglucose isomerase) proceeds through such an enediol.

**Non-enzymatic glycation (the Maillard reaction):** the aldehyde group of the open form of glucose forms a **Schiff base** with the free amino group of a protein (nucleophilic addition followed by loss of water); this rearranges into a stable **Amadori product** (this is exactly how HbA~1c~ is formed). Later, with oxidation and cross-linking, irreversible **advanced glycation end products** accumulate.

parts.text: Advanced glycation end products cross-link collagen and basement membranes, making them stiff and brittle; they take part in the late complications of diabetes mellitus — retinopathy, nephropathy, atherosclerosis and cataract. The browning and aroma of food during cooking are also the result of the Maillard reaction.

blocks.text: **Formation of maltose from starch:** salivary and pancreatic **α-amylase** hydrolyzes the internal α-1,4-glycosidic bonds of starch; maltose, maltotriose and α-dextrins are formed, and these are broken down to glucose in the intestine by **maltase** and isomaltase. In theory, maltose can be obtained from two molecules of α-D-glucopyranose by removing water (from the hydroxyls at C-1 of the first and C-4 of the second).

parts.text: **Lactase deficiency** (lactose intolerance): lactose is not broken down in the small intestine, passes into the large intestine and is fermented by bacteria — bloating, pain and diarrhea. In most adults (especially in Asian peoples) lactase activity falls with age. Treatment: lactose-free milk, fermented dairy products, lactase preparations.

blocks.text: Monosaccharides pass into enterocytes: glucose and galactose **together with Na^+^** (the SGLT1 transporter, secondary active transport), and fructose by facilitated diffusion through GLUT5. All of them leave the cell for the blood through GLUT2. The absorption of glucose together with Na^+^ is the basis of **oral rehydration solutions**: glucose increases the absorption of Na^+^ and, with it, of water.

blocks.text: In the clinic glucose is determined by the **glucose oxidase** method: glucose + O~2~ → gluconolactone + H~2~O~2~; the H~2~O~2~ formed oxidizes a chromogen with the help of **peroxidase** to give a colored product whose absorbance is proportional to the glucose content. Glucometers measure the electric current of the same reaction.

parts.text: **Hypoglycemia** (glucose < 3.0 mmol/L) — sweating, tremor, hunger, behavior changes, and in severe cases seizures and coma. Because the brain depends entirely on glucose, this condition is dangerous even faster than hyperglycemia: if the patient is conscious — a sweet drink or 15–20 g of glucose; if unconscious — 40 % glucose intravenously or glucagon intramuscularly.

blocks.text: Each glucose residue of cellulose has three free OH groups; they form esters with acids.

items: **Cellulose acetates** (with acetic anhydride): acetate rayon, films, formerly hemodialysis membranes; tablet coatings (cellulose acetate phthalate — an enteric coating).

**Cellulose nitrates** (with nitric acid): the lightly nitrated form is **pyroxylin (colloxylin)**; its solution in ether–alcohol is **collodion**, used as a sealing coat for small wounds and surgical sutures. The fully nitrated form is explosive guncotton.
**Methyl- and carboxymethylcellulose** — thickeners and artificial tears in eye drops, ointments and tablets.

blocks.text: **Glycosaminoglycans** (mucopolysaccharides) are heteropolysaccharides built from repeating disaccharide units (uronic acid + amino sugar) and strongly negatively charged because of their sulfate and carboxyl groups. They bind a lot of water and form the gel medium of connective tissue.

Disaccharide unit

rows: synovial fluid, vitreous body, skin; lubrication, shock absorption
mast cells; an **anticoagulant** — activates antithrombin III

parts.text: **Heparin** is the most negatively charged biomolecule; it binds to antithrombin III and rapidly inactivates thrombin and factor Xa — it is used to treat thrombosis and embolism; its antidote is the positively charged **protamine sulfate**. When lysosomal enzymes are deficient, glycosaminoglycans accumulate and hereditary **mucopolysaccharidoses** (Hurler and Hunter syndromes) develop.

blocks.text: Glycoproteins and blood group antigens

Short, branched oligosaccharide chains covalently attached to proteins form **glycoproteins** (immunoglobulins, hormones, membrane receptors, mucus — mucins). Oligosaccharides are attached to the protein through the hydroxyl of serine or threonine (**O-glycosidic** bond) or through the amide nitrogen of asparagine (**N-glycosidic** bond). In **proteoglycans**, by contrast, long glycosaminoglycan chains are attached to a protein core and carbohydrate makes up most of the mass.

parts.text: The A and B antigens differ by only **one monosaccharide** — the type of glycosyltransferase that attaches it to the H chain is inherited. Even such a small chemical difference causes a strong immune response and severe hemolysis in an incompatible blood transfusion.

skills.title: Skill: detecting reducing carbohydrates (the Trommer reaction)

items: Put 1 mL of carbohydrate solution and 1 mL of 10 % NaOH into a test tube.
Add 5 % CuSO~4~ dropwise — the Cu(OH)~2~ that first forms dissolves on shaking and a blue solution forms (a property of polyhydric alcohols).
Heat the upper part of the solution.
If the carbohydrate is reducing, a yellow CuOH and then a brick-red Cu~2~O precipitate forms.
With sucrose the reaction is negative; if you first hydrolyze it with acid and test again, it is positive.

skills.title: Skill: analyzing the formula of a disaccharide

items: Identify the two monosaccharide residues in the molecule (pyranose or furanose; glucose, galactose or fructose).
Find the carbons that form the glycosidic bond (1→4, 1→2, 1→1).
Determine the anomeric configuration of the bond (α or β).
Check whether a free hemiacetal OH is present — if so, the sugar is reducing.
Name the disaccharide and say which enzyme breaks it down.

skills.title: Skill: detecting ketoses with Seliwanoff’s reaction

items: Pour 1 mL each of glucose and fructose solutions (or the test sample) into two test tubes.
Add 1 mL of Seliwanoff’s reagent (resorcinol in HCl) to each.
Place the tubes in a boiling water bath at the same time and observe the color after 1 minute.
Fructose gives a **red** color within 30–60 seconds; glucose gives only a weak pink color after prolonged heating (as it isomerizes to fructose).
Conclude from the result whether the sample contains a ketose (for example, the fructose in honey).

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A 22-year-old student complains of bloating, pain and loose stools 1–2 hours after drinking milk. He tolerates kefir and cheese well.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain the chemical mechanism.
cases.answer: **Lactase deficiency** (lactose intolerance). Lactose is a disaccharide of galactose and glucose with a β-1,4-glycosidic bond; it is broken down by **lactase** (β-galactosidase) of the small intestinal mucosa. When the enzyme is lacking, lactose is not absorbed; being osmotically active, it draws water into the intestine (diarrhea), and in the large intestine bacteria ferment it into gases (H~2~, CO~2~, CH~4~) and acids (bloating, pain). In kefir and cheese lactose has been partly broken down by bacteria, so they are well tolerated.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: A patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus has fasting glucose of 8.2 mmol/L and HbA~1c~ = 8.5 %.
cases.ask: How is HbA~1c~ formed and what does it show? Which property of carbohydrates is involved?
cases.answer: The open (aldehyde) form of glucose condenses non-enzymatically with the amino group of the N-terminal valine of the hemoglobin β-chain (Schiff base → Amadori rearrangement) — **glycated hemoglobin** is formed. The reaction depends on blood glucose concentration and time, and since red cells live ≈ 120 days, HbA~1c~ reflects the mean glycemia over the last 2–3 months. 8.5 % means the diabetes is poorly controlled (the target is usually < 7 %); treatment should be adjusted.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient with deep vein thrombosis was given heparin. A few hours later signs of bleeding appeared.
cases.ask: Explain the chemical structure and mechanism of action of heparin. How does the antidote act?
cases.answer: Heparin is a highly sulfated glycosaminoglycan built from glucosamine and uronic acids; it is the most strongly negatively charged biomolecule. Through a specific pentasaccharide sequence it binds to **antithrombin III** and increases a thousandfold the rate at which antithrombin inactivates thrombin and factor Xa — blood clotting slows. The antidote is the positively charged protein **protamine sulfate**: it forms an electrostatic complex with heparin and neutralizes it.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: A two-week-old infant vomits after breastfeeding and does not gain weight; there is jaundice and an enlarged liver, and a cataract is beginning to form. The urine contains a reducing substance, but the glucose oxidase test is negative.
cases.ask: Which inherited disease is suspected? What is the chemical cause of the cataract? How is it treated?
cases.answer: **Galactosemia** — deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase. Galactose formed from milk lactose cannot be converted into glucose and accumulates. The reducing substance in the urine is **galactose** (glucose oxidase does not act on it, so the test is negative). In the lens, aldose reductase reduces galactose to **galactitol**; it cannot leave the cell and draws in water osmotically — the lens swells and becomes cloudy (**cataract**). Galactose 1-phosphate is toxic to the liver and brain. Treatment: immediately exclude milk and lactose completely and switch to soy-based formulas.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: An overweight 45-year-old woman underwent a glucose tolerance test: fasting venous plasma glucose 6.4 mmol/L, 2 hours after drinking 75 g of glucose 9.2 mmol/L.
cases.ask: Interpret the result. What is recommended for the patient?
cases.answer: Fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L — **impaired fasting glucose** (6.1–6.9); the 2-hour value 9.2 mmol/L — **impaired glucose tolerance** (7.8–11.0). This is **prediabetes**: the criteria for diabetes mellitus (≥ 7.0 and ≥ 11.1) are not yet met, but the risk of developing type 2 diabetes in future is high. Recommendations: lose 5–7 % of body weight, physical activity (≥ 150 minutes a week), limit rapidly absorbed carbohydrates, check HbA~1c~ and monitor yearly.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: A patient on insulin skipped dinner and lost consciousness. The glucometer shows 1.9 mmol/L. The ambulance team gave 40 mL of 40 % glucose intravenously.
cases.ask: How much glucose was given to the patient? Why is hypoglycemia dangerous faster than hyperglycemia?
cases.answer: m = 0.40 · 40 = **16 g** of glucose (the usual dose for quickly correcting hypoglycemia is 15–20 g). The brain cannot store glucose itself and gets its energy almost exclusively from blood glucose; if glucose falls sharply, neuronal function is disturbed within minutes — seizures and coma, and if it lasts long, irreversible damage. After regaining consciousness the patient is given food with slowly absorbed carbohydrates, because the action of insulin is still continuing.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: A patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus was prescribed dapagliflozin (an SGLT2 inhibitor). A week later the urine test showed a lot of glucose, while blood glucose had decreased.
cases.ask: Explain the appearance of glucose in the urine. Is this a worrying sign?
cases.answer: In the proximal renal tubules glucose is reabsorbed from the filtrate mainly through the **SGLT2** transporter (together with Na^+^); normally there is almost no glucose in the urine. Glucose passes into the urine only when its blood level exceeds ≈ 10 mmol/L (the **renal threshold**). Dapagliflozin blocks SGLT2 and excretes glucose in the urine even below the threshold — this is the **expected effect** of the drug and its mechanism for lowering blood glucose. However, glucose in the urine increases the risk of genitourinary infections, so attention is paid to hygiene.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A laboratory assistant was given two unlabeled bottles: one contains glucose solution and the other diluted honey (mainly fructose). Both gave a positive Trommer reaction.
cases.ask: How can they be distinguished? Why is Trommer’s reaction positive for both?
cases.answer: Glucose is an aldose and fructose a ketose, but in an alkaline medium fructose isomerizes to an aldose via an **enediol**, so both reduce Cu^2+^ — Trommer’s reaction does not distinguish them. **Seliwanoff’s reaction** is used to tell them apart: on heating with resorcinol and HCl, fructose (honey) gives a red color within 1 minute, while glucose does not. In addition, a glucose oxidase test strip is positive only for glucose.

topics.title: Amino acids. Peptides and proteins. Structure and properties

goals.text: To teach the student the concept of biopolymers and bioregulators, the structure, classification, physicochemical properties and biological functions of α-amino acids, the peptide bond and biologically active peptides, the primary and spatial structure, classification, functions, molecular mass and colloidal properties of proteins, and to develop the skills of performing qualitative reactions of amino acids and determining serum protein by the biuret method.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the structure of proteinogenic amino acids, their classification by side chain, and the essential amino acids;
the amphoteric nature of amino acids, the zwitterion and the isoelectric point;
the chemical reactions and biological functions of amino acids;
the structure of the peptide bond and biologically active peptides;
the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure of proteins;
the classification, functions, molecular mass and colloidal properties of proteins.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: perform the qualitative reactions of amino acids and proteins and explain the result;
determine and interpret total serum protein by the biuret method;
carry out protein precipitation experiments (salting out, denaturation);
calculate the isoelectric point of an amino acid and determine its charge at a given pH.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In blood serum **total protein is 65–85 g/L** and albumin 35–50 g/L. The **biuret reaction** detects at least two peptide bonds — that is why free amino acids and dipeptides do not give this reaction.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The 8 essential amino acids for adults: **“Very Lazy Ice Tigers Meet Lions For Tea”** — Valine, Leucine, Isoleucine, Threonine, Methionine, Lysine, Phenylalanine, Tryptophan; histidine is also essential for children.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: At its **isoelectric point** (pI) a protein has zero net charge, its lowest solubility and does not move in an electric field. Protein precipitation and separation by electrophoresis are based on this very property.

sections.title: 1. The concept of biopolymers and bioregulators

blocks.text: **Biopolymers** are natural high-molecular compounds built from monomers: **proteins** (monomer — α-amino acids), **nucleic acids** (nucleotides) and **polysaccharides** (monosaccharides). **Bioregulators** are substances that control the activity of cells and organs in small amounts: hormones, neurotransmitters, vitamins, regulatory peptides, prostaglandins.

sections.title: 2. Structure and classification of α-amino acids

blocks.text: Proteins contain 20 **α-amino acids**; their general formula is H~2~N−CH(R)−COOH. In all of them except glycine (R = H) the α-carbon is chiral, and natural amino acids belong to the **L series**. They differ from each other only in the side chain (R).

blocks.title: Table 13.1. Classification of amino acids by side-chain polarity
head: Group
Amino acids
rows: glycine, alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, proline, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan
serine, threonine, cysteine, tyrosine, asparagine, glutamine

blocks.text: Amino acids that are not synthesized in the body and must come with food are called **essential**: in adults — valine, leucine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, lysine, phenylalanine, tryptophan; in the growing organism — also histidine (and partly arginine).

sections.title: 3. Physical and chemical properties of amino acids

blocks.text: Amino acids are **amphoteric**: −COOH gives acidic and −NH~2~ basic properties. In solution and in crystals they exist as a **zwitterion** (dipolar ion): ^+^H~3~N−CH(R)−COO^−^. That is why they dissolve well in water, melt (decompose) at high temperature and dissolve poorly in organic solvents.

The **isoelectric point** (pI) is the pH at which an amino acid has zero net charge: for neutral amino acids pI = (pK~1~ + pK~2~) / 2. For example, for glycine pK~1~ (COOH) = 2.34 and pK~2~ (NH~3~^+^) = 9.60, so pI = 5.97. At pH < pI the amino acid is positively charged, at pH > pI negatively charged.

blocks.caption: Dependence of the net charge of glycine on pH: a cation in an acidic medium, a zwitterion (charge 0) at pI = 5.97, an anion in an alkaline medium (calculated with the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation).

sections.title: 4. Amino acid metabolism, nitrogen balance and ammonia

blocks.text: Proteins are constantly renewed in the body: in adults ≈ 300–400 g of protein is broken down and resynthesized daily. The nitrogen of the released amino acids is excreted mainly as **urea** in the urine. The ratio of nitrogen taken in with food to nitrogen excreted is called the **nitrogen balance** (≈ 16 % of protein mass is nitrogen, i.e. nitrogen · 6.25 = protein).

items: **Positive nitrogen balance** (intake > output): growth, pregnancy, recovery from illness, increase in muscle mass.
**Nitrogen equilibrium** (intake = output): healthy adults.
**Negative nitrogen balance** (output > intake): starvation, burns, severe infections and operations, cancer cachexia, treatment with glucocorticoids.

blocks.text: **Transaminases** are enzymes that transfer an amino group from an amino acid to a keto acid (coenzyme — pyridoxal phosphate): **ALT** (alanine aminotransferase, mainly in the liver) and **AST** (aspartate aminotransferase, in the liver, heart and skeletal muscles). When cells are damaged they are released into the blood; the normal level of each is up to ≈ 40 U/L. The **De Ritis ratio** (AST / ALT ≈ 1.3) helps to estimate the site of damage: < 1 in viral hepatitis (ALT predominates), > 2 in alcoholic liver damage and myocardial infarction.

**Ammonia** (NH~3~), formed in the deamination of amino acids, is a potent neurotoxin: in the brain it binds α-ketoglutarate into glutamate and glutamine, slowing the Krebs cycle, and causes osmotic swelling of astrocytes. In the liver ammonia is converted into harmless urea in the **urea cycle**: 2NH~3~ + CO~2~ → (NH~2~)~2~CO + H~2~O (ATP is consumed in the cycle). The normal blood ammonia level is < 50 µmol/L.

parts.text: **Hepatic encephalopathy:** in cirrhosis or acute liver failure urea synthesis decreases and ammonia accumulates in the blood — drowsiness, confusion, “flapping” tremor (asterixis), coma. **Lactulose** is used in treatment: in the colon it is broken down by bacteria into lactic and acetic acids and acidifies the contents; NH~3~ becomes ionized to NH~4~^+^, is not absorbed into the blood and is excreted in the feces.

items: **Building blocks** of proteins and peptides.
**Neurotransmitters:** glutamate (excitatory), glycine and GABA (inhibitory).

**Precursors of biologically active substances:** tyrosine → catecholamines, thyroxine, melanin; tryptophan → serotonin, melatonin, nicotinic acid; histidine → histamine; glycine → heme, creatine, glutathione, bile acid conjugates; arginine → nitric oxide (NO), urea.
**An energy source** (through gluconeogenesis in starvation) and nitrogen carriers (glutamine, alanine).

parts.text: **Phenylketonuria** is an inherited deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase: phenylalanine is not converted to tyrosine, accumulates in the blood and disturbs brain development (intellectual disability). Newborns are screened; treatment is a phenylalanine-restricted diet. **Homocystinuria, alkaptonuria and maple syrup urine disease** are other aminoacidopathies.

blocks.text: The −CO−NH− bond formed with loss of water between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another is called the **peptide bond**. It has partial double-bond character (C−N mesomerism), so it is **planar** and rotation around it is restricted; in peptides it is mostly in the **trans** configuration. A peptide chain has a free amino group at its start (**N-terminus**) and a free carboxyl at its end (**C-terminus**).

sections.title: 7. Primary and spatial structure of proteins

blocks.title: Table 13.4. Levels of protein structure
head: Level
Essence

rows: the sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain
folding of parts of the chain into an α-helix (3.6 residues per turn) or a β-sheet

blocks.text: The spatial structure of a protein, and hence its function, is **determined by its primary structure** (C. Anfinsen’s experiment). An example of quaternary structure is **hemoglobin** (2 α- and 2 β-chains, α~2~β~2~): the protomers interact when binding oxygen (cooperativity).

parts.text: **Sickle cell anemia:** at position 6 of the hemoglobin β-chain **glutamate is replaced by valine** (HbS). This single change in the primary structure creates a hydrophobic “sticky” patch in the deoxy form; the molecules polymerize, red cells take a sickle shape and block the capillaries. In **prion diseases**, on the other hand, the primary structure of the protein is unchanged, but its secondary structure switches from α-helix to β-sheet.

sections.title: 8. Fibrous proteins and disorders of protein folding

blocks.text: **Collagen** is the most abundant protein in the body (≈ 25–30 % of total protein). Each of its chains contains repeating **Gly−X−Y** (X is often proline, Y — hydroxyproline or hydroxylysine); three left-handed chains form a right-handed **triple helix**. Only the smallest amino acid — glycine — fits inside the helix. The enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine require **ascorbic acid** (vitamin C) and Fe^2+^; the hydrogen bonds of hydroxyproline stabilize the triple helix.

Correct protein folding in the cell is assisted by **chaperones** (heat shock proteins). Misfolded proteins are usually degraded in the proteasome; if they accumulate and form insoluble β-sheet fibrils, **amyloidosis** and neurodegenerative diseases develop.

sections.title: 9. Classification, functions, molecular mass and colloidal properties of proteins

items: **Simple proteins** — consist only of amino acids: albumins, globulins, histones, protamines, scleroproteins (collagen, keratin, elastin).
**Conjugated proteins** — protein + prosthetic group: glycoproteins, lipoproteins, nucleoproteins, chromoproteins (hemoglobin), phosphoproteins (casein), metalloproteins (ferritin).

**Functions:** catalytic (enzymes), structural (collagen), transport (hemoglobin, albumin), protective (immunoglobulins, fibrinogen), regulatory (insulin), contractile (actin, myosin), receptor, storage (ferritin, casein).

blocks.text: The molecular mass of proteins ranges from ≈ 6 000 (insulin ≈ 5 800) to several million daltons. It is determined by **ultracentrifugation** (sedimentation constant, Svedberg unit), **gel filtration**, **electrophoresis** (with sodium dodecyl sulfate) and mass spectrometry.

Protein solutions are **lyophilic colloids**: the particles are 1–100 nm, they give the Tyndall effect, do not pass through membranes and are highly viscous. Their stability has two factors — **charge** and the **hydration shell**. Removing them precipitates the protein: **salting out** (ammonium sulfate — reversible; globulins precipitate at half saturation, albumins at full saturation), **isoelectric precipitation**, **denaturation** (heating, strong acids and alkalis, heavy-metal salts, alcohol — the spatial structure is destroyed, often irreversibly).

parts.text: In poisoning with salts of heavy metals (mercury, lead, copper), **milk** or **egg white** is given as emergency first aid: the proteins form insoluble compounds with the metal ions, bind them in the gut and reduce their absorption; then the stomach is washed out.

blocks.text: Nutritional value of proteins and protein deficiency

The daily protein requirement for adults is **0.8–1 g/kg** body weight; in pregnancy, lactation, periods of growth, severe illness and burns it rises to 1.2–2 g/kg. Animal proteins (eggs, milk, meat, fish) contain all the essential amino acids and are well digested; plant proteins are low in some of them (lysine in cereals, methionine in legumes).

parts.text: In kwashiorkor the liver cannot export triglycerides because it lacks protein (apoproteins) for lipoprotein synthesis — a **fatty liver** develops. The edema is explained by the fall in albumin and oncotic pressure (topic 2).

blocks.text: Determination of total serum protein by the biuret method

**Principle of the method:** in an alkaline medium the peptide bonds of protein form a violet complex with Cu^2+^; the color intensity (optical density at 540 nm) is proportional to the protein concentration.

items: Prepare three tubes: test (0.1 mL serum), standard (0.1 mL of 70 g/L albumin solution) and blank (0.1 mL of 0.9 % NaCl).
Add 5 mL of biuret reagent to each and mix.
Leave at room temperature for 30 minutes.
Measure the optical density against the blank on a photoelectric colorimeter with a green filter (540 nm).
Calculate: C = (E~test~ / E~standard~) · C~standard~ (g/L).

parts.text: **Hypoproteinemia** (< 65 g/L) occurs in starvation, liver cirrhosis (reduced synthesis), nephrotic syndrome and burns (loss); oncotic pressure falls and **edema** appears. **Hyperproteinemia** (> 85 g/L) occurs in dehydration (relative) and multiple myeloma (paraprotein).

blocks.text: Study of the physicochemical properties of proteins

items: **Salting out:** add an equal volume of saturated (NH~4~)~2~SO~4~ to egg white solution — the globulins precipitate; saturate the filtrate with crystalline salt — the albumins precipitate. When water is added the precipitate dissolves again (a reversible process).
**Denaturation by heating:** boil the protein solution — turbidity and clots appear; they do not dissolve on cooling.
**Precipitation by heavy metals:** add drops of CuSO~4~ or lead acetate to the protein solution — a precipitate forms.
**With acids:** carefully layer protein solution over conc. HNO~3~ — a white ring forms at the boundary (Heller’s test — detection of protein in urine).

sections.title: 11. Production of artificial protein foods and future prospects (independent work)

blocks.text: Population growth and the ecological burden of livestock farming (land and water use, greenhouse gases) have made the search for **alternative protein sources** urgent.

parts.text: The completeness of a protein is judged by its **essential amino acid** content and its digestibility. Eating different plant proteins together (for example, cereals + legumes) makes up for each other’s missing amino acids.

skills.title: Skill: determining total protein by the biuret method

items: Label the tubes: test, standard, blank.
Measure 0.1 mL of the corresponding sample into each accurately with a micropipette.
Add 5 mL of biuret reagent, mix and wait 30 minutes.
Zero the photometer with the blank and measure E~test~ and E~standard~ at 540 nm.
Calculate with the formula C = (E~test~ / E~standard~) · 70 g/L and compare with the normal range (65–85 g/L).

skills.title: Skill: determining the isoelectric point and charge of an amino acid

items: Write the pK values of all ionizable groups of the amino acid.
For a neutral amino acid pI = (pK~COOH~ + pK~NH3+~) / 2.
For an acidic amino acid pI is the mean of the two acidic pK values; for a basic one, the mean of the two basic pK values.
If the given pH < pI, the net charge is positive; if pH > pI, negative.
Determine toward which electrode it moves in electrophoresis.

skills.title: Skill: calculating nitrogen balance

items: Determine the daily protein intake (from the diet or parenteral nutrition).
Calculate the nitrogen intake: N~in~ = protein (g) / 6.25.
Determine the urea nitrogen (g) in the daily urine and add ≈ 4 g for other losses through urine, feces and skin: N~out~ = urea nitrogen + 4.
Find the nitrogen balance: NB = N~in~ − N~out~.
Assess the result: positive — anabolism, negative — protein catabolism; with a negative balance an increase in dietary protein is planned.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: Serum protein of a patient was determined by the biuret method. For the standard albumin solution (70 g/L) E = 0.35, for the serum E = 0.24. The patient has edema of the legs and face and 6 g of protein in the urine per day.
cases.ask: Calculate the total protein. Explain the mechanism of the edema.
cases.answer: C = (0.24 / 0.35) · 70 = 48 g/L — **hypoproteinemia** (normal 65–85 g/L). Heavy loss of protein (mainly albumin) in the urine is typical of **nephrotic syndrome**. Albumin creates most of the oncotic pressure of plasma; when it falls, water passes from the capillaries into the interstitial space — **oncotic edema** appears.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: The pK values of glutamic acid are: α-COOH 2.19; γ-COOH 4.25; α-NH~3~^+^ 9.67. Electrophoresis is carried out at pH 7.0.
cases.ask: Find the isoelectric point of glutamic acid and say toward which electrode it moves at pH 7.0.
cases.answer: For an acidic amino acid pI is the mean of the pK values of the two acidic groups: pI = (2.19 + 4.25) / 2 = 3.22. pH 7.0 > pI, so glutamate has a net **negative** charge (both carboxyls ionized, the amino group protonated: net charge −1) and moves toward the **anode (+)**.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A chemical plant worker accidentally swallowed some mercury(II) chloride solution. Before the ambulance arrived, a colleague gave him 3 raw egg whites mixed together to drink.
cases.ask: What is the chemical basis of this measure?
cases.answer: Heavy-metal ions such as mercury bind to the SH, carboxyl and imidazole groups of proteins, **denature** them and form insoluble metal–protein compounds (a precipitate). The proteins of egg white (ovalbumin) bind the Hg^2+^ ions in the stomach and reduce their interaction with the proteins of the mucosa and their absorption. Then the stomach is washed out and specific antidotes (unithiol, dimercaprol) are given.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: An elderly man living alone who for a long time ate only bread, potatoes and tea has bleeding, swollen gums, loose teeth, pinpoint hemorrhages in the skin, and small wounds that heal slowly.
cases.ask: Deficiency of which vitamin? Explain the molecular cause of the signs in terms of collagen structure.
cases.answer: This is **scurvy** — **vitamin C** deficiency. Ascorbic acid is required for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases: it keeps the iron of the enzyme in the Fe^2+^ state. Without vitamin C, proline and lysine in collagen chains are not hydroxylated and the hydroxyproline hydrogen bonds do not form — the **triple helix is unstable** and collagen fibers are fragile. As a result the vessel walls weaken (hemorrhages, bleeding gums), the periodontal ligament loosens and wounds do not heal. Treatment — vitamin C and a diet rich in fruit and vegetables.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: Blood tests of two patients: the first has ALT 820 U/L, AST 610 U/L and jaundice; the second has ALT 60 U/L, AST 180 U/L and a history of many years of alcohol use.
cases.ask: Calculate the De Ritis ratio for each patient and assess the nature of the damage.
cases.answer: Patient 1: AST / ALT = 610 / 820 ≈ **0.74** (< 1) — ALT predominates, the cytoplasm of liver cells is massively damaged; this is typical of **acute viral hepatitis**. Patient 2: 180 / 60 = **3** (> 2) — AST predominates; part of AST is located in mitochondria, which alcohol damages, and in addition B~6~ deficiency in alcoholism reduces ALT synthesis — typical of **alcoholic liver damage**. In both cases the diagnosis is confirmed by other tests.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: A patient with severe burns receives 75 g of protein a day by parenteral nutrition. The daily urine contains 18 g of urea nitrogen.
cases.ask: Calculate and assess the nitrogen balance.
cases.answer: N~in~ = 75 / 6.25 = **12 g**. N~out~ = 18 + 4 = **22 g**. Nitrogen balance = 12 − 22 = **−10 g/day** — sharply negative. In burns, stress hormones cause rapid breakdown of muscle proteins, and protein is also lost from the burn surface. Each 1 g of nitrogen corresponds to ≈ 6.25 g of protein or ≈ 30 g of muscle tissue, so the patient is losing ≈ 300 g of muscle a day. The protein intake should be increased to 1.5–2 g/kg.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: A 2-year-old child weaned early from breast milk and fed mainly rice porridge has swollen legs and face, a large abdomen, sparse discolored hair and is apathetic. Blood albumin is 18 g/L.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain the biochemical cause of the edema and the enlarged abdomen.
cases.answer: This is **kwashiorkor** — enough energy (carbohydrate) but a severe lack of protein. The liver cannot synthesize enough albumin — albumin is 18 g/L, the **oncotic pressure has fallen**, and water stays in the tissues — edema and ascites. Because apoproteins are lacking, the liver cannot export triglycerides as lipoproteins — a **fatty liver** enlarges, and the abdomen looks big. Treatment: feeding with milk-based therapeutic formulas, increasing protein and energy gradually, and treating infections.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A patient with liver cirrhosis became drowsy and confused after bleeding from esophageal varices; there is a “flapping” tremor of the hands. Blood ammonia is 140 µmol/L (normal < 50).
cases.ask: How did the bleeding cause the rise in ammonia? How does lactulose help?
cases.answer: Blood in the intestine is a large amount of **protein**: bacteria break it down and produce a lot of **ammonia**. In cirrhosis the liver cannot detoxify ammonia in the urea cycle, and in addition blood bypasses the portal system — ammonia reaches the brain and causes **hepatic encephalopathy**. **Lactulose** is broken down by bacteria in the colon into organic acids, and the contents become acidic: NH~3~ + H^+^ → NH~4~^+^; ionized ammonium is not absorbed into the blood and is excreted in the feces, while the laxative effect of lactulose cleans out the intestine. In addition, an antibiotic that reduces intestinal bacteria (rifaximin) is given.

topics.title: Nucleosides. Nucleotides. Nucleic acids

goals.text: To teach the student the structure and properties of nucleosides and nucleotides, their antimetabolites and nucleoside antibiotics, nucleoside polyphosphates (AMP, ADP, ATP) and high-energy bonds, cyclic nucleotides, nucleotide coenzymes (NAD^+^, NADP^+^, FAD), the polynucleotide chain, the primary and spatial structure of nucleic acids, their hydrolysis, denaturation and renaturation, hybridization, DNA synthesis and the chemical basis of mutations.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the composition of nucleosides and nucleotides, the N-glycosidic and phosphoester bonds and their naming;
the principle of action of nucleoside antimetabolites and antibiotics;
the structure of ATP, high-energy bonds and the function of cAMP and cGMP;
the structure of NAD^+^, NADP^+^ and FAD and their role in oxidation–reduction;
the primary and secondary structure of DNA and RNA and Chargaff’s rules;
the hydrolysis, denaturation and renaturation of nucleic acids and the chemical causes of mutations.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: draw the formula of a nucleotide and write its name;
write the complementary strand from a DNA sequence;
calculate base proportions with Chargaff’s rules;
explain the mechanism of action of mutagens and antimetabolite drugs.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Nucleoside** = nitrogenous base + pentose (N-glycosidic bond); **nucleotide** = nucleoside + phosphate (phosphoester bond). In DNA A–T (2 hydrogen bonds), G–C (3 hydrogen bonds); the strands are **antiparallel** (5′→3′ and 3′→5′).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Chargaff’s rule: **“Apples in the Tree, Car in the Garage”** — A = T, G = C; purines = pyrimidines (A + G = T + C).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: RNA is easily hydrolyzed by alkali (because of the 2′-OH group of ribose), while DNA is resistant to alkali — that is why DNA is the more stable molecule for storing hereditary information. In acid, on the other hand, the **purine bases** are released from DNA first.

sections.title: 1. Structure and properties of nucleosides and nucleotides

blocks.text: A **nucleoside** is a purine or pyrimidine base joined to ribose or 2′-deoxyribose by a **β-N-glycosidic bond**: atom N-9 of purines or N-1 of pyrimidines is bound to atom C-1′ of the pentose. A **nucleotide** is a phosphate ester of a nucleoside (most often at the 5′-OH).

blocks.title: Table 14.1. Naming of nucleosides and nucleotides
head: Base
Ribonucleoside
Deoxyribonucleoside
Nucleotide (5′-monophosphate)

blocks.text: Because of the phosphate residue, nucleotides are **acidic** and negatively charged at physiological pH. The N-glycosidic bond is hydrolyzed in acid (more easily in purines than in pyrimidines). The aromatic rings of the bases absorb ultraviolet light strongly at **260 nm** — the spectrophotometric determination of nucleic acids is based on this.

blocks.title: Table 14.2. Drugs of nucleoside and nucleotide nature
head: Drug
Natural “look-alike”
Mechanism of action
Use
rows: N~3~ instead of 3′-OH — the DNA chain is terminated (reverse transcriptase)
no cyclic pentose — a chain terminator
arabinose instead of ribose — DNA polymerase is blocked
terminates the peptide chain on the ribosome prematurely

parts.text: Many antiviral drugs are **chain terminators**: they are added to DNA as nucleotides, but because they lack the 3′-OH group to which the next nucleotide is attached, chain elongation stops.

sections.title: 3. Nucleoside polyphosphates. High-energy bonds. Cyclic nucleotides

blocks.text: One or two more phosphate residues may be attached to the 5′-phosphate of a nucleotide by **phosphoanhydride** bonds: AMP → ADP → ATP. Bonds whose hydrolysis releases much energy (ΔG°′ < −25 kJ/mol) are called **high-energy (macroergic)** and are shown with the sign “∼”: A−P∼P∼P.

items: ATP + H~2~O → ADP + P~i~; ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ/mol.
ATP + H~2~O → AMP + PP~i~; ΔG°′ = −45.6 kJ/mol (pyrophosphate is then hydrolyzed, making the reaction irreversible).
Reasons for the high energy: mutual repulsion of the negative charges of the phosphate residues, resonance stabilization and stronger hydration of the products.
Other high-energy compounds: GTP, UTP, CTP, creatine phosphate, phosphoenolpyruvate, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, acetyl-CoA.

blocks.label: Figure 14.1
blocks.caption: Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — a nucleotide with two high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds — and cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), a second messenger molecule (structural formulas drawn with RDKit).

blocks.text: **Cyclic nucleotides:** **cAMP** (3′,5′-cyclic AMP) is formed from ATP by **adenylate cyclase** and acts as a **second messenger** that carries the effect of hormones such as epinephrine and glucagon into the cell; it is broken down to AMP by phosphodiesterase. **cGMP** is formed by guanylate cyclase (activated by NO) and relaxes smooth muscle.

parts.text: **Caffeine and theophylline** block phosphodiesterase and slow the breakdown of cAMP (bronchodilation, CNS stimulation). **Sildenafil** blocks type 5 phosphodiesterase, which breaks down cGMP. **Cholera toxin** permanently activates adenylate cyclase: cAMP rises sharply in intestinal cells and Cl^−^ and water are lost — severe diarrhea.

head: Coenzyme
Composition
Function

synthetic reactions (fatty acids, cholesterol), antioxidant defense (NADPH)
complex I of the respiratory chain

blocks.text: The active part of NAD^+^ is atom C-4 of the nicotinamide ring: it accepts a **hydride ion** (H^−^) from the substrate and becomes NADH, while the second proton goes into solution: NAD^+^ + 2H → NADH + H^+^. NADH absorbs light at 340 nm (NAD^+^ does not) — many enzyme activities (ALT, AST, LDH) are measured this way. FAD adds two hydrogen atoms at atoms N-1 and N-5 of the isoalloxazine ring.

sections.title: 5. The polynucleotide chain. Primary and spatial structure of nucleic acids

blocks.text: Nucleotides join through **3′,5′-phosphodiester bonds** to form a polynucleotide chain: the 3′-OH of the pentose of one nucleotide binds to the 5′-phosphate of the next. One end of the chain has a free 5′-phosphate and the other a free 3′-OH; the sequence is written in the **5′→3′** direction. The nucleotide sequence is the **primary structure** of a nucleic acid.

blocks.title: Table 14.4. Differences between DNA and RNA
head: Feature
DNA
RNA
rows: storage and transmission of hereditary information
carrying out the information: mRNA, tRNA, rRNA

blocks.text: **The DNA double helix** (J. Watson and F. Crick, 1953): two **antiparallel** strands are twisted to the right around a common axis; the bases are inside and the phosphate–sugar backbone outside. The bases pair **complementarily**: A–T (2 hydrogen bonds), G–C (3 hydrogen bonds). In the B form there are ≈ 10 base pairs per turn, the pitch is 3.4 nm and the diameter 2 nm. The helix is held by hydrogen bonds and base **stacking** interactions.

parts.text: **Chargaff’s rules:** in DNA A = T and G = C; the number of purines equals the number of pyrimidines. DNA rich in G–C pairs is more stable (three hydrogen bonds) and “melts” at a higher temperature.

blocks.text: **Other forms of DNA and supercoiling.** Besides the B form, a shorter and wider **A form** occurs in a less hydrated medium (RNA–DNA hybrids and double-stranded RNA also have this form), and a left-handed **Z form** occurs in G–C-rich sequences. In the cell, long DNA is further twisted (**supercoiled**) and compacted; the degree of twisting is controlled by **topoisomerases**, which temporarily cut and rejoin the strands.

parts.text: Topoisomerases are important drug targets: **fluoroquinolones** block bacterial DNA gyrase (a type II topoisomerase) and topoisomerase IV; the anticancer **anthracyclines** (doxorubicin) and **etoposide** inhibit human topoisomerase II, and **irinotecan** inhibits topoisomerase I — irreparable breaks remain in the DNA.

sections.title: 6. Hydrolysis of nucleic acids. Denaturation, renaturation and hybridization. DNA synthesis

items: **Acid hydrolysis:** in weak acid the purine bases are released first (apurinic DNA); complete hydrolysis gives nitrogenous bases, pentose and phosphoric acid.
**Alkaline hydrolysis:** RNA is broken down through 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotides into 2′- and 3′-nucleotides; DNA is resistant.
**Enzymatic hydrolysis:** nucleases — DNase, RNase (endo- and exonucleases); **restriction enzymes** cut DNA at specific sequences (genetic engineering).

blocks.text: **Denaturation (“melting”):** heating, alkali or urea break the hydrogen bonds and the double helix separates into two strands; absorbance at 260 nm rises by 30–40 % (the **hyperchromic effect**). The temperature at which half the strands separate is the **melting temperature** (T~m~); it rises with the G–C content. On slow cooling the complementary strands rejoin — **renaturation** (annealing). The joining of complementary strands from different sources is **hybridization** (DNA–DNA, DNA–RNA).

**DNA synthesis (replication)** is **semiconservative**: each new molecule consists of one old and one new strand (the Meselson–Stahl experiment). DNA polymerase synthesizes the new strand only in the **5′→3′** direction, starting from an RNA primer, from deoxynucleoside triphosphates; the lagging strand is made as Okazaki fragments that are joined by ligase.

parts.text: Denaturation and hybridization underlie the **polymerase chain reaction** (PCR): denaturation at 94–95 °C, primer annealing at 50–65 °C, and chain extension at 72 °C by heat-stable Taq polymerase. In 30–35 cycles a DNA fragment is copied billions of times — it is used for infections (COVID-19, tuberculosis, HIV), hereditary diseases and forensic examination.

blocks.text: Hereditary information is expressed in the direction **DNA → RNA → protein** (the central dogma of molecular biology). In **transcription**, RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA complementary to one (template) strand of DNA in the 5′→3′ direction; synthesis starts at a **promoter**. In eukaryotes the primary transcript undergoes **processing**: a “cap” (7-methylguanosine) is added to the 5′ end and a poly(A) tail to the 3′ end, and in **splicing** the introns are cut out and the exons joined.

**Translation** takes place on ribosomes: every three nucleotides of mRNA — a **codon** — specify one amino acid. Amino acids are brought to the ribosome by **tRNA**; the **anticodon** of tRNA pairs complementarily with the mRNA codon. The peptidyl transferase center of the ribosome (rRNA — a ribozyme) forms the peptide bond.

head: Substance
Target

rows: toxin of the death cap mushroom — liver necrosis
protein synthesis stops and the cell dies

parts.text: The selective action of antibiotics is based on the difference in structure between bacterial (70S: 30S + 50S) and eukaryotic (80S: 40S + 60S) ribosomes. Mitochondrial ribosomes resemble bacterial ones — some side effects of antibiotics (for example, the effect of chloramphenicol on bone marrow) are related to this.

blocks.title: Table 14.7. Chemical and physical mutagens
head: Mutagen
Change in DNA
Result
rows: deaminates cytosine to uracil and adenine to hypoxanthine

blocks.text: The chemical causes of mutations are changes in the structure of the bases (deamination, alkylation, oxidation), mispairing due to wrong tautomeric forms (lactim, imino) and physical damage to the strand. The cell has many **repair** systems; inherited defects in them (for example, **xeroderma pigmentosum**) sharply increase the tendency to cancer.

sections.title: 9. Metabolism of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides

blocks.text: Nucleotides are formed in two ways. In **de novo synthesis** the rings are built from simple substances: the purine ring is assembled on activated ribose 5-phosphate (**PRPP**) from glycine, glutamine, aspartate, CO~2~ and folate derivatives, while the pyrimidine ring is first assembled separately (from carbamoyl phosphate and aspartate) and then attached to PRPP. In the **salvage pathway** ready-made bases released from degraded nucleotides are converted back into nucleotides with PRPP (for example, by hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase — HGPRT).

**Purine catabolism:** AMP → IMP → inosine → hypoxanthine → xanthine → **uric acid** (the last two steps are catalyzed by xanthine oxidase). Humans lack the enzyme uricase, so uric acid is the end product. **Pyrimidines**, by contrast, are broken down to the water-soluble β-alanine, β-aminoisobutyric acid, CO~2~ and NH~3~ — they do not accumulate and cause disease.

blocks.title: Table 14.8. Disorders of uric acid metabolism

inherited deficiency of HGPRT — purines are not salvaged

parts.text: **Allopurinol** blocks xanthine oxidase. This enzyme also breaks down the anticancer and immunosuppressive drugs **6-mercaptopurine** and **azathioprine**. If they are given together with allopurinol without reducing their dose, they accumulate in the blood and severely suppress the bone marrow.

skills.title: Skill: writing the complementary strand and the Chargaff calculation

items: Write the given strand in the 5′→3′ direction (for example, 5′-ATGCCGTA-3′).

By Chargaff’s rule: if A = 30 %, then T = 30 %, G + C = 40 %, and G = C = 20 %.
Remember that U is written instead of T for RNA.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A fragment of one DNA strand: 5′-ATGGCTAACG-3′.
cases.ask: Write the complementary strand. Check the base composition of the fragment by Chargaff’s rule and write the mRNA sequence synthesized from this fragment (if this strand is the template).
cases.answer: Complementary strand: 3′-TACCGATTGC-5′ (in the 5′→3′ direction: 5′-CGTTAGCCAT-3′). In the double-stranded fragment (20 bases): A = T = 5, G = C = 5 — consistent with Chargaff’s rule. If the given strand is the template, the mRNA is complementary to it and contains uracil instead of thymine: 5′-CGUUAGCCAU-3′.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: A patient with HIV infection was prescribed zidovudine (3′-azido-3′-deoxythymidine).
cases.ask: How does the drug work? Explain in terms of its chemical structure.
cases.answer: Zidovudine is a thymidine analog: an azido group (−N~3~) replaces the 3′-OH of deoxyribose. In the cell it is phosphorylated to the triphosphate and incorporated into the DNA chain in place of dTMP by the viral **reverse transcriptase**. Because there is no 3′-OH to attach the next nucleotide, no phosphodiester bond can form — **the chain is terminated** and viral DNA is not synthesized. Reverse transcriptase uses zidovudine much more readily than human DNA polymerases, which ensures selective action.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient with cholera has up to 10–15 L a day of “rice-water” diarrhea and severe dehydration.
cases.ask: Explain the molecular mechanism of the disease in terms of cyclic nucleotides.
cases.answer: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gs protein that controls **adenylate cyclase** in the intestinal epithelium and leaves it permanently active. As a result **cAMP** is formed from ATP continuously; via protein kinase A, cAMP activates the CFTR chloride channels — Cl^−^, Na^+^ and a lot of water pour into the intestinal lumen. The basis of treatment is rehydration with oral or intravenous water–electrolyte (glucose–salt) solutions, plus antibiotics.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: Members of a family who ate a dish made from mushrooms picked in the forest developed severe vomiting and diarrhea 8–12 hours later; after 2–3 days jaundice appeared and the liver enzymes rose sharply.
cases.ask: Poisoning with which toxin is suspected? What is its molecular mechanism of action and why is the liver specifically damaged?
cases.answer: The clinical picture (late onset, liver failure after a “false recovery”) is typical of the **death cap** toxin **α-amanitin**. It strongly blocks eukaryotic **RNA polymerase II** — mRNA synthesis stops, and the cell, unable to make new proteins, dies. The toxin is absorbed from the intestine and reaches the liver first, where hepatocytes actively take it up; it is excreted in bile and absorbed again (enterohepatic circulation) — that is why the liver is damaged most. Treatment: repeated activated charcoal, silibinin, and in severe cases liver transplantation.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: A patient taking azathioprine after a kidney transplant had an attack of gout and was prescribed allopurinol. Two weeks later the white cells and platelets fell sharply.
cases.ask: Explain the biochemical cause of the damage to the blood system.
cases.answer: Azathioprine is converted in the body into **6-mercaptopurine**; its main route of inactivation is oxidation by **xanthine oxidase**. **Allopurinol** blocks this enzyme — 6-mercaptopurine is not broken down, accumulates in the blood and excessively suppresses purine synthesis in bone marrow cells: **leukopenia and thrombocytopenia** develop. In this combination the azathioprine dose is reduced 3–4 times or another drug is chosen.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: An mRNA fragment: 5′-AUG GCU UGG AAA UAG-3′. As a result of a mutation the second G nucleotide in the UGG codon was replaced by A.
cases.ask: What peptide is formed from the normal and the mutant mRNA? What type of mutation is this?
cases.answer: Normally: AUG — Met, GCU — Ala, UGG — Trp, AAA — Lys, UAG — stop. Peptide: **Met–Ala–Trp–Lys**. In the mutant UGG → **UAG** — a stop codon; the peptide consists of **Met–Ala** and is terminated prematurely. This is a **nonsense mutation**: a codon specifying an amino acid becomes a stop codon and the protein is truncated and usually inactive (for example, some β-thalassemias and Duchenne muscular dystrophy are associated with such mutations).

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: Tetracycline was going to be prescribed to an 8-year-old child for pneumonia, but the pediatrician chose another antibiotic.
cases.ask: What is the mechanism of action of tetracycline on bacteria? Why is it not recommended for children under 8?
cases.answer: Tetracycline binds to the **30S subunit** of the bacterial ribosome and blocks the binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to the ribosome — protein synthesis stops (bacteriostatic effect). It has little effect on the eukaryotic 80S ribosome. In children, however, tetracycline forms a **chelate with Ca^2+^** in growing teeth and bone and accumulates there: the teeth become permanently stained yellow-brown, enamel hypoplasia and temporary slowing of bone growth occur. That is why it is not used in children under 8 or in pregnancy.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A 1-year-old boy has delayed development and involuntary movements, and later began to injure his lips and fingers by biting; orange “sand” crystals are seen in his diapers.
cases.ask: Which inherited disease is this? Explain its biochemical basis.
cases.answer: This is **Lesch–Nyhan syndrome** — an X-linked deficiency of **HGPRT** (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase). Purine bases are not converted into nucleotides by the salvage pathway and are broken down to **uric acid**; in addition, unused PRPP accumulates and stimulates de novo purine synthesis. The result is marked **hyperuricemia** — the orange crystals in the diapers are urate, later gout and kidney stones follow. The mechanism of the neurological disturbances is not fully understood. Allopurinol lowers uric acid but does not affect the neurological signs.

topics.title: Lipids. Saponifiable simple and complex lipids. Nonsaponifiable lipids

goals.text: To teach the student the classification of lipids, the saponification reaction, natural saturated and unsaturated fatty acids, mono-, di- and triglycerides, the chemical properties and nutritional value of fats, essential fatty acids, phospholipids, sphingolipids and glycolipids, terpenes and carotenoids, and the structure and medical significance of steroids (sex hormones, corticosteroids, bile acids, cholesterol, ergosterol, calciferol).
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the division of lipids into saponifiable (simple and complex) and nonsaponifiable groups;
the main fatty acids, the ω-3 and ω-6 series and the essential fatty acids;
the structure of triglycerides and the hydrolysis, hydrogenation and peroxidation of fats;
phospholipids, the formation of glycerol 3-phosphate, sphingolipids and glycolipids;
the classification of terpenes and carotenoids;
steroids: cholesterol, bile acids, steroid hormones and vitamin D.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write the saponification reaction of a triglyceride;
determine the structure of a fatty acid from its shorthand (C18:2, ω-6);
assess the unsaturation of a fat from its iodine number;
explain the medical significance of disorders of lipid metabolism and of lipid-based drugs.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Linoleic (ω-6)** and **α-linolenic (ω-3)** acids are not synthesized in the human body — they are **essential** and must come with food. The double bonds of natural unsaturated fatty acids are in the **cis** configuration.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Terpenes by the number of isoprene (C~5~) units: **“mono — 10, sesqui — 15, di — 20, tri — 30, tetra — 40”** carbons; squalene (a triterpene) → cholesterol, β-carotene (a tetraterpene) → vitamin A.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Industrial partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils (margarine) produces **trans fatty acids**: they raise LDL cholesterol, lower HDL and increase the risk of cardiovascular disease.

sections.title: 1. Classification of lipids. The saponification reaction

blocks.text: **Lipids** are natural compounds that are insoluble in water and soluble in nonpolar organic solvents (ether, chloroform, benzene). They serve as an energy store (1 g of fat — 38.9 kJ), as components of membranes, as thermal and mechanical protection, and as precursors of hormones, vitamins and signal molecules.

blocks.title: Table 15.1. Classification of lipids
head: Group
Subgroup
Examples
rows: carotenes, cholesterol, bile acids, steroid hormones, vitamins A, D, E, K

blocks.text: **Saponification** is the hydrolysis of ester bonds in the presence of an alkali: triglyceride + 3NaOH → glycerol + 3R−COONa (soap). Sodium salts are hard soaps, potassium salts liquid soaps. Nonsaponifiable lipids have no ester bond and are not broken down by alkali.

Natural fatty acids are usually unbranched monocarboxylic acids with an **even number** (C~14~–C~24~) of carbon atoms. Shorthand: C18:2 means 18 carbons and 2 double bonds; the **ω** (n) number shows the position of the first double bond counted from the methyl end.

blocks.label: Figure 15.1
blocks.caption: Saturated stearic acid (a straight chain) and oleic and linoleic acids with cis double bonds (a bent chain) (structural formulas drawn with RDKit from PubChem data).

blocks.text: A cis double bond creates a “kink” in the chain and prevents tight packing of the molecules — that is why vegetable **oils**, rich in unsaturated acids, are **liquid**, and animal **fats**, rich in saturated acids, are **solid**. Unsaturated fatty acids in membranes provide their fluidity.

sections.title: 3. Mono-, di- and triglycerides. Chemical properties of fats

blocks.text: **Acylglycerols** are esters of glycerol with fatty acids: mono-, di- and **triglycerides** (triacylglycerols). If all three acyl residues are the same, the triglyceride is **simple** (tripalmitin); if they differ, it is **mixed**; natural fats consist mainly of mixed triglycerides.

blocks.title: Table 15.3. Chemical properties of fats
head: Reaction
Essence
Significance
rows: lipase breaks a triglyceride into fatty acids and glycerol
digestion (pancreatic lipase), mobilization of fat from adipose tissue
soap making; the **saponification number** shows the mean molecular mass
addition of hydrogen to double bonds (Ni catalyst)
margarine; formation of trans fatty acids
the **iodine number** — a measure of unsaturation: olive oil ≈ 80–90, sunflower oil ≈ 125–140, beef tallow ≈ 30–45
radical oxidation of unsaturated chains by O~2~
rancidity of fat; damage to membrane lipids (oxidative stress)

parts.text: **Lipid peroxidation** (LPO) proceeds as a chain reaction in the polyunsaturated fatty acids of membranes under the action of reactive oxygen species; its product is malondialdehyde. It increases in atherosclerosis, ischemic injury, aging and inflammation. Protection comes from antioxidants: **vitamin E** (tocopherol), vitamin C, glutathione and selenium-containing glutathione peroxidase.

blocks.text: **Nutritional value of fats:** fats should provide ≈ 25–30 % of dietary energy; they are a source of the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and of the **essential fatty acids** (linoleic, α-linolenic — formerly called “vitamin F”). Their deficiency leads to dermatitis, growth retardation and slow wound healing.

Because fats are insoluble in water, their digestion and transport require special mechanisms. In the small intestine **bile acids** emulsify fats, and pancreatic **lipase** (with the help of colipase) breaks triglycerides down into 2-monoacylglycerol and fatty acids. The digestion products form **mixed micelles** with bile acids and reach the enterocytes; there triglycerides are resynthesized and released into the lymph in **chylomicrons**.

In the blood lipids are transported as **lipoproteins**: in the center of the spherical particle are the nonpolar triglycerides and cholesterol esters, and on the surface are phospholipids, free cholesterol and proteins — **apolipoproteins**. The greater the lipid fraction, the lower the density.

blocks.title: Table 15.4. Blood lipoproteins
head: Lipoprotein
Main lipid
Main apoprotein
Function
rows: transport dietary fats from the intestine to tissues
return excess cholesterol from tissues to the liver — “good cholesterol”

blocks.text: **Lipoprotein lipase** on the vascular endothelium (activated by apo C-II) breaks down the triglycerides of chylomicrons and VLDL; the fatty acids pass into muscle and adipose tissue, and VLDL is gradually converted into LDL. LDL enters the vessel wall and is oxidized; macrophages engulf it and become “foam cells” — the beginning of an **atherosclerotic plaque**.

parts.text: LDL cholesterol is often calculated with the **Friedewald formula** (in mmol/L): LDL = total cholesterol − HDL − triglycerides / 2.2 (when triglycerides < 4.5 mmol/L). **Atherogenic index** = (total cholesterol − HDL) / HDL; normally less than 3.

blocks.text: **Glycerophospholipids** are derivatives of phosphatidic acid: fatty acids at positions 1 and 2 of glycerol, and at position 3 a phosphate with an amino alcohol or another group attached to it. They are **diphilic** molecules: two hydrophobic “tails” and a polar “head” — that is why in water they form the lipid bilayer (membrane) and liposomes.

blocks.text: **L-Glycerol 3-phosphate is formed in the body in two ways:** 1) phosphorylation of glycerol by ATP (**glycerol kinase**, mainly in the liver and kidney): glycerol + ATP → L-glycerol 3-phosphate + ADP; 2) reduction of the glycolytic intermediate dihydroxyacetone phosphate (**glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase**, NADH): dihydroxyacetone phosphate + NADH + H^+^ → L-glycerol 3-phosphate + NAD^+^ (in adipose tissue and muscle). Triglycerides and phospholipids are synthesized from it.

**Eicosanoids** are locally acting hormone-like substances formed from 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acids, mainly **arachidonic acid**. Arachidonic acid is released from membrane phospholipids by **phospholipase A~2~** and is then converted by two pathways.

parts.text: **ω-3 fatty acids** (EPA, DHA) are also substrates of COX and lipoxygenase, but the eicosanoids formed from them stimulate inflammation and thrombus formation more weakly. This is how a fish-rich diet is linked to a lower risk of cardiovascular disease.

blocks.text: **Sphingolipids** contain the 18-carbon amino alcohol **sphingosine** instead of glycerol. When the amino group of sphingosine forms an amide bond with a fatty acid, a **ceramide** results; ceramide joined with phosphocholine is **sphingomyelin** (the myelin sheath of nerve fibers).

items: **Cerebrosides** (galactocerebrosides) — ceramide + one galactose (or glucose); abundant in myelin and nervous tissue.
**Gangliosides** — ceramide + an oligosaccharide containing sialic (N-acetylneuraminic) acid; in nerve cell membranes, with receptor and cell–cell recognition functions.
**Sulfatides** — sulfated cerebrosides.

parts.text: **Sphingolipidoses** are inherited deficiencies of the lysosomal enzymes that break down sphingolipids: **Gaucher disease** (glucocerebrosidase — glucocerebroside accumulates; enzyme replacement therapy exists), **Tay–Sachs disease** (hexosaminidase A — GM~2~ ganglioside accumulates in brain neurons), **Niemann–Pick disease** (sphingomyelinase).

blocks.text: **Terpenes** are compounds built from **isoprene** (C~5~H~8~) units. They are divided into monoterpenes (C~10~: menthol, camphor, limonene), sesquiterpenes (C~15~), diterpenes (C~20~: retinol), triterpenes (C~30~: squalene — the precursor of cholesterol) and tetraterpenes (C~40~: carotenoids). In the body isoprenoids are synthesized from acetyl-CoA by the **mevalonate** pathway.

items: **β-Carotene** is split in two in the intestinal wall to give two molecules of **vitamin A** (retinal); carrots, pumpkin, apricots.
**Lycopene** (tomatoes), **lutein** and **zeaxanthin** (the macula of the retina) are antioxidants.
Vitamin A (retinol) is part of the visual pigment **rhodopsin** and controls epithelial differentiation; its deficiency causes “night blindness” (hemeralopia) and xerophthalmia.

parts.text: **Statins** (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin) block **HMG-CoA reductase**, the key enzyme of the mevalonate pathway, and reduce cholesterol synthesis in the liver — LDL cholesterol falls; they are the main drug group for preventing atherosclerosis and its complications (myocardial infarction, stroke).

sections.title: 9. Steroids: cholesterol, bile acids, steroid hormones, vitamin D

blocks.text: **Steroids** are compounds with the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene (sterane) skeleton: three six-membered (A, B, C) and one five-membered (D) ring. The precursor of them all is **cholesterol**.

blocks.caption: Steroids: cholesterol, cortisol (a glucocorticoid) and estradiol (an estrogen) — the common sterane skeleton (structural formulas drawn with RDKit from PubChem data).

blocks.text: **Formation of vitamin D:** in the skin, 7-dehydrocholesterol has its B ring opened by solar ultraviolet (UVB) light and becomes **cholecalciferol (D~3~)**; when ergosterol (in plants and fungi) is irradiated, **ergocalciferol (D~2~)** is formed. The active form is **calcitriol** (1,25-dihydroxy-D~3~), produced after 25-hydroxylation in the liver and 1α-hydroxylation in the kidney.

parts.text: Normal blood lipid values (adults): total cholesterol < 5.2 mmol/L, LDL cholesterol < 3.0 mmol/L, HDL cholesterol > 1.0 mmol/L (men), triglycerides < 1.7 mmol/L. When cholesterol in bile exceeds bile acids and phospholipids, **cholesterol gallstones** form; ursodeoxycholic acid is used to dissolve small stones. Vitamin D deficiency leads to **rickets** in children and osteomalacia in adults.

blocks.text: Cholesterol balance and familial hypercholesterolemia

The adult body synthesizes ≈ 1 g of cholesterol a day (mainly in the liver) and takes in 0.3–0.5 g with food. The steran ring is not broken down in the body: cholesterol is excreted with bile into the intestine mainly as **bile acids** and unchanged; ≈ 95 % of bile acids are reabsorbed in the terminal small intestine and return to the liver (**enterohepatic circulation**).

Cells take up LDL by endocytosis through special **LDL receptors**. When cholesterol in the cell increases, the synthesis of HMG-CoA reductase and the number of receptors decrease — this is **negative feedback**. Statins reduce cellular cholesterol and increase the number of LDL receptors in the liver — more LDL is taken up from the blood.

parts.text: **Familial hypercholesterolemia** is a mutation of the LDL receptor gene: LDL is not removed from the blood and its cholesterol rises sharply (5–10 in heterozygotes, > 13 mmol/L in homozygotes). **Xanthomas** in tendons, xanthelasmas around the eyes and myocardial infarction at a young age (in homozygotes even in childhood) develop. Treatment: statins, ezetimibe (blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption), PCSK9 inhibitors.

items: Write the formula of the triglyceride: the glycerol residue and three acyl groups (R~1~CO−, R~2~CO−, R~3~CO−).

skills.title: Skill: analyzing the shorthand of a fatty acid

items: The first number is the number of carbon atoms (C18).
The number after the colon is the number of double bonds (C18:2 — two).
The ω number is the position of the first double bond from the methyl end (ω-6).
In natural acids the double bonds are cis and separated by a methylene group (−CH=CH−CH~2~−CH=CH−).
The ω-3 and ω-6 series do not interconvert in the body — both must come with food.

skills.title: Skill: assessing a lipid profile

items: Write down the total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and triglyceride values in mmol/L.
Calculate LDL cholesterol with the Friedewald formula: LDL = TC − HDL − TG / 2.2 (if TG < 4.5 mmol/L).
Find the atherogenic index: AI = (TC − HDL) / HDL.
Compare each value with the norm: TC < 5.2; LDL < 3.0; HDL > 1.0 (men), > 1.2 (women); TG < 1.7 mmol/L; AI < 3.
Assess the cardiovascular risk together with the patient’s other risk factors (smoking, arterial hypertension, diabetes, age).
